# "Walled garden" in The Verge's Epic v. Google coverage: a closed platform controlling distribution and payment

In its December 12, 2023 account of Epic's jury verdict against Google, The Verge sets "walled garden" in quotation marks as a descriptor for Apple — Epic's "rival," which the piece notes "almost entirely won a similar case two years ago." In that usage, the term denotes a closed mobile platform whose owner controls both app distribution and in-app payment: the same two powers the nine-person federal jury found Google held an illegal monopoly over, in "Android app distribution and in-app payment systems," and had illegally tied together through "its Google Play billing system to its app store." Apple's verdict, by contrast, went Epic's way only in part.


---


# The store–billing relation: how Epic v. Google's two findings form one loop

Read as a single structure rather than two verdicts, the findings a federal jury returned against Google — reported by Tim Sweeney of Epic Games in The Verge, 2023-12-12 — describe one loop with two ends.

One end is the monopolised product: Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. The other end is the tied product: Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The relation between the ends is the model. Whichever product a developer must accept to reach Android users also becomes the channel through which that developer's money moves, so control of distribution converts into control of payment — and the payment share Sweeney calls "huge taxes" paid to a few gatekeepers reinforces the distribution hold. Two holdings, one circuit.

If it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape; Epic claims illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing." Sections: legal theory and statutes (Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2, Cartwright Act, Unfair Competition Law, the Microsoft/Netscape precedent); the two relevant markets; commissions and User Choice Billing; OEM agreements, AFAs and Project Hug; and Google's defenses.

# Contents index: TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup of US v Google

This TechCrunch roundup of November 13, 2023 indexes five sections. First, why US v Google matters and the remedies at stake before Judge Amit Mehta: sharing APIs, bans on anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, and surrendering data — the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. Second, Google's concurrent antitrust matters: the Match Group settlement and the November 6 trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games over Google Play. Third, the declassified list of 20 search terms ordered by revenue for the week of September 22, 2018, and vertical search. Fourth, Jamie Rosenberg's November 8 testimony on MADA (11 pre-loaded Google apps) and RSA mechanics. Fifth, Expedia and Barry Diller on ad load.

# Epic's Google case rests on the Microsoft browser-monopoly precedent

Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google, which began on November 6, 2023 and concerns Google Play's app distribution and its 15% to 30% commissions, is analogically dependent on the Microsoft antitrust rulings, as reported by TechCrunch. In those earlier cases, courts found that Microsoft had a monopoly over the operating system and was abusing it by making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. The analogy carries weight because Android, unlike Apple's iOS, permits sideloading — so Epic's theory of the case runs on a dominant platform owner's agreements constraining rivals rather than on the absence of any alternative.


---


# US v Google's ripple effect on parallel Big Tech antitrust cases

A ruling in US v Google may have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases, since enforcers need one landmark judgment to demonstrate antitrust law remains relevant. The parallel matters named in a TechCrunch roundup dated 2023-11-13: the FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power; the DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products; and there's an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, wherein the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp. The proposition is falsified if those cases proceed and settle unaffected by the Google judgment. Judge Amit Mehta hears the Google case.


---


# Sherman Act: the U.S. antitrust statute behind Epic's claims against Google

The Sherman Act is the U.S. antitrust statute Epic Games planned to invoke against Google at the trial that began November 6, 2023, taking Section 1 and Section 2 claims alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. Section 1 concerns restraints of competition; Section 2 concerns monopolization. Epic's case rested on arguing that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.


---


# Epic's Twin Antitrust Suits Diverged: Apple Settled in 2021, Google Waited to 2023

Epic Games sued Apple and Google on the same day, August 13th, 2020, both over in-app payment fees critics call the "Apple tax" and "Google tax," but the two cases then moved at wildly different speeds. The Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021, and a ruling came down that September mostly in Apple's favor, with both parties still waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in. The Google suit never got its day in court during those years, delayed again and again, so that Epic v. Google trial beginning November 6th, 2023 arrived "a mere 1,180 days" after Epic filed, per The Verge's article dated 2023-11-05.

# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.

# Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.

# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."

# DOJ's theory in *US v. Google*: default deals capture search entry points

In *US v. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. Reporting on Apple executive Eddy Cue's testimony on 2023-09-26, The Verge states that the Justice Department is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.

# Google's Drummond Called Microsoft's Search Default Anticompetitive in 2005

In 2005, after Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, Google legal chief David Drummond wrote to Microsoft arguing that the default was anticompetitive, according to a TechCrunch report dated 2023-10-31 on the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google. Drummond's letter rested on a claim about user behavior: most end users "do not change defaults," so the engine picked at the outset keeps the searches.

# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

Read as a single structure rather than two verdicts, the findings a federal jury returned against Google — reported by Tim Sweeney of Epic Games in The Verge, 2023-12-12 — describe one loop with two ends.

qid: Which company, scrutinized in articles from both 'The Age' and 'TechCrunch', is not only accused of potentially unfair practices to maintain its dominance as a default search engine but also faces allegations of harming news publishers' revenues and audiences through its operations?
context:
# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# Complaint's core allegation: Google is "starving the free press" at a cost of billions

The central harm asserted in the class action antitrust complaint filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. is that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars." The plaintiff, Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, brings the claim against Google and parent company Alphabet under the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust law, framing Google's redistribution of news content inside its own products as anticompetitive conduct that diverts publishers' content, readers and ad revenue.


---


# Wired removed Megan Gray's article alleging Google rewrites search queries for ad revenue

In October 2023, Wired published an opinion piece by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the US antitrust trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear". Google rejected the piece as misleading and inaccurate, denying it ever alters search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards.


---


# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# Google Search Antitrust Trial: the 2020 Dominance Claim

The U.S. antitrust trial being heard in October 2023 is the 2020 claim over Google's dominance in the online search market, in which Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified on the Monday covered by TechCrunch's Oct. 31, 2023 report, defending the deals that make Google the default search engine. It is distinct from the separate claim filed in January 2023 by the Department of Justice with eight states, including New York, California and Colorado, which seeks to break Google's monopoly in digital advertising, not search.


---


# Reach of the retracted Wired piece on Google query manipulation, October 2023

In October 2023, Wired published, then removed for not meeting its standards, an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had revealed during the US antitrust trial that it manipulates search queries for ad revenue — for example replacing "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear". The Age reports that the extent of its sharing on social media and boosting in write-ups at other outlets shows how willing people are to accept foul play by Google, amid a standing suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling.

SOURCE: The Age, "Is Google Search better than the rest? And is that fair?", 2023-10-22.


---


# Google's rebuttal to Megan Gray's Wired query-rewrite allegation

In October 2023, in response to the Wired opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray — which alleged, on the example of a search for "children's clothing" being replaced with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear", that Google manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — Google rejected the piece in very strong terms, calling it misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards.


---


# DOJ's Theory of Harm in the Google Antitrust Case: Defaults Cut Rivals Off From Data

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The theory therefore runs in two linked steps: owned distribution plus paid defaults deny rivals visibility, and denied visibility denies them the query data that would let their products reach a quality high enough to challenge Google. The claim over Google's dominance in the online search market was filed in 2020. It is separate from a claim filed in January by the Department of Justice along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind its monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising. Google's counter is that it is simply doing business, since partners want the best default engine.


---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Revenue-ranked queries as evidence of Google's vertical search dominance

In TechCrunch's 2023-11-13 roundup of the US v Google trial, the reporter interprets a publicly released list of the 20 search terms that made Google the most money during the week of September 22, 2018 — a list Judge Amit Mehta ruled to make public, with per-term revenue and query counts redacted — as proof of Google's dominance of vertical search, meaning search in very specific market categories. The warrant is saturation: the terms are concentrated in the categories where advertisers pay most — "Auto Insurance," "Car Insurance," "Car Insurance Quotes," "Cheap Car Insurance," "Insurance Quotes," "Cheap Flights," "DirecTV," "AT&T," "Spectrum," "Comcast," "Xfinity," "Hulu," "Free Credit Report," "LifeLock." The iPhone 8 aside concedes the list is unsurprising, since "September 22, 2017 was the official release date of the iPhone 8" and Google and Apple maintain a mutually beneficial relationship even while competing. The reporter also attributes "LifeLock" to the 2017 Equifax breach. The whole reading rests on one week in 2018.

qid: Has the description of ChatGPT's capabilities by TechCrunch remained consistent between the article published on September 28 and the subsequent article on November 30?
context:
# TechCrunch's ChatGPT coverage: living timeline plus companion FAQ

TechCrunch's hub article "ChatGPT: Everything you need to know about the AI-powered chatbot" (published 2023-09-28) splits into two navigational layers. The first is a timeline of ChatGPT product updates and releases ordered with the latest entries at the top — December 2023 entries such as the reopened ChatGPT Plus subscriptions lead the list — which TechCrunch states it has "been updating throughout the year," so it is a living page rather than a fixed record. The second is a cross-linked ChatGPT FAQ pointed to from the same intro paragraph for definitional and how-to questions.


---


# TechCrunch contrasts ChatGPT's minimal launch with an unsourced "fastest-growing consumer app" claim

TechCrunch's case for ChatGPT's significance on its first birthday (November 30, 2023) rests on a contrast between an unpromising origin and a superlative outcome. The chatbot shipped a year earlier as a "low-key research preview" — initially only a basic free-to-use, web-based, chat-focused interface on top of GPT-3.5, one of OpenAI's existing models. From that, the article asserts, it became OpenAI's most popular product ever and "the fastest-growing consumer app in history," a record stated without naming the data behind it. Sam Altman's retrospective tweet that evening — "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt … what a year it's been…" (@sama, November 30, 2023) — supplies the humble-origin half of the argument.


---


# ChatGPT's year-one capability set is a strict superset of its GPT-3.5 chat-only launch state

ChatGPT's feature set as of TechCrunch's 2023-11-30 one-year report contains everything it launched with, plus layers added on top. A year earlier, OpenAI had released ChatGPT as a "low-key research preview" — initially a basic free-to-use, web-based and chat-focused interface on top of one of OpenAI's existing models, GPT-3.5. In the months following its launch, ChatGPT gained paid tiers with additional features, including a plan geared toward enterprise customers. OpenAI also upgraded ChatGPT with web searching, document analyzing and image creating (via DALL-E 3) capabilities. And, leaning on speech recognition, voice synthesis and text-image understanding models developed in house, OpenAI gave ChatGPT the ability to "hear," "speak," "see" and take actions. The chat interface on GPT-3.5 remains the substrate; the later functions are additions, not replacements.


---


# ChatGPT Redirected the AI Field by Lowering the Skill Barrier

Stella Biderman, an AI researcher at Booz Allen Hamilton and the open research group EleutherAI, told TechCrunch on 2023-11-30 that ChatGPT's influence on the AI field came from lowering a barrier to use, not from a jump in capability. She does not consider it an AI breakthrough per se, but a "user experience breakthrough" that took generative AI mainstream — and its primary effect, she says, was "encouraging people training AIs to try to mimic it, or encouraging people studying AIs to use it as their central object of study." The mechanism she gives: "Previously you needed to have some skill, albeit not be an expert, to consistently get usable stuff out of [text-generating models]." Once that requirement disappeared, ChatGPT "brought a very large amount of attention to and discussion about the technology."


---


# Biderman's "User Experience Breakthrough" vs. an AI Breakthrough

In an interview published by TechCrunch on 2023-11-30, Stella Biderman, an AI researcher at Booz Allen Hamilton and the open research group EleutherAI, separated an "AI breakthrough" from what she called a bonafide "user experience breakthrough." The second is a change in how already-existing capability is reached and consumed by ordinary people, not a leap in the capability itself. ChatGPT, released a year earlier as a "low-key research preview," was that: a free, web-based, chat-focused interface on top of OpenAI's existing model GPT-3.5, taking generative AI mainstream. Previously, she said, "you needed to have some skill, albeit not be an expert, to consistently get usable stuff out of [text-generating models]." OpenAI has released dozens of research papers on its models but never one on ChatGPT.


---


# More than 92% of Fortune 500 Companies Use ChatGPT (TechCrunch, 2023)

According to TechCrunch's ChatGPT explainer, dated 2023-09-28, more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies use ChatGPT, OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot. The figure describes how far the product had spread beyond its origins: TechCrunch characterises ChatGPT as having started as a tool to hyper-charge productivity through writing essays and code with short text prompts, then evolving into a behemoth that those large employers deploy for more wide-ranging needs. The article was last updated through December 2023.


---


# OpenAI never published a research paper on ChatGPT itself

Stella Biderman, an AI researcher at Booz Allen Hamilton and the open research group EleutherAI, observes pointedly that OpenAI — despite having released dozens of research papers on its models — never published one on ChatGPT. She made that remark in a TechCrunch article dated November 30, 2023, marking ChatGPT's first anniversary, while stopping short of calling ChatGPT an AI breakthrough per se.


---


# ChatGPT Summarized the News Prompt Gemini Pro Deflected

In a news-summary test described in a TechCrunch article published on 2023-12-07, the author asked Bard, running Google's Gemini Pro, to recap a topical story, and got a response matching Gemini Pro's pattern, as the author characterizes it, of declining to comment on potentially controversial news topics and telling users to Google it themselves instead. As a control, the author ran the same prompt through ChatGPT, which returned a bullet-list summary with citations to news articles.


---


# ChatGPT Plus

ChatGPT Plus is OpenAI's paid subscription tier for ChatGPT, the AI chatbot used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies. Its defining differentiator is access to GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo, described in a TechCrunch article published 2023-09-28. GPT-4 writes more naturally and fluently than previous models and remains largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users. OpenAI paused Plus sign-ups in November 2023 citing a "surge of usage"; CEO Sam Altman announced subscriptions re-enabled on December 13, 2023, after the company "found more gpus".


---


# Facets covered in TechCrunch's one-year ChatGPT retrospective

TechCrunch's "One year later, ChatGPT is still alive and kicking" (2023-11-30) covers ChatGPT's first year across eight facets: OpenAI's launch of it as a "low-key research preview" and the data-gathering rationale leadership gave; the adoption record plus third-party traffic figures from Similarweb and Data.ai; the capability expansion into web search, document analysis, DALL-E 3 image creation, and hearing, speaking and seeing; ChatGPT becoming priority number one inside OpenAI; competitor responses including Google's Bard, Amazon Q and DeepMind's Gemini; Stella Biderman's reframing of it as a "user experience breakthrough" rather than an AI one; the psychology of conversational interfaces per Ruoxi Shang and Adam Hyland; and measured productivity effects.


---


# OpenAI connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users

OpenAI connected ChatGPT to the live internet for all users, according to TechCrunch's running explainer on the chatbot (dated 2023-09-28). The rollout is notable for who it covered. Unlike GPT-4, which the article says "remains largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users" — reachable free of charge only through Microsoft's Bing Chat in the Edge, Google Chrome and Safari browsers — the internet connection went to the entire user base rather than to subscribers alone. qid: After TechCrunch reported on November 6, 2023, that Google provided extensive evidence to counter Epic Games' claims in their antitrust battle, did the consistency of Google's stance on antitrust issues remain unchanged according to a later report by TechCrunch on December 15, 2023, regarding a class action lawsuit filed by a news publisher against Google?
context:
# Google faced three search and app-store antitrust trials at once in mid-November 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was simultaneously litigating three antitrust matters touching search and app distribution, according to a TechCrunch report dated November 13, 2023. First, the Justice Department's landmark case against Google over search was roughly two months in, before Judge Amit Mehta. Second, Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the previous week. Third, on November 6, 2023 Google went to trial against Fortnite maker Epic Games, which sought to prove Google engages in anticompetitive behavior regarding its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure.


---


# Publisher's Google antitrust suit alleges spoliation of chat messages, echoing Epic Games case

The class action antitrust suit that Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023 alleges evidence of improper spoliation by Google — specifically the destruction of chat messages. The complaint ties that allegation to a known precedent: the same issue of destroyed chat messages was raised in Epic Games' recent lawsuit against Google over app-store antitrust conduct, a case Epic won. The spoliation claim sits alongside the suit's other concerns, including allegedly changed AdSense rates, and appears among the counts supporting its requests for damages and injunctive relief against Google.


---


# Google antitrust actions surrounding the Helena World Chronicle publisher suit, December 2023

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and covered by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, arrived while several other Google proceedings were live. This note indexes that surrounding docket.

- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (digital ad technology): the DOJ's monopoly suit over Google's ad-tech stack, pending alongside the publisher case in late 2023.
- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (2020): the earlier civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.
- Epic Games v. Google: the app-store antitrust case, which Epic won; the Helena complaint borrows its finding of improper spoliation of evidence — Google's destruction of chat messages.
- Canada settlement (November 2023): Google agreed to pay Canadian media $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) a year, distributed by newsroom headcount. Meta's negotiations remained unresolved; Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August.


---


# Epic v. Google as a Four-Year Sequence, Originating in a September 2019 Plan Email

The Epic Games v. Google antitrust proceeding reads as a dated four-year chain rather than a single lawsuit. Its causal origin is a September 2019 email surfaced in discovery, describing Epic's plan to draw Google into a legal battle over antitrust — the document that predates and sets up everything after it. That plan became a four-week federal antitrust trial before a nine-person jury, which found on Monday, December 11, 2023 that Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems and illegally tied Google Play billing to its app store. The Verge's December 12, 2023 interview with Epic CEO Tim Sweeney frames the verdict as "four years in the making." Sweeney dates his own suspicion of Google's practices to 2018, one year earlier than the email.


---


# Epic's Twin Antitrust Suits Diverged: Apple Settled in 2021, Google Waited to 2023

Epic Games sued Apple and Google on the same day, August 13th, 2020, both over in-app payment fees critics call the "Apple tax" and "Google tax," but the two cases then moved at wildly different speeds. The Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021, and a ruling came down that September mostly in Apple's favor, with both parties still waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in. The Google suit never got its day in court during those years, delayed again and again, so that Epic v. Google trial beginning November 6th, 2023 arrived "a mere 1,180 days" after Epic filed, per The Verge's article dated 2023-11-05.


---


# Epic v. Google after openings: what the evidence phase must settle

Following both sides' opening statements to the jury in early November 2023 — Epic Games' on Monday, 2023-11-06, and Google's later the same week, lasting 45 minutes — the Epic v. Google antitrust trial moves to its evidence phase, with several disputes deferred to later weeks. Testimony must first settle Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's claim that "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete," including the alleged $360 million payment that kept Activision from opening an app store competing with Google Play; Activision told The Verge in 2022 it "never entered into an agreement that Activision would not open its own app store." The trial must also resolve whether Android is open: Bornstein promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option," while Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz points to over a billion users installing outside Play.

SOURCE: The Verge, "The Epic v. Google trial may come down to simple v. complicated," 2023-11-07


---


# Epic v. Google reached trial 1,180 days after Epic first sued

Epic v. Google went to trial on 2023-11-06, "a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued," according to The Verge's 2023-11-05 explainer. The delay is the comparison: Epic's parallel antitrust suit against Apple — both filed after the 2020-08-13 Fortnite hotfix and the app stores' removal of the game — went to court in 2021, with a ruling that September mostly in Apple's favor. The Google case was "delayed again and again" until late 2023.


---


# Epic v. Google trial notes index — November 6, 2023

These notes cover TechCrunch's November 6, 2023 report on Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google, which began November 6, 2023 over Google Play and its commission structure. Sections: legal theory and statutes (Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2, Cartwright Act, Unfair Competition Law, the Microsoft/Netscape precedent); the two relevant markets; commissions and User Choice Billing; OEM agreements, AFAs and Project Hug; and Google's defenses.


---


# Sherman Act: the U.S. antitrust statute behind Epic's claims against Google

The Sherman Act is the U.S. antitrust statute Epic Games planned to invoke against Google at the trial that began November 6, 2023, taking Section 1 and Section 2 claims alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. Section 1 concerns restraints of competition; Section 2 concerns monopolization. Epic's case rested on arguing that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.


---


# Epic's OEM evidence: the cancelled OnePlus deal and the Google–Samsung agreement

Epic Games' antitrust case against Google, tried from November 6, 2023, leads with an agreement theory, because Android allows sideloading and Epic cannot claim, as it did against Apple, that no other way exists to load apps. Two episodes carry that theory. Epic had an agreement with the device maker OnePlus to make Epic games available on OnePlus devices through the Epic Games app, and OnePlus cancelled the deal over concerns that the arrangement would have it bypassing the Google Play Store. The trial will also examine a deal between Google and Samsung that Epic says was designed to prevent the Galaxy Store from becoming a competitive threat and to require Google Play Billing on apps distributed by Samsung. Epic places both inside the "Anti-Fragmentation Agreements" (AFAs) it cites, which prevent Android OEMs from modifying Android to allow frictionless downloading of apps outside Google Play.


---


# Google Search Antitrust Trial: the 2020 Dominance Claim

The U.S. antitrust trial being heard in October 2023 is the 2020 claim over Google's dominance in the online search market, in which Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified on the Monday covered by TechCrunch's Oct. 31, 2023 report, defending the deals that make Google the default search engine. It is distinct from the separate claim filed in January 2023 by the Department of Justice with eight states, including New York, California and Colorado, which seeks to break Google's monopoly in digital advertising, not search.

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. TechCrunch reported this on 2023-10-31, describing Pichai's testimony that Monday, two days after search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on 2023-10-28 that Google had paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default placement. Line shopping — checking the posted lines and odds for the same prospective bet at multiple sportsbooks — is not confined to one market. # "Walled garden" in The Verge's Epic v. Google coverage: a closed platform controlling distribution and payment

In its December 12, 2023 account of Epic's jury verdict against Google, The Verge sets "walled garden" in quotation marks as a descriptor for Apple — Epic's "rival," which the piece notes "almost entirely won a similar case two years ago." In that usage, the term denotes a closed mobile platform whose owner controls both app distribution and in-app payment: the same two powers the nine-person federal jury found Google held an illegal monopoly over, in "Android app distribution and in-app payment systems," and had illegally tied together through "its Google Play billing system to its app store." Apple's verdict, by contrast, went Epic's way only in part.


---


# Index: The Verge's "Epic v. Google, explained" (Sean Hollister, 2023-11-05)

Navigation for "Epic v. Google, explained," Sean Hollister's reader-facing explainer at The Verge, published 2023-11-05 ahead of the trial that opened November 6th — "a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued"; Hollister appended a December 15th, 2023 update marking it superseded. Notes grouped by the question each answers:

- **Background — the August 13th, 2020 trigger**: Epic's hotfix letting Fortnite V-Bucks be bought at a discount outside app store fees, Apple and Google pulling Fortnite, Epic's two lawsuits and the "Llamacorn" attack ad.
- **Competing legal claims**: Epic's monopoly and Play-payments-tying allegations versus Google's sideloaded-app-safety and free-app-store defenses.
- **Market definition**: "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing" versus phones and app stores generally.
- **Apple-case precedent**: the September 2021 ruling mostly in Apple's favor, with the Supreme Court possibly weighing in.


---


# The store–billing relation: how Epic v. Google's two findings form one loop

Read as a single structure rather than two verdicts, the findings a federal jury returned against Google — reported by Tim Sweeney of Epic Games in The Verge, 2023-12-12 — describe one loop with two ends.

One end is the monopolised product: Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. The other end is the tied product: Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The relation between the ends is the model. Whichever product a developer must accept to reach Android users also becomes the channel through which that developer's money moves, so control of distribution converts into control of payment — and the payment share Sweeney calls "huge taxes" paid to a few gatekeepers reinforces the distribution hold. Two holdings, one circuit.


---


# Epic's Android App Distribution Monopoly Claim Against Google

In Epic Games' antitrust suit against Google, whose trial began on November 6th, 2023, Epic's core argument concerns Android app distribution. Epic argues that Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that Google has created an illegal monopoly. The claimed harms are twofold: the monopoly unjustly enriches Google, and it artificially drives up app prices, because other app stores can't compete. Epic calls the standard in-app payment fees the "Google tax". The remedy Epic seeks is to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods, so that developers aren't stuck paying that tax or passing the fee along to players.

Source: The Verge, "Epic v. Google, explained" (2023-11-05).


---


# Epic's stake in v. Google: break up the Android app distribution and in-app payment monopolies

Epic Games' interest in Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023 — 1,180 days after Epic first sued — is the break-up of what it calls Google's illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing." Epic charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal. The theory is straightforward: if those two monopolies are dismantled, developers buying or selling on Android are no longer stuck paying the "Google tax," the 30%-style in-app payment fee critics named — and therefore no longer pass that fee along to consumers in higher app prices. Both Epic and Google agreed the trial could decide the future of Google's app store.


---


# Google argues its Play commission pays for more than billing

In Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google, which began November 6, 2023, Google contests the framing that the 15% to 30% commission it charges app developers on the sales it processes through Google Play's required first-party billing system is payment-processing markup. Its argument is that the commission instead funds other features and controls that keep Android users safe and guide them toward discovering new applications, plus the tools and services developers need to build and grow their apps. Google claims credit for reach beyond the mobile phone too: Android support across platforms, ranging from tablets to TVs to autos and more. It narrows the burden by noting that 99% of its developers qualify for a commission of 15% or less, based on their revenues.


---


# Complaint's core allegation: Google is "starving the free press" at a cost of billions

The central harm asserted in the class action antitrust complaint filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. is that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars." The plaintiff, Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, brings the claim against Google and parent company Alphabet under the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust law, framing Google's redistribution of news content inside its own products as anticompetitive conduct that diverts publishers' content, readers and ad revenue.


---


# Google's counter-argument: iPhone substitution, not Android app stores, defines the market

Google rebutted Epic's market definition in Epic v. Google — which went to trial on Nov. 6, 2023, some 1,180 days after Epic first sued — by arguing the real competition is Apple, because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead. On that view, Google's app store competes with Apple's across platforms, so it is "pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general." Epic's contrary position: Android app distribution and Android in-app payment processing are each their own market.


---


# Epic v. Google's outcome hinges on which market the court defines

In Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023, the trial's outcome turns on the market definition the court adopts — the line of argument The Verge names "market definition." If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google's on the road to victory, since Google argues the real competition is Apple and buyers can choose an iPhone instead. If it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape; Epic claims illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing." The hypothesis is falsified by whichever definition the judge records, including a different one entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up picking.


---


# Market Definition in Epic v. Google: Narrow Android Market vs. All Smartphones

In Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023, "market definition" is the name The Verge gives to the question that decides the case: a monopoly on what? Epic claims Google holds illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing", so anyone who buys or develops for Android phones is stuck paying the "Google tax". Google answers that the real competition is Apple, because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead. The same conduct is lawful or unlawful depending on the boundary drawn: if the court holds the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, Google is "on the road to victory"; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic is in better shape. The court could also pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in Epic's Apple case did.

As of the week ending 7 October 2023, the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried — the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of cryptocurrency exchange FTX — was in session at the Manhattan Federal Court, and TechCrunch reported that its team had been stationed there to cover the proceedings. The observation appears in TechCrunch's Week in Review digest of that week, in the item headlined "SBF allegedly tried to buy off Trump," which described the trial as the setting for emerging details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings.


---


# Bankman-Fried Visibly Upset During Wang's Testimony, October 2023

CNBC's courtroom report of 5–6 October 2023 records that Sam Bankman-Fried, 31, stayed mostly quiet at his fraud trial, listening intently to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys. But as Gary Wang testified against him, Bankman-Fried looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's appearance and demeanor in court, 2023-10-04

Fortune's account of day two of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial in New York on 2023-10-04 records what it observed in the courtroom: his cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, and he spent most of his day there staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys.


---


# Bankman-Fried Faced Seven Counts at Close of Prosecution's Case, October 2023

At the close of the prosecution's case in October 2023, Sam Bankman-Fried faced seven counts: two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges, according to The Verge's reporting on 2023-10-26. The trial concerned fraud at the FTX exchange and his trading firm Alameda Research.


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried Faces Seven Federal Charges Carrying Life Exposure, October 2023

As his fraud trial over the collapsed crypto exchange FTX proceeded on 6 October 2023, Sam Bankman-Fried, 31, faced seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering — charges that could put him in prison for the rest of his life.


---


# Bankman-Fried on trial for seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy, October 2023

As reported by The Verge on 2023-10-10, Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, was standing trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. In the same passage, The Verge records the Securities and Exchange Commission's allegation that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The report places the trial in progress on the day Caroline Ellison took the stand.


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried fraud trial opened at Manhattan Federal Court on 3 October 2023

Sam Bankman-Fried, the cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history" through the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the exchange he founded and led, stood trial from Tuesday 3 October 2023 at Manhattan Federal Court. Bankman-Fried had pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

# Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial began with jury selection on 3 October 2023

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-06 that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO and co-founder of the collapsed crypto exchange FTX, kicked off with jury selection on October 3. The case against him involves seven counts tied to fraud and money laundering at FTX and sister company Alameda. Courtroom access is limited, with no devices allowed.

# Index: The Seven People Closest to Sam Bankman-Fried in the October 2023 FTX Trial Record

This index scopes the individuals named in a The Verge article dated 2023-10-26 as the people who loved or worked with Sam Bankman-Fried and appeared in the FTX trial record. The source lists them in order of testimony and relationship: Adam Yedidia and Gary Wang (college roommates), Nishad Singh (longtime family friend), Caroline Ellison (ex-girlfriend), his parents Joe Bankman and Barbara Fried, and his brother Gabe Bankman-Fried. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are felons; the article's closing paragraph covers their sentencing exposure, restitution, job bars, and reputational damage.


---


# Bankman-Fried's public claims of innocence after FTX's collapse

Sam Bankman-Fried maintained his innocence after FTX collapsed in late 2022. Appearing virtually from the Bahamas at The New York Times' DealBook Summit, the former FTX CEO said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month." In a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter, he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." Reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-01, ahead of his criminal trial on seven counts of fraud and conspiracy.


---


# Bankman-Fried's Physical Demeanour Shifted Between Two Testimonies, 2023-10-10

In The Verge's courtroom coverage of 2023-10-10 — the fifth day of Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial, in which he faces seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — the reporter recorded a change in the defendant's posture as the witnesses changed. Bankman-Fried "had been vibrating slightly" during the testimony of Gary Wang, FTX's chief technology officer. During Caroline Ellison's testimony later the same day, the reporter wrote, "his bouncing became more noticeable." By day's end, the defence's cross-examination of Wang "seemed like a sideshow." The observation is the journalist's own visual impression, not a measured or courtroom-documented fact.


---


# Bankman-Fried Could Not Recall Who Decided to Spend $8 Billion of FTX Customer Funds

During his trial testimony on October 31, 2023, Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of the collapsed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, said he could not recall knowing anything about who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, as prosecutor Danielle Sassoon questioned him in the wire fraud trial. Asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, and whether there were rules for risk management, Bankman-Fried answered only, "I was concerned with overall risk management." He also said he wasn't trying to build blame for the spending, and had fired no one.


---


# Bankman-Fried's "we" sometimes meant only himself

During his direct examination at the FTX trial, reported by The Verge on 2023-10-28, Sam Bankman-Fried on occasion used the first-person plural "we" while referring only to himself, the court correspondent notes. His lawyer Mark Cohen was the one asking the questions at that point in the testimony.

# SEC alleges FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a multi-billion-dollar shortfall from customer funds

The Securities and Exchange Commission alleges that FTX, the cryptocurrency exchange Sam Bankman-Fried founded in 2019, was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to his crypto trading firm Alameda Research, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds," according to reporting by The Verge on 2023-09-28, shortly before Bankman-Fried's trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy began.


---


# SEC Alleges FTX Was a Fraud "From the Start," Caused by Bankman-Fried's Own Misappropriation

The SEC's allegation against Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, goes further than the criminal charges he was facing at trial — seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. The Securities and Exchange Commission alleges that FTX was a fraud “from the start,” which frames the misstatement as running through the exchange's whole existence rather than arising only as it collapsed. The element that separates the SEC's theory from a plain story of a failed exchange is the source of the shortfall: it alleges a “multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds,” naming Bankman-Fried personally and specifying customer money as what went missing.


---

Sam Bankman-Fried is defined here as the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX and the defendant in a criminal fraud trial, as reported by The Verge on 2023-10-10. He was on trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. The Securities and Exchange Commission alleges that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." Those characterizations come from the government's allegations, not from findings the article reports as settled.

# Sam Bankman-Fried charged with seven federal counts: two wire fraud, five conspiracy

Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX and of the crypto trading firm Alameda Research, faced seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy, The Verge reported on 2023-09-28. The allegation was reported by The Verge on 2023-09-28, ahead of his trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy.

As reported by The Verge on 2023-10-10, Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, was standing trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. # FTX indictment alleges $100M+ in customer funds went to political contributions, uncharged but admissible

The August 14th superseding indictment against Sam Bankman-Fried alleges he used more than $100 million of misappropriated FTX customer funds to make political contributions — a use of customer money distinct from the real estate (more than $200 million), investments, and Alameda lender repayments also cited. Those contributions are not among the seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy charged in his trial, which began in late September 2023, but prosecutors may still introduce evidence of them; a second trial with additional charges was scheduled for March 2024 (The Verge, 2023-09-28).


---


# Ellison's named-but-unpaid role at Alameda is the Verge author's worst-ex-boyfriend test case

In its October 10, 2023 report on Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial, The Verge's author bases her verdict that Caroline Ellison is the paradigmatically terrible ex-boyfriend case on a single swapped pair: Ellison was made the named head of Alameda Research, the hedge fund at the center of the FTX collapse, while being refused equity — the author's formulation is that no ex of hers "made me the CEO of their sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give me equity." The claim's force comes from a reversal of ownership and accountability, the person whose name carried the fund's sins holding none of its upside. The author confines the argument to her personal standing as a spurned partner, not the legal record: Ellison had already pleaded guilty to fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering before testifying that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes."


---


# Notre Dame professor Easton traced billions between Alameda Research and FTX to customer deposits

In week three of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, University of Notre Dame professor Peter Easton, who helped the government prosecutions of Enron and WorldCom, testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX (TechCrunch, Oct. 6, 2023). Easton testified that much of that funding came from customers, and that user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments, or direct funding toward political causes and charities. The reported coverage placed his testimony early in that week of proceedings.


---


# The Verge's Assessment: Prosecution Built a Strong Case of Orchestration and Direct Participation by Bankman-Fried

In a column published 2023-10-26, as the government's case against Sam Bankman-Fried neared its end, The Verge argued that the prosecution "has made a strong case" that Bankman-Fried presided over the various forms of fraud played out at his trading firm Alameda Research and at the FTX exchange — orchestrating some of that conduct and engaging in some of it directly. Bankman-Fried then faced seven counts: two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges. The claim's scope is explicitly limited to the trial evidence presented up to that date, and it is a journalist's assessment of the government's persuasiveness rather than any verdict — testimony still to come included from former colleagues who had already pleaded guilty and were felons.


---


# FTX's Collapse Traced to Alameda Research Drawing on Customer Funds

In The Verge's 2023-10-26 account of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, FTX collapsed as the result of Bankman-Fried's trading firm Alameda Research purloining the exchange's customers' funds. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, testified that Alameda took customer funds and that Bankman-Fried knew about it and even invested them against her advice; she also described the seven phony balance sheets she had created. Gary Wang, co-founder of FTX and Alameda Research, testified about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code. Customers who had money trapped on the FTX exchange when it collapsed lost access to funds that should have been available at any time they wanted it, even if the bankruptcy proceedings later make them whole.

# Sweeney: Google leaked private Epic conversations to reporters, confirmed at trial

In a *The Verge* interview published 2023-12-12, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney said the evidence presented at the Epic v. Google antitrust trial confirmed practices he had suspected "since 2018 or so," when Epic first began confronting Google. One was Google leaking Epic–Google conversations to reporters in order to get negative stories written about Epic. Sweeney had been called a conspiracy theorist for believing it, and the four-week trial proved him right.


---


# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Epic's own mention of Project Liberty blunts Google's bad-faith angle

Google's attempt to cast Epic's Project Liberty as proof of bad faith runs into one complication: in the opening statements of Epic's 2020 monopoly suit against Google, reported by The Verge on 2023-11-07, Epic mentioned Project Liberty in its own opening. A fact the jury hears first from the side it is supposed to embarrass lands as disclosure, not exposure — so the same detail is a weaker sting when Google reaches for it later. Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein spoke first, portraying Google as a bully that pays competitors not to compete.


---


# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# Contents index: TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup of US v Google

This TechCrunch roundup of November 13, 2023 indexes five sections. First, why US v Google matters and the remedies at stake before Judge Amit Mehta: sharing APIs, bans on anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, and surrendering data — the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. Second, Google's concurrent antitrust matters: the Match Group settlement and the November 6 trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games over Google Play. Third, the declassified list of 20 search terms ordered by revenue for the week of September 22, 2018, and vertical search. Fourth, Jamie Rosenberg's November 8 testimony on MADA (11 pre-loaded Google apps) and RSA mechanics. Fifth, Expedia and Barry Diller on ad load.


---


# SEO's Spread Has Made Ordinary Searches commercially Shaped (The Verge, 2023)

Reporting for The Verge on 2023-11-01 argues that the harm from search engine optimization is no longer confined to sites built for it. The article states that "over time, SEO techniques have spread and become insidious, such that googling anything can now feel like looking up 'sneaker' in the dictionary and finding a definition that sounds both incorrect and suspiciously as though it were written by someone promoting Nike." By 2023, users described Google Search results as "absolutely unusable," "garbage," and "a nightmare" because "a lot of the content doesn't feel authentic." Since Google holds a 90 percent market share for online search, that commercial shaping reaches nearly every informational query, destroying "the illusion that the internet was ever about anything other than selling stuff."

# Verge's "Epic v. Google, explained" Is Flagged Outdated and Left Unfinished

The Verge's explainer "Epic v. Google, explained," published 2023-11-05 ahead of the trial that began November 6th, 2023, was revised on December 15th, 2023 with the banner: "It's basically over now. What happened? Read this, this, and this to get the whole picture." That banner replaces outcome reporting with three unlabeled links. The body below it still speaks in future tense and makes two promises it never keeps: the verdict and remedies, and the "juicy dirt on both companies" — teased with "More on that later!" and absent from the text.

# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# DOJ's theory in *US v. Google*: default deals capture search entry points

In *US v. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. Reporting on Apple executive Eddy Cue's testimony on 2023-09-26, The Verge states that the Justice Department is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.


---


# US v Google's ripple effect on parallel Big Tech antitrust cases

A ruling in US v Google may have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases, since enforcers need one landmark judgment to demonstrate antitrust law remains relevant. The parallel matters named in a TechCrunch roundup dated 2023-11-13: the FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power; the DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products; and there's an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, wherein the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp. The proposition is falsified if those cases proceed and settle unaffected by the Google judgment. Judge Amit Mehta hears the Google case.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. That same roundup reported Google had tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Both facts were carried into TechCrunch's roundup published on November 13, 2023.

# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# DOJ's Theory of Harm in the Google Antitrust Case: Defaults Cut Rivals Off From Data

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The theory therefore runs in two linked steps: owned distribution plus paid defaults deny rivals visibility, and denied visibility denies them the query data that would let their products reach a quality high enough to challenge Google. The claim over Google's dominance in the online search market was filed in 2020. It is separate from a claim filed in January by the Department of Justice along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind its monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising. Google's counter is that it is simply doing business, since partners want the best default engine.


---


# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# Remedies floated against Google if Judge Mehta finds liability

In TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup of the US v. Google antitrust trial, the remedies sketched for Google all hinge on one condition: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google. The article names three. First, Google may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers. Second, it may be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and with wireless carriers. Third, Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines, so those rivals can improve their products and attract more users. The DOJ has said that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday, and the government's case is that Google uses its platforms and partner deals to block competition in search and advertising, cutting rivals off from the data they would need to improve their products.


---


# The Article's Argument: The Burden of Proof Makes the Google Case an Uphill Battle

In "Is Google Search better than the rest? And is that fair?", published by The Age on 22 October 2023, the author argues that the US antitrust suit against Google "could be an uphill battle" because the government "has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo" — that is, show that Google's dominance as the default search provider was unlawfully won rather than earned by being, as Google contends, simply the best product. The same paragraph grants the case a countervailing value: for everyone outside the courtroom it "offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share," specifically whether Google is still focused on being the best, or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money even at the expense of product quality, and how "organic" its results are.


---


# Complaint's core allegation: Google is "starving the free press" at a cost of billions

The central harm asserted in the class action antitrust complaint filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. is that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars." The plaintiff, Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, brings the claim against Google and parent company Alphabet under the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust law, framing Google's redistribution of news content inside its own products as anticompetitive conduct that diverts publishers' content, readers and ad revenue.

# Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. # Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." # Rehn's Core Allegation: SBF's Success "Was Built on Lies"

In his roughly 30-minute government opening statement on Oct. 4, 2023, in Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial, prosecutor Thane Rehn's central claim was that Bankman-Fried's apparent success — "all of that, all of it, was built on lies" — because "behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." The warrant is the divergence between Bankman-Fried repeatedly telling FTX customers their money was "safe and secure" and his alleged "secret access" to that customer money via Alameda Research.


---


# Adversarial proximity: FTX co-defendants and housemates testify against Bankman-Fried, October 2023

In October 2023, FTX's trial in Manhattan turned on adversarial proximity. Gary Wang and Nishad Singh — Sam Bankman-Fried's former MIT classmates, co-workers, and housemates in the Bahamas — testified against their former classmate, confidant and boss, in a case alleging a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars.
