# Some Sports Betting Apps Copy Lines Rather Than Set Their Own

As of Sporting News' line-shopping guide dated 2023-11-06, sportsbook pricing is not uniform across the market. The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services, which use computer models and algorithms weighing analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, to set their lines and odds. Other sports betting apps, by contrast, simply copy those lines rather than produce prices of their own.


---


# Sportsbook Opening Lines Come From Computer Models Run by Oddsmakers

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), the best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and dedicated oddsmaking services to produce their lines and odds. Those oddsmakers and oddsmaking services run computer models and algorithms that weigh analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, among other inputs, to develop the lines and odds before betting opens. Not every operator does this work itself: other sports betting apps simply copy the lines that the oddsmakers and oddsmaking services set. The models' inputs are therefore the origin point for the prices that later move on public betting.


---


# Sports Betting Lines Move With Public Action and New Information

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), betting lines and odds are not static once posted by sportsbooks. They are subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that comes to light ahead of the game — sportsbooks will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side. Because the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook, one may be forced to move a line while another is not.


---


# The Sportsbook Business Model: Balanced Action Wins Either Way

Per Sporting News (2023-11-06), a sportsbook's objective on each market is balanced action, not picking winners. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," which lets it earn the profit already built into the odds and lines — the margin commonly called the vig — without worrying about which side wins. Lines move when the public bets heavily on one side; the originals come from oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms fed by analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data.


---


# Offshore Sportsbooks Are Illegal and Fraud-Exposed, So They Cannot Enter the ROTY Odds Comparison

Comparing NBA Rookie of the Year odds across every "online sportsbook" reachable on the open internet is unsound. Sporting News' NBA ROTY guide of 2023-10-04 concedes that offshore sportsbooks "advertise widely on the internet, but they are illegal and offer no protection against fraud and other criminal activities." The obligation it states is to use "only legal online sportsbooks for any type of betting," so the permissible set for ROTY futures is the licensed, regulated books — for that piece, DraftKings and FanDuel — not the cheapest quoted price wherever it appears.


---


# Futures Odds Diverge Across Sportsbooks Because of Liability, So Timing Matters

In a guide to line shopping published by Sporting News on 2023-11-06, a model of sportsbook pricing explains why futures are the exception to the usual uniformity of odds. Most game lines are similar at different sportsbooks, but the odds in futures markets can vary significantly. The mechanism is liability: sportsbooks sometimes have higher liabilities for specific teams and offer better odds on others to lay that off. Timing is everything. Getting it right lets a bettor take advantage of changes in different futures markets due to liability, and the only way to find these opportunities is shopping lines.


---


# Procedure: Betting NBA Rookie of the Year Futures (Sporting News, 2023-10-04)

Sporting News (2023-10-04) gives these steps for an NBA Rookie of the Year futures bet, once you hold a funded account at a legal online sportsbook:

1. Open the basketball section of the sportsbook website.
2. Select the NBA.
3. Enter the futures tab, where Rookie of the Year odds and NBA MVP odds are posted.
4. Choose your Rookie of the Year selection — Victor Wembanyama was the early favorite, with Scoot Henderson and Chet Holmgren also cited.
5. Enter the stake amount and finalize the bet slip.

Postcondition: a recorded futures ticket on that player, settling at season's end. Offshore sportsbooks are illegal and offer no fraud protection.


---


# Line Shopping: Checking Odds Across Multiple Sportsbooks

Line shopping is the practice of checking the lines and odds for a prospective bet at multiple online sports betting sites. Sporting News' guide to line shopping, published 6 Nov 2023, defines the process this way and describes its result as "quite often better odds and improved lines." The aim is to book a wager at improved odds or a more favourable line than a single sportsbook would offer, since betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook.


---


# Why the Same Bet Is Priced Differently at Every Sportsbook

The Sporting News guide to line shopping (Nov 6, 2023) argues that price differences between sportsbooks are structural, not accidental, and that this is the reason line shopping "always makes sense."

Each sportsbook sets its own market: some employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms, while other betting apps simply copy those lines. Some books therefore open at different prices "right from the jump." Then each book responds to its own money. Since a sportsbook's goal is to even out betting on both sides so it can earn the profit built into the odds without worrying which side wins, it moves a line or changes odds when the public bets heavily on one side.

The decisive point is independence: one sportsbook may be forced to move a line because of betting, while another is not. That produces a divergence on the identical bet, and the divergence is the opportunity — a chance to lay less, win more, and improve your chances.


---


# Live Odds Feeds Are the Easiest Line-Shopping Method

Sporting News (2023-11-06) names a live odds feed as the easiest way to shop lines in US sports betting. Such a feed displays the differences in lines and odds for the same bet across many of the top sportsbooks in the country in one place — a "one-stop shop" where comparing prices takes just seconds rather than manually hopping between apps. The feed works for moneylines, point spreads, totals and prop bets. The trade-off: manual shopping across multiple downloaded sportsbook apps takes longer but can reach more books, or the few that consistently offer the best lines and odds.


---


# Navigating Sporting News' 2023-10-04 NBA Rookie of the Year odds page

Sporting News' page "NBA Rookie of the Year Odds – Wembanyama the early favorite," dated 2023-10-04, indexes the pre-season 2023-24 NBA Rookie of the Year futures market in four sections: "Current NBA ROTY odds" (odds by player), "Who are the NBA RoY odds favorites?" (the case for Victor Wembanyama, Scoot Henderson and Chet Holmgren), "How to bet on NBA Rookie of the Year" (sportsbook mechanics), and "Best sportsbooks for NBA Rookie of the Year odds" (DraftKings, FanDuel).

# DraftKings Runs More Open Betting Markets Than Most Online Sportsbooks

qid: Which company, recently compared for its Gemini Pro performance to OpenAI's GPT-3.5 by TechCrunch, is also mentioned by The Verge as both altering the internet's appearance and potentially winning a court case if all phones and app stores are considered the relevant market?
context:
# Vendor capability claims and user outcomes are weakly coupled — Gemini Pro, December 2023

The weakness of benchmark-derived vendor claims as evidence about real use shows up sharply in the Gemini Pro launch. In blog posts and press materials released the week of 2023-12-07, according to TechCrunch's "Early impressions of Google's Gemini aren't great," Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities and claimed the model meets or exceeds the performance of leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4. The end-user evidence that a "lite" version, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard on 2023-12-06 does not refute those claims, and that is precisely the problem. Users posting on X reported wrong 2023 Oscar winners, a seven-letter answer to a request for a six-letter French word, stale Ukraine summaries, and failed Python and HTML coding attempts. Blog-asserted capability and observed outcome are only weakly related.


---


# GPT store launch delayed past December 2023 by OpenAI's C-suite crisis

TechCrunch's predictions piece of 2023-12-19 reports that OpenAI's GPT store was originally planned for launch in December but was "understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas" — the leadership shake-up of November 2023. The article describes the store as an "app store for AI" that OpenAI will push hard as the platform for AI tools.


---


# GPT Store: OpenAI's Marketplace for User-Built, Monetizable Custom GPTs

The GPT store is an OpenAI marketplace where users can create and monetize their own custom versions of GPT. OpenAI announced it on November 6 at OpenAI DevDay, the company's first developer conference, as part of a slew of updates coming to GPT that also included GPT-4 Turbo (super-charged versions of GPT-4, OpenAI's latest language-writing model) and a multimodal API. TechCrunch reported the announcement in its continuously updated ChatGPT timeline, noting the DevDay news arrived before the leadership turmoil surrounding CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return.


---


# Hypothesis: OpenAI's GPT store becomes the default "app store for AI" in 2024

In a TechCrunch piece dated 2023-12-19, the prediction is that OpenAI will push its GPT store hard through 2024 as the default "app store for AI" — the platform people get their AI tools from — following Apple's store model "all the way to the bank," and at the expense of Hugging Face and open-source models. Originally planned for a December launch, the store was delayed by the November C-suite upheaval that left Sam Altman more fully in charge, accelerating OpenAI's shift toward a "ship it" mindset.

Falsification: the store fails to ship, or becomes only a minor distribution channel for AI tools.


---


# Epic v. Google's outcome hinges on which market the court defines

In Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023, the trial's outcome turns on the market definition the court adopts — the line of argument The Verge names "market definition." If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google's on the road to victory, since Google argues the real competition is Apple and buyers can choose an iPhone instead. If it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape; Epic claims illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing." The hypothesis is falsified by whichever definition the judge records, including a different one entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up picking.


---


# Market Definition in Epic v. Google: Narrow Android Market vs. All Smartphones

In Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023, "market definition" is the name The Verge gives to the question that decides the case: a monopoly on what? Epic claims Google holds illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing", so anyone who buys or develops for Android phones is stuck paying the "Google tax". Google answers that the real competition is Apple, because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead. The same conduct is lawful or unlawful depending on the boundary drawn: if the court holds the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, Google is "on the road to victory"; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic is in better shape. The court could also pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in Epic's Apple case did.


---


# Bard: Google's ChatGPT competitor and the consumer surface for Gemini Pro

Bard is Google's consumer chatbot, which TechCrunch on 2023-12-07 describes as "Google's ChatGPT competitor," the counterpart to OpenAI's ChatGPT. It is one of the range of products and services that Gemini — Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled the same week and pitched as meeting or exceeding models like OpenAI's GPT-4 — was meant to power. A "lite" version of that model, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard the day before publication, on 2023-12-06, making Bard the surface through which ordinary users first reached Gemini Pro.


---


# OpenAI's product-company turn: Altman's post-November 2023 authority displaces board caution with appetite for markets

TechCrunch's 2023-12-19 predictions essay argues that OpenAI will run as a product company in 2024 because the leadership shake-up in November 2023 left Sam Altman more fully in charge, displacing the previous board. The consequence trickles down at every level of the company as a "ship it" mindset, exemplified by the GPT store — the "app store for AI" originally planned for launch in December but delayed due to the C-suite fracas — which OpenAI will push hard as the place to get AI toys and tools, never mind Hugging Face or any open source models. The mechanism is a swap of governing temperament: the caution and academic reserve that the previous board exerted gives way, in TechCrunch's phrasing, to an unseemly lust for markets and customers.


---


# ChatGPT's Launch Reset Competitor Roadmaps: Bard, Amazon Q and Gemini

As ChatGPT became OpenAI's top priority, its success propagated through rivals' product roadmaps in what TechCrunch described on 2023-11-30 as a competition-driven marketplace. Google scrambled to answer it, releasing Bard, "a more or less comparable AI chatbot," in February 2023. Countless other ChatGPT rivals and derivatives reached market afterward, the most recent being Amazon Q, a more business-oriented take on ChatGPT. DeepMind, Google's premier AI research lab, was expected to debut a next-gen chatbot, Gemini, before the end of 2023. The pattern set by these three responses is that a breakout consumer product supplies the template competitors copy and reposition rather than a market they vacate.


---


# Google's opening argument: Play Store dominance is the fruit of competing with the iPhone

In his opening statement for Google in the Epic v. Google trial, lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz told the jury that Google's dominance over the Android app market "isn't anything nefarious but simply the natural outcome of Google fiercely competing with the iPhone and its iOS App Store, where Google would like the court to believe that competition truly lies." His stated warrant, reported by The Verge on 2023-11-07, was that "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other." The argument's leverage is definitional: on that framing the relevant market is phones and ecosystems, where Google plainly lacks a monopoly, rather than Android app stores alone. The reporter judged it potentially "a winning argument in the case" if the jury accepts it, while noting Google spent much of its 45 minutes explaining away apparently bad behavior as normal business practice and "didn't always succeed out of the gate."


---


# ChatGPT Summarized the News Prompt Gemini Pro Deflected

In a news-summary test described in a TechCrunch article published on 2023-12-07, the author asked Bard, running Google's Gemini Pro, to recap a topical story, and got a response matching Gemini Pro's pattern, as the author characterizes it, of declining to comment on potentially controversial news topics and telling users to Google it themselves instead. As a control, the author ran the same prompt through ChatGPT, which returned a bullet-list summary with citations to news articles.

qid: Between the report from The Age on October 22, 2023, regarding Google's manipulation of search results to maximize ad revenue, and the TechCrunch report on December 15, 2023, about a class action antitrust suit filed against Google citing AI's harms to news publishers' bottom lines, is the portrayal of Google's business practices consistent?
context:
# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# Reach of the retracted Wired piece on Google query manipulation, October 2023

In October 2023, Wired published, then removed for not meeting its standards, an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had revealed during the US antitrust trial that it manipulates search queries for ad revenue — for example replacing "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear". The Age reports that the extent of its sharing on social media and boosting in write-ups at other outlets shows how willing people are to accept foul play by Google, amid a standing suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling.

SOURCE: The Age, "Is Google Search better than the rest? And is that fair?", 2023-10-22.


---


# Google antitrust actions surrounding the Helena World Chronicle publisher suit, December 2023

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and covered by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, arrived while several other Google proceedings were live. This note indexes that surrounding docket.

- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (digital ad technology): the DOJ's monopoly suit over Google's ad-tech stack, pending alongside the publisher case in late 2023.
- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (2020): the earlier civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.
- Epic Games v. Google: the app-store antitrust case, which Epic won; the Helena complaint borrows its finding of improper spoliation of evidence — Google's destruction of chat messages.
- Canada settlement (November 2023): Google agreed to pay Canadian media $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) a year, distributed by newsroom headcount. Meta's negotiations remained unresolved; Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August.


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# The DOJ's Separate Google Ad-Tech Lawsuit (January 2023)

Distinct from the online search monopoly case tried in 2023 is a separate antitrust suit the U.S. Department of Justice filed in January 2023 together with eight states, including New York, California and Colorado. That ad-tech action aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising," according to TechCrunch's October 31, 2023 report on the search trial. The two cases therefore target different markets — search versus digital advertising — even though both stem from the government's broader claims about Google's platforms and partner deals blocking competition.


---


# The Article's Argument: The Burden of Proof Makes the Google Case an Uphill Battle

In "Is Google Search better than the rest? And is that fair?", published by The Age on 22 October 2023, the author argues that the US antitrust suit against Google "could be an uphill battle" because the government "has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo" — that is, show that Google's dominance as the default search provider was unlawfully won rather than earned by being, as Google contends, simply the best product. The same paragraph grants the case a countervailing value: for everyone outside the courtroom it "offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share," specifically whether Google is still focused on being the best, or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money even at the expense of product quality, and how "organic" its results are.


---


# Google Search Antitrust Trial: the 2020 Dominance Claim

The U.S. antitrust trial being heard in October 2023 is the 2020 claim over Google's dominance in the online search market, in which Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified on the Monday covered by TechCrunch's Oct. 31, 2023 report, defending the deals that make Google the default search engine. It is distinct from the separate claim filed in January 2023 by the Department of Justice with eight states, including New York, California and Colorado, which seeks to break Google's monopoly in digital advertising, not search.


---


# Complaint's core allegation: Google is "starving the free press" at a cost of billions

The central harm asserted in the class action antitrust complaint filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. is that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars." The plaintiff, Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, brings the claim against Google and parent company Alphabet under the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust law, framing Google's redistribution of news content inside its own products as anticompetitive conduct that diverts publishers' content, readers and ad revenue.


---


# Hausfeld frames the Google publishers suit as a fight for AI-era press competition

Housefeeds counsel Hausfeld, in the website announcement accompanying the class action filed the week of 2023-12-15 in the U.S. District Court in D.C., cast the case against Google and parent Alphabet as necessary to restore competition in the digital news and reference publishing markets and to establish guardrails for the free marketplace of ideas in the AI era. The suit, brought on behalf of Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle and a class of news publishers, invokes both the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act. Hausfeld's framing positions the relief sought — class-wide damages plus an injunction governing how Google uses publisher content in AI products — as a structural remedy for press sustainability, not merely a compensation claim.


---


# Google calls Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit "meritless"

A Google spokesperson rejected the Helena World Chronicle class action filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. (TechCrunch, 2023-12-15) as "meritless," denying the complaint's central allegations — that Google breaks the Sherman Act by "siphoning off" publishers' content, readers and ad revenue, and that AI products including Search Generative Experience and Bard worsen the harm.

qid: Did the 'Fortune' article suggest that Sam Bankman-Fried openly conducted all business dealings without using Caroline Ellison as a front for illicit activities involving customer funds at Alameda Research, while the 'TechCrunch' articles focus on his alleged intentions to use wealth for altruistic purposes and accusations of committing fraud for personal gain, without mentioning the use of a front person?
context:
# Caroline Ellison: Alameda CEO at the Centre of Both Sides' FTX Trial Story

Caroline Ellison is the figure both sides leaned on in the opening statements of Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial, as reported by Fortune on 2023-10-04. She was the CEO of Alameda Research, the crypto hedge fund Bankman-Fried also owned, and his on-again off-again girlfriend. Prosecutor Thane Rehn alleged that Bankman-Fried used Ellison as a front to get "secret access" to customer money — both cash and crypto. Defence lawyer Mark Cohen answered that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and pointed the finger at Ellison, who, he said, did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. By then she was a former lieutenant turned government cooperator, which is why she was not among the prosecution's first two witnesses.


---


# Caroline Ellison's testimony on phony balance sheets and Alameda's use of customer funds

Caroline Ellison, Sam Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, testified at his trial that she created seven phony balance sheets. Writing in The Verge on 2023-10-26, the account of her testimony records that she was clear on two points: Alameda Research took customer funds, and Bankman-Fried knew about it. He even invested those customer funds against her advice. Ellison, alongside Gary Wang and Nishad Singh, is now a felon, with their lives irrevocably changed by possible imprisonment, house arrest, restitution requirements, barred job categories, and the publicity.


---


# Ellison's named-but-unpaid role at Alameda is the Verge author's worst-ex-boyfriend test case

In its October 10, 2023 report on Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial, The Verge's author bases her verdict that Caroline Ellison is the paradigmatically terrible ex-boyfriend case on a single swapped pair: Ellison was made the named head of Alameda Research, the hedge fund at the center of the FTX collapse, while being refused equity — the author's formulation is that no ex of hers "made me the CEO of their sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give me equity." The claim's force comes from a reversal of ownership and accountability, the person whose name carried the fund's sins holding none of its upside. The author confines the argument to her personal standing as a spurned partner, not the legal record: Ellison had already pleaded guilty to fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering before testifying that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes."


---


# Caroline Ellison: Alameda's former head and cooperating witness against Bankman-Fried

Caroline Ellison led Alameda Research, the hedge fund at the center of the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX, and is the former girlfriend of its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried. She has already pleaded guilty to criminal charges in the case: fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering. Testifying for the prosecution on 2023-10-10, the first day she took the stand in Bankman-Fried's criminal trial, she listed those crimes and said that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes," adding, "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back." Bankman-Fried is the defendant on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy.

SOURCE: The Verge, "Sam Bankman-Fried was a terrible boyfriend," 2023-10-10


---


# The government's model of the Bankman-Fried scheme: Alameda as the conduit

In his opening statement on 2023-10-04, Fortune reported, prosecutor Thane Rehn identified Alameda Research, "a crypto hedge fund he also owned," as "the key to his alleged scheme." Using Caroline Ellison, his on-again off-again girlfriend and Alameda's CEO, as a front, Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money — both cash and crypto.


---


# Caroline Ellison: Alameda Research head and prosecution's star witness in the FTX trial

Caroline Ellison ran Alameda Research, the sister hedge fund of the crypto exchange FTX, and had been a girlfriend of FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried. Per a CNBC report dated 2023-10-06 covering Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, she and FTX co-founder Gary Wang were integral members of Bankman-Fried's personal and professional inner circles, and both pleaded guilty in December 2022. Ellison is considered the prosecution's star witness and was expected to take the stand under a cooperation arrangement similar to Wang's.


---


# Bankman-Fried's own definition of "risk-neutral": a world-destroying coin flip

In her testimony on 2023-10-10, Alameda Research's former head Caroline Ellison described a coin-flip thought experiment Sam Bankman-Fried used: if tails destroyed the world and heads made it twice as good, he would still flip. He called that stance being "risk-neutral" — a term The Verge read as a fancy way of saying he was a gambling addict. Ellison, who pleaded guilty to fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering, said Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes," and put the figure at "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."


---


# Defence's counter: Alameda's risk failure lay with CEO Caroline Ellison, not Bankman-Fried's design

Countering the prosecution's Alameda-centred account, Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, told the jury on Oct. 4, 2023 at the FTX founder's trial that Caroline Ellison, the former chief executive of Alameda Research, did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. Alameda, he said, was a successful hedge fund, not a subterranean or shady front, and business practices between it and FTX were reasonable; Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor and market maker. Locating the failure in Ellison's risk management, rather than in Bankman-Fried's design, Cohen framed working at a startup as "like building a plane as you're flying it," adding that businesses sometimes fail.


---


# Cohen's Closing Argument: Bankman-Fried Gave Up Wealth Rather Than Steal, Fortune Says

Mark Cohen, defending Sam Bankman-Fried at FTX's criminal trial in New York, argued in his opening statement on 2023-10-04 that when the walls came closing in and his "plane approached the 'eye of the storm'," Bankman-Fried behaved as an innocent would, being willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. Cohen concluded that the founder of two billion-dollar businesses "didn't steal any money."

Source: Fortune, 2023-10-04.


---


# Caroline Ellison's $14 Billion Testimony, Week Two of the SBF Trial

In week two of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud and money laundering trial, reported by TechCrunch's Jacquelyn Melinek on 2023-10-06, the standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison. She claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. The case against Bankman-Fried covers seven counts tied to fraud and money laundering.


---


# Caroline Ellison's "$14 billion" figure on the stand, 2023-10-10

Testifying at Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial on 2023-10-10, Caroline Ellison — head of Alameda Research during the implosion of Alameda and FTX, already pleaded guilty to fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — said Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes" and stated: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back." The remark, quoted at the end of The Verge's fifth paragraph, was repeated in the seventh as she described the losses.


---


# Rehn's Opening: Three Alleged Destinations for FTX Customer Funds

In his roughly 30-minute opening statement on Oct. 4, 2023, prosecutor Thane Rehn told the jury that Sam Bankman-Fried allegedly stole FTX customer funds for three purposes: to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, to donate millions of dollars to political candidates, and to finance risky bets made through Alameda Research, the crypto hedge fund he also owned.

# Epic's Android App Distribution Monopoly Claim Against Google

In Epic Games' antitrust suit against Google, whose trial began on November 6th, 2023, Epic's core argument concerns Android app distribution. Epic argues that Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that Google has created an illegal monopoly. The claimed harms are twofold: the monopoly unjustly enriches Google, and it artificially drives up app prices, because other app stores can't compete. Epic calls the standard in-app payment fees the "Google tax". The remedy Epic seeks is to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods, so that developers aren't stuck paying that tax or passing the fee along to players.

# Google's counter-argument: iPhone substitution, not Android app stores, defines the market

Google rebutted Epic's market definition in Epic v. Google — which went to trial on Nov. 6, 2023, some 1,180 days after Epic first sued — by arguing the real competition is Apple, because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead. On that view, Google's app store competes with Apple's across platforms, so it is "pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general." Epic's contrary position: Android app distribution and Android in-app payment processing are each their own market.

# "Walled garden" in The Verge's Epic v. Google coverage: a closed platform controlling distribution and payment

In its December 12, 2023 account of Epic's jury verdict against Google, The Verge sets "walled garden" in quotation marks as a descriptor for Apple — Epic's "rival," which the piece notes "almost entirely won a similar case two years ago." In that usage, the term denotes a closed mobile platform whose owner controls both app distribution and in-app payment: the same two powers the nine-person federal jury found Google held an illegal monopoly over, in "Android app distribution and in-app payment systems," and had illegally tied together through "its Google Play billing system to its app store." Apple's verdict, by contrast, went Epic's way only in part.


---


# Epic's stake in v. Google: break up the Android app distribution and in-app payment monopolies

Epic Games' interest in Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023 — 1,180 days after Epic first sued — is the break-up of what it calls Google's illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing." Epic charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal. The theory is straightforward: if those two monopolies are dismantled, developers buying or selling on Android are no longer stuck paying the "Google tax," the 30%-style in-app payment fee critics named — and therefore no longer pass that fee along to consumers in higher app prices. Both Epic and Google agreed the trial could decide the future of Google's app store.


---


# Google argues its Play commission pays for more than billing

In Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google, which began November 6, 2023, Google contests the framing that the 15% to 30% commission it charges app developers on the sales it processes through Google Play's required first-party billing system is payment-processing markup. Its argument is that the commission instead funds other features and controls that keep Android users safe and guide them toward discovering new applications, plus the tools and services developers need to build and grow their apps. Google claims credit for reach beyond the mobile phone too: Android support across platforms, ranging from tablets to TVs to autos and more. It narrows the burden by noting that 99% of its developers qualify for a commission of 15% or less, based on their revenues.


---


# The store–billing relation: how Epic v. Google's two findings form one loop

Read as a single structure rather than two verdicts, the findings a federal jury returned against Google — reported by Tim Sweeney of Epic Games in The Verge, 2023-12-12 — describe one loop with two ends.

One end is the monopolised product: Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. The other end is the tied product: Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The relation between the ends is the model. Whichever product a developer must accept to reach Android users also becomes the channel through which that developer's money moves, so control of distribution converts into control of payment — and the payment share Sweeney calls "huge taxes" paid to a few gatekeepers reinforces the distribution hold. Two holdings, one circuit.


---


# Epic v. Google after openings: what the evidence phase must settle

Following both sides' opening statements to the jury in early November 2023 — Epic Games' on Monday, 2023-11-06, and Google's later the same week, lasting 45 minutes — the Epic v. Google antitrust trial moves to its evidence phase, with several disputes deferred to later weeks. Testimony must first settle Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's claim that "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete," including the alleged $360 million payment that kept Activision from opening an app store competing with Google Play; Activision told The Verge in 2022 it "never entered into an agreement that Activision would not open its own app store." The trial must also resolve whether Android is open: Bornstein promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option," while Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz points to over a billion users installing outside Play.

SOURCE: The Verge, "The Epic v. Google trial may come down to simple v. complicated," 2023-11-07

# Rosenberg's Nov 8 Defense of Google's Android Pre-install and RSA Payments

In the US v Google antitrust trial, Jamie Rosenberg, a Google employee who focuses on Android and Google Play, testified on November 8, 2023 in Google's defense that the deals putting Google Search and Chrome on Android amount to fair competition rather than exclusion. Rosenberg described a mobile app distribution agreement (MADA) that requires Android smartphone makers such as Samsung or Oppo to pre-load a bundle of 11 Google apps, including Search, Chrome and Play, and stressed that those apps need not be the default choices, according to Bloomberg's account of the testimony. Rosenberg also cited revenue share agreements (RSAs) with smartphone makers and wireless carriers such as Verizon — payments that, in Google's telling, reward partners for building and selling more Android devices, in a rivalry with Apple he called "as intense as it gets."


---


# Epic's Core Argument: Google's OEM and Developer Agreements Are Unlawful Restraints

Epic Games' claim against Google, tried from November 6, 2023, rests on one argument: Google's agreements with Android device manufacturers and app developers are anticompetitive restraints under Sections 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act and under California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law, regardless of whether Android permits sideloading.

That sideloading point matters because it distinguishes this case from Epic's suit against Apple, where Epic alleged there was no other way to load apps. Here Android does allow sideloading, so Epic contends those agreements — not the absence of alternatives — are what restrain competition in two markets: distribution of apps to Android users, and payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps. # Sportsbook Opening Lines Come From Computer Models Run by Oddsmakers

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), the best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and dedicated oddsmaking services to produce their lines and odds. Those oddsmakers and oddsmaking services run computer models and algorithms that weigh analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, among other inputs, to develop the lines and odds before betting opens. Not every operator does this work itself: other sports betting apps simply copy the lines that the oddsmakers and oddsmaking services set. The models' inputs are therefore the origin point for the prices that later move on public betting.


---


# Sports Betting Lines Move With Public Action and New Information

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), betting lines and odds are not static once posted by sportsbooks. They are subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that comes to light ahead of the game — sportsbooks will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side. Because the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook, one may be forced to move a line while another is not.


---


# A Placed Bet Locks In the Odds or Line Posted at Wagering

Sporting News (2023-11-06), in its guide to line shopping, states the rule in one sentence: "When you bet, you lock in the odds or line as currently posted." A ticket is priced at the moment it is accepted. Subsequent moves — a spread shifting because the public bet heavily on one side, or odds changing on fresh injury and roster news — apply to bets still to come, not to the wager already placed, whether those later changes would have helped or hurt.


---


# Procedure: Betting NBA Rookie of the Year Futures (Sporting News, 2023-10-04)

Sporting News (2023-10-04) gives these steps for an NBA Rookie of the Year futures bet, once you hold a funded account at a legal online sportsbook:

1. Open the basketball section of the sportsbook website.
2. Select the NBA.
3. Enter the futures tab, where Rookie of the Year odds and NBA MVP odds are posted.
4. Choose your Rookie of the Year selection — Victor Wembanyama was the early favorite, with Scoot Henderson and Chet Holmgren also cited.
5. Enter the stake amount and finalize the bet slip.

Postcondition: a recorded futures ticket on that player, settling at season's end. Offshore sportsbooks are illegal and offer no fraud protection.


---


# Line Shopping Extends to Every Priced Market, and How to Execute It

Line shopping — checking the posted lines and odds for the same prospective bet at multiple sportsbooks — is not confined to one market. Sporting News' line-shopping guide (2023-11-06) states that you can shop around for moneylines, point spreads, totals bets, prop bets, and more, adding that finding the best line or better odds on any bet "is like finding money." The workflow it prescribes: pick a side, then use the drop-down menus and tabs — on a live odds feed or on several sportsbook apps installed on your phone — to reveal that bet's odds and lines across books, and bet when one shows better odds or an improved line than the competition.


---


# Some Sports Betting Apps Copy Lines Rather Than Set Their Own

As of Sporting News' line-shopping guide dated 2023-11-06, sportsbook pricing is not uniform across the market. The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services, which use computer models and algorithms weighing analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, to set their lines and odds. Other sports betting apps, by contrast, simply copy those lines rather than produce prices of their own.


---


# The Sportsbook Business Model: Balanced Action Wins Either Way

Per Sporting News (2023-11-06), a sportsbook's objective on each market is balanced action, not picking winners. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," which lets it earn the profit already built into the odds and lines — the margin commonly called the vig — without worrying about which side wins. Lines move when the public bets heavily on one side; the originals come from oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms fed by analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data.


---


# Offshore Sportsbooks Are Illegal and Fraud-Exposed, So They Cannot Enter the ROTY Odds Comparison

Comparing NBA Rookie of the Year odds across every "online sportsbook" reachable on the open internet is unsound. Sporting News' NBA ROTY guide of 2023-10-04 concedes that offshore sportsbooks "advertise widely on the internet, but they are illegal and offer no protection against fraud and other criminal activities." The obligation it states is to use "only legal online sportsbooks for any type of betting," so the permissible set for ROTY futures is the licensed, regulated books — for that piece, DraftKings and FanDuel — not the cheapest quoted price wherever it appears.


---


# Line Shopping: Checking Odds Across Multiple Sportsbooks

Line shopping is the practice of checking the lines and odds for a prospective bet at multiple online sports betting sites. Sporting News' guide to line shopping, published 6 Nov 2023, defines the process this way and describes its result as "quite often better odds and improved lines." The aim is to book a wager at improved odds or a more favourable line than a single sportsbook would offer, since betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook.


---


# NBA Futures Markets Span the Whole Season, Including Rookie of the Year

NBA Rookie of the Year is one of the NBA futures markets, so wagering opens before the start of the NBA regular season and continues throughout the year, as with other NBA futures odds. Sporting News described (4 October 2023) these markets as settled on season-long outcomes, with odds posted at online sportsbooks and grouped under the NBA futures tab.


---


# Live Odds Feeds Are the Easiest Line-Shopping Method

Sporting News (2023-11-06) names a live odds feed as the easiest way to shop lines in US sports betting. Such a feed displays the differences in lines and odds for the same bet across many of the top sportsbooks in the country in one place — a "one-stop shop" where comparing prices takes just seconds rather than manually hopping between apps. The feed works for moneylines, point spreads, totals and prop bets. The trade-off: manual shopping across multiple downloaded sportsbook apps takes longer but can reach more books, or the few that consistently offer the best lines and odds.


---


# Why the Same Bet Is Priced Differently at Every Sportsbook

The Sporting News guide to line shopping (Nov 6, 2023) argues that price differences between sportsbooks are structural, not accidental, and that this is the reason line shopping "always makes sense."

Each sportsbook sets its own market: some employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms, while other betting apps simply copy those lines. Some books therefore open at different prices "right from the jump." Then each book responds to its own money. Since a sportsbook's goal is to even out betting on both sides so it can earn the profit built into the odds without worrying which side wins, it moves a line or changes odds when the public bets heavily on one side.

The decisive point is independence: one sportsbook may be forced to move a line because of betting, while another is not. That produces a divergence on the identical bet, and the divergence is the opportunity — a chance to lay less, win more, and improve your chances.


---


# Why Line Shopping Pays for the Time It Costs

The argument for line shopping is a mismatch between what it gains and what it costs. Sporting News's guide "Line Shopping in Sports Betting – How to Find the Best Odds" (2023-11-06) puts the cost at "just seconds" when a bettor uses a live odds feed showing differences between sportsbooks, or longer when working manually by installing more than one sports betting app on a phone and tapping among them to compare.

The gain is larger. Betting volume is rarely the same at every sportsbook, so one may be forced to move a line or change odds while another is not; prices may also differ from the opening. Caesars Sportsbook's point spreads can be "a half-point to two points better than the competition's," and its moneyline odds may be more favorable. A half-point at that size changes which side of a posted number a spread wager settles on. As the guide puts it, shopping around lets a bettor "lay less, win more, and improve your chances."

qid: What type of businesses, frequently covered by Sporting News, are known to change their betting lines based on events like injuries or roster changes, and also alter the odds for awards like the NBA Rookie of the Year based on collected data?
context:
# Sports Betting Lines Move With Public Action and New Information

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), betting lines and odds are not static once posted by sportsbooks. They are subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that comes to light ahead of the game — sportsbooks will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side. Because the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook, one may be forced to move a line while another is not.


---


# Some Sports Betting Apps Copy Lines Rather Than Set Their Own

As of Sporting News' line-shopping guide dated 2023-11-06, sportsbook pricing is not uniform across the market. The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services, which use computer models and algorithms weighing analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, to set their lines and odds. Other sports betting apps, by contrast, simply copy those lines rather than produce prices of their own.


---


# Sportsbook Opening Lines Come From Computer Models Run by Oddsmakers

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), the best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and dedicated oddsmaking services to produce their lines and odds. Those oddsmakers and oddsmaking services run computer models and algorithms that weigh analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, among other inputs, to develop the lines and odds before betting opens. Not every operator does this work itself: other sports betting apps simply copy the lines that the oddsmakers and oddsmaking services set. The models' inputs are therefore the origin point for the prices that later move on public betting.


---


# The Sportsbook Business Model: Balanced Action Wins Either Way

Per Sporting News (2023-11-06), a sportsbook's objective on each market is balanced action, not picking winners. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," which lets it earn the profit already built into the odds and lines — the margin commonly called the vig — without worrying about which side wins. Lines move when the public bets heavily on one side; the originals come from oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms fed by analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data.


---


# A Placed Bet Locks In the Odds or Line Posted at Wagering

Sporting News (2023-11-06), in its guide to line shopping, states the rule in one sentence: "When you bet, you lock in the odds or line as currently posted." A ticket is priced at the moment it is accepted. Subsequent moves — a spread shifting because the public bet heavily on one side, or odds changing on fresh injury and roster news — apply to bets still to come, not to the wager already placed, whether those later changes would have helped or hurt.


---


# Procedure: Betting NBA Rookie of the Year Futures (Sporting News, 2023-10-04)

Sporting News (2023-10-04) gives these steps for an NBA Rookie of the Year futures bet, once you hold a funded account at a legal online sportsbook:

1. Open the basketball section of the sportsbook website.
2. Select the NBA.
3. Enter the futures tab, where Rookie of the Year odds and NBA MVP odds are posted.
4. Choose your Rookie of the Year selection — Victor Wembanyama was the early favorite, with Scoot Henderson and Chet Holmgren also cited.
5. Enter the stake amount and finalize the bet slip.

Postcondition: a recorded futures ticket on that player, settling at season's end. Offshore sportsbooks are illegal and offer no fraud protection.


---


# Live Odds Feeds Are the Easiest Line-Shopping Method

Sporting News (2023-11-06) names a live odds feed as the easiest way to shop lines in US sports betting. Such a feed displays the differences in lines and odds for the same bet across many of the top sportsbooks in the country in one place — a "one-stop shop" where comparing prices takes just seconds rather than manually hopping between apps. The feed works for moneylines, point spreads, totals and prop bets. The trade-off: manual shopping across multiple downloaded sportsbook apps takes longer but can reach more books, or the few that consistently offer the best lines and odds.


---


# Line Shopping Extends to Every Priced Market, and How to Execute It

Line shopping — checking the posted lines and odds for the same prospective bet at multiple sportsbooks — is not confined to one market. Sporting News' line-shopping guide (2023-11-06) states that you can shop around for moneylines, point spreads, totals bets, prop bets, and more, adding that finding the best line or better odds on any bet "is like finding money." The workflow it prescribes: pick a side, then use the drop-down menus and tabs — on a live odds feed or on several sportsbook apps installed on your phone — to reveal that bet's odds and lines across books, and bet when one shows better odds or an improved line than the competition.


---


# NBA Futures Markets Span the Whole Season, Including Rookie of the Year

NBA Rookie of the Year is one of the NBA futures markets, so wagering opens before the start of the NBA regular season and continues throughout the year, as with other NBA futures odds. Sporting News described (4 October 2023) these markets as settled on season-long outcomes, with odds posted at online sportsbooks and grouped under the NBA futures tab.


---


# BetMGM Offers Consistently Competitive Lines Plus Frequent Promos and Odds Boosts

Sporting News, writing on 2023-11-06 in its guide to line shopping, reports that the lines and odds at BetMGM Sportsbook are consistently competitive. The publication adds that sports betting promos and odds boosts abound at BetMGM, so a bettor will find a better price on many bets there. Sporting News names BetMGM among the top online sportsbooks for line shopping.


---


# Sporting News' Line Shopping Guide — Section Map and Cross-Links (2023-11-06)

Sporting News' "Line Shopping in Sports Betting - How to Find the Best Odds" (2023-11-06) is ordered as: how sportsbooks set odds and lines; shopping for the best lines at online sportsbooks, covering the best way to shop lines and the recommended sportsbooks Caesars Sportsbook, BetMGM Sportsbook, DraftKings Sportsbook and FanDuel Sportsbook; how to find the best lines and odds for any bet; line shopping for futures; whether you can get a better line or odds after you've already bet; and value.

Two "See more" cross-links branch outward: "How to bet on sports in the US" follows the odds-setting section, and "NFL futures bets" closes the futures section.


---


# Offshore Sportsbooks Are Illegal and Fraud-Exposed, So They Cannot Enter the ROTY Odds Comparison

Comparing NBA Rookie of the Year odds across every "online sportsbook" reachable on the open internet is unsound. Sporting News' NBA ROTY guide of 2023-10-04 concedes that offshore sportsbooks "advertise widely on the internet, but they are illegal and offer no protection against fraud and other criminal activities." The obligation it states is to use "only legal online sportsbooks for any type of betting," so the permissible set for ROTY futures is the licensed, regulated books — for that piece, DraftKings and FanDuel — not the cheapest quoted price wherever it appears.


---


# Why the Same Bet Is Priced Differently at Every Sportsbook

The Sporting News guide to line shopping (Nov 6, 2023) argues that price differences between sportsbooks are structural, not accidental, and that this is the reason line shopping "always makes sense."

Each sportsbook sets its own market: some employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms, while other betting apps simply copy those lines. Some books therefore open at different prices "right from the jump." Then each book responds to its own money. Since a sportsbook's goal is to even out betting on both sides so it can earn the profit built into the odds without worrying which side wins, it moves a line or changes odds when the public bets heavily on one side.

The decisive point is independence: one sportsbook may be forced to move a line because of betting, while another is not. That produces a divergence on the identical bet, and the divergence is the opportunity — a chance to lay less, win more, and improve your chances.

Two related figures from the same reporting set the stakes — Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, per data from Similarweb, and when online magazine The Atlantic modeled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website.

The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.

In a search-engine comparison published in The Age on 2023-10-22, the author writes that the test "did remind me how much data Google collects — not just my searches but anything I say to a smart speaker, any search result or ad that I click." That accumulated behavioural data is the mechanism the article names for relevance: it "does also mean that Google (not just search but also mobile widgets and other services) personalises to me more effectively." Personalisation in the article's account is therefore compounded across surfaces rather than confined to the search results page.

A hypothesis drawn from a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: advocacy groups have raised concerns that Meta's partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform's policy decisions. Extending that concern into a testable claim, the partnerships shift content-policy outcomes against Palestinian expression — the same user group reported for posting Palestine-related content regardless of whether it violates Meta's policies, and restricted from features such as posting or commenting for 24 hours.

The hypothesis is falsified if removal and restriction rates for comparable Palestine-related content show no association with escalation in those agency channels: more reports or referrals routed through partner agencies, but unchanged enforcement rates, would sever the claimed link.

Scope: Meta's platforms, notably Instagram, in the period following Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade of Gaza.

By 2023, users were calling search results "absolutely unusable", "garbage", and "a nightmare", and googling anything could feel like looking up "sneaker" in a dictionary and finding an entry written by someone promoting Nike. A November 2023 Verge feature on the people accused of ruining the internet describes the professionals turning online life into what one tech writer recently called a "search-optimized hellhole" — a phrase capturing internet content reshaped to satisfy search algorithms and earn traffic rather than inform.

# The SEO Business Model: Ranking High to Convert Google's Objectivity Into Ad Traffic

In The Verge's article "The people who ruined the internet" (published 2023-11-01), the distinction between SEO and paid search placement is the core of the model. In the author's phrasing, it is "more like the Wizard of Oz projecting his voice to magnify his authority" — the practitioner's goal is to tell the algorithm whatever it needs to hear for a site to appear as high up as possible in search results. Findability inside a search engine and index is maximized; discoverability to a passer-by and to word-of-mouth is what gets spent to buy it. The Verge reported this on 2023-10-26. A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. # Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. # Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. # Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

In the U.S. antitrust trial over Google's search dominance, CEO Sundar Pichai defended what Google spends on default placement with a self-reinforcing account of why the money is justified. Being the default on other companies' browsers, phones and platforms produces more searches; more searches mean more data taken in; more data make Google the best engine across those devices; and being the best explains why partners choose it and why further default payments are reasonable. ---


# ChatGPT — OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot

ChatGPT is OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot. It began as a tool to hyper-charge productivity: users write essays and code by feeding it short text prompts, and it composes the prose in response. In TechCrunch's description of it on 2023-09-28, that prompting-and-generation pattern is the core capability that made the chatbot widely known.

From that start, ChatGPT grew into something used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies for more wide-ranging needs, and it reached 100 million weekly active users since its initial launch nearly a year before that writing. Its underlying latest language-writing model is GPT-4.


---


# ChatGPT Hit 100 Million Weekly Active Users About a Year After Launch

As of TechCrunch's coverage dated 2023-09-28, ChatGPT had reached 100 million weekly active users, roughly one year after its initial launch — the timeline described as "nearly a year ago." ---


# Shang: ChatGPT's target shifted from domain-specific chatbots to general-purpose systems via prompting

Ruoxi Shang, a third-year PhD student at the University of Washington studying human-AI interaction, attributes part of ChatGPT's enduring popularity in a TechCrunch article published 2023-11-30 to a change in what such systems were built to be. Chatbots had existed for decades, but the models behind ChatGPT were far more sophisticated than what users were accustomed to. Training on vast data moved the design target away from specialized, domain-specific chatbots toward general-purpose systems that people drive through instruction prompting, on the condition that users need learn no new interaction language. Shang notes that "AI models have enabled conversational agents to conduct conversations nearly indistinguishable from human dialogues."


---


# Shang: Conversational Interface Research Explains ChatGPT's "Convincingly Real" Dialogue

Ruoxi Shang, a third-year PhD student at the University of Washington studying human-AI interaction, named ChatGPT's ability to conduct conversations that are "convincingly real" as one reason for the chatbot's enduring popularity, in TechCrunch's coverage of its first anniversary on 2023-11-30.

Shang grounded that explanation in earlier work: "Human-computer interaction researchers have studied how conversational interfaces can improve understandability of information, and the socialization aspects of chatbots bring increased engagement." She continued: "Now, AI models have enabled conversational agents to conduct conversations nearly indistinguishable from human dialogues."

The contrast Shang drew is with chatbots that had existed for decades but ran on models much less sophisticated than those powering ChatGPT, so the same two interface properties now operate at far higher fidelity.

It orders the day's four movements: jury selection that Wednesday morning; the government's opening by prosecutor Thane Rehn, portraying Bankman-Fried as a lying "man" who stole billions; the defense opening by Mark Cohen countering with a good-faith "boy" startup founder; and the prosecution's first two witnesses, beginning with FTX customer Marc-Antoine Julliard, a London-based cocoa trader who said he never recovered almost $100,000. The article closes before the day's adjournment.

# The Verge's Assessment: Prosecution Built a Strong Case of Orchestration and Direct Participation by Bankman-Fried

In a column published 2023-10-26, as the government's case against Sam Bankman-Fried neared its end, The Verge argued that the prosecution "has made a strong case" that Bankman-Fried presided over the various forms of fraud played out at his trading firm Alameda Research and at the FTX exchange — orchestrating some of that conduct and engaging in some of it directly. Bankman-Fried then faced seven counts: two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges. The claim's scope is explicitly limited to the trial evidence presented up to that date, and it is a journalist's assessment of the government's persuasiveness rather than any verdict — testimony still to come included from former colleagues who had already pleaded guilty and were felons.


---


# Caroline Ellison: Alameda Research head and prosecution's star witness in the FTX trial

Caroline Ellison ran Alameda Research, the sister hedge fund of the crypto exchange FTX, and had been a girlfriend of FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried. Per a CNBC report dated 2023-10-06 covering Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, she and FTX co-founder Gary Wang were integral members of Bankman-Fried's personal and professional inner circles, and both pleaded guilty in December 2022. Ellison is considered the prosecution's star witness and was expected to take the stand under a cooperation arrangement similar to Wang's.


---

Court coverage of the Sam Bankman-Fried fraud trial on 2023-10-10 records a juror who had dozed off while testimony turned to the FTT token snapping awake when Caroline Ellison — head of Alameda Research, already pleaded guilty to fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud and money laundering — began testifying about her relationship with Bankman-Fried, the defendant facing seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy.


---


# Caroline Ellison: Alameda's former head and cooperating witness against Bankman-Fried

Caroline Ellison led Alameda Research, the hedge fund at the center of the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX, and is the former girlfriend of its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried. She has already pleaded guilty to criminal charges in the case: fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering. Wire-fraud liability turns on what a defendant knew and when he asked — so Bankman-Fried's quarrels over precision ("hole isn't really the word I would use"; wanting "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it") wrote the jury the record of his own inquiry. # Market Definition in Epic v. Google: Narrow Android Market vs. All Smartphones

In Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023, "market definition" is the name The Verge gives to the question that decides the case: a monopoly on what? Epic claims Google holds illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing", so anyone who buys or develops for Android phones is stuck paying the "Google tax". Google answers that the real competition is Apple, because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead. The same conduct is lawful or unlawful depending on the boundary drawn: if the court holds the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, Google is "on the road to victory"; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic is in better shape. The court could also pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in Epic's Apple case did.

# Judge Rogers' Market Definition Gave Apple the Epic Case — and Haunts Google

In Epic's antitrust case against Apple, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers defined the relevant market for Fortnite as "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than iPhone apps, and that definitional choice carried much of Apple's mostly favorable September 2021 victory. It is the precedent hanging over Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023 — a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued. There, Epic's proposed markets are "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing"; Google counters that the real competition is the iPhone.


---


# Google's counter-argument: iPhone substitution, not Android app stores, defines the market

Google rebutted Epic's market definition in Epic v. Google — which went to trial on Nov. 6, 2023, some 1,180 days after Epic first sued — by arguing the real competition is Apple, because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead. On that view, Google's app store competes with Apple's across platforms, so it is "pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general." Epic's contrary position: Android app distribution and Android in-app payment processing are each their own market.


---


# "Walled garden" in The Verge's Epic v. Google coverage: a closed platform controlling distribution and payment

In its December 12, 2023 account of Epic's jury verdict against Google, The Verge sets "walled garden" in quotation marks as a descriptor for Apple — Epic's "rival," which the piece notes "almost entirely won a similar case two years ago." In that usage, the term denotes a closed mobile platform whose owner controls both app distribution and in-app payment: the same two powers the nine-person federal jury found Google held an illegal monopoly over, in "Android app distribution and in-app payment systems," and had illegally tied together through "its Google Play billing system to its app store." Apple's verdict, by contrast, went Epic's way only in part.

# Epic's Core Argument: Google's OEM and Developer Agreements Are Unlawful Restraints

Epic Games' claim against Google, tried from November 6, 2023, rests on one argument: Google's agreements with Android device manufacturers and app developers are anticompetitive restraints under Sections 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act and under California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law, regardless of whether Android permits sideloading.

That sideloading point matters because it distinguishes this case from Epic's suit against Apple, where Epic alleged there was no other way to load apps. Here Android does allow sideloading, so Epic contends those agreements — not the absence of alternatives — are what restrain competition in two markets: distribution of apps to Android users, and payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps. Epic cites Anti-Fragmentation Agreements blocking OEMs from modifying Android for frictionless downloading outside Google Play, through which 90% of apps are still downloaded.


---


# Epic's case against Google is weakened by never naming a reasonable store fee

Epic Games' antitrust case against Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023 — 1,180 days after Epic originally sued — argues that Google holds illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," and that developers buying for or publishing on Android are stuck paying the "Google tax." One criticism aimed at Epic's position is that it wants something for nothing: Epic has never stated what fee it would consider reasonable for Google to charge for placement in the Google Play app store. Rather than naming a defensible figure, Epic CEO Tim Sweeney instead implies that a developer who uses its own payment system should pay Google nothing at all for store listing. That silence leaves Epic's target vague: it opposes the current fee without ever describing the competitive price a court could order.


---


# Epic's Android App Distribution Monopoly Claim Against Google

In Epic Games' antitrust suit against Google, whose trial began on November 6th, 2023, Epic's core argument concerns Android app distribution. Epic argues that Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that Google has created an illegal monopoly. The claimed harms are twofold: the monopoly unjustly enriches Google, and it artificially drives up app prices, because other app stores can't compete. Epic calls the standard in-app payment fees the "Google tax". The remedy Epic seeks is to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods, so that developers aren't stuck paying that tax or passing the fee along to players.

Source: The Verge, "Epic v. Google, explained" (2023-11-05).

# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Google's opening argument: Play Store dominance is the fruit of competing with the iPhone

In his opening statement for Google in the Epic v. Google trial, lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz told the jury that Google's dominance over the Android app market "isn't anything nefarious but simply the natural outcome of Google fiercely competing with the iPhone and its iOS App Store, where Google would like the court to believe that competition truly lies." His stated warrant, reported by The Verge on 2023-11-07, was that "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other." The argument's leverage is definitional: on that framing the relevant market is phones and ecosystems, where Google plainly lacks a monopoly, rather than Android app stores alone. The U.S. antitrust trial being heard in October 2023 is the 2020 claim over Google's dominance in the online search market, in which Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified on the Monday covered by TechCrunch's Oct. 31, 2023 report, defending the deals that make Google the default search engine. It is distinct from the separate claim filed in January 2023 by the Department of Justice with eight states, including New York, California and Colorado, which seeks to break Google's monopoly in digital advertising, not search.
