# DOJ's Theory of Harm in the Google Antitrust Case: Defaults Cut Rivals Off From Data

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The theory therefore runs in two linked steps: owned distribution plus paid defaults deny rivals visibility, and denied visibility denies them the query data that would let their products reach a quality high enough to challenge Google. The claim over Google's dominance in the online search market was filed in 2020. It is separate from a claim filed in January by the Department of Justice along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind its monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising. Google's counter is that it is simply doing business, since partners want the best default engine.

# Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.

- **The ISA**: the Information Services Agreement making Google default search on all Apple devices, in place since 2002 and renegotiated by Cue with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016.
- **The 2016 revenue-share renegotiation**: Apple sought a larger share of Google's search revenue from Apple-directed users; specific numbers were reserved for closed court sessions.

Google plans to push back against Epic's claim that it faces no competition in the app store business. Beyond that, Google will point out that Android also supports competitive app stores, specifically Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore. This counters Epic's assertion that Google restrains competition in the market for distributing apps to Android users. Epic's anticipated response is that Google makes it hard for those alternative app stores to succeed and reach consumers.

# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

They compromised on a figure neither disclosed in open court: on 26 September 2023, in US v. Google before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, Cue testified that discussion of specific numbers was reserved for closed court sessions. # The Article's Argument: The Burden of Proof Makes the Google Case an Uphill Battle

In "Is Google Search better than the rest? And is that fair?", published by The Age on 22 October 2023, the author argues that the US antitrust suit against Google "could be an uphill battle" because the government "has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo" — that is, show that Google's dominance as the default search provider was unlawfully won rather than earned by being, as Google contends, simply the best product. The same paragraph grants the case a countervailing value: for everyone outside the courtroom it "offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share," specifically whether Google is still focused on being the best, or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money even at the expense of product quality, and how "organic" its results are.


---


# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Google's behavioural data as the personalisation engine across Search, mobile widgets and other services

In a search-engine comparison published in The Age on 2023-10-22, the author writes that the test "did remind me how much data Google collects — not just my searches but anything I say to a smart speaker, any search result or ad that I click." That accumulated behavioural data is the mechanism the article names for relevance: it "does also mean that Google (not just search but also mobile widgets and other services) personalises to me more effectively." The competing service in the same test, DuckDuckGo, collects less but "didn't perform as well and is harder to read." Personalisation in the article's account is therefore compounded across surfaces rather than confined to the search results page.


---


# Web Growth, Not Monetisation, Is The Simpler Explanation For "Google Search Was A Lot Better 10 Years Ago"

Running through the discussion of Google's search dominance in *The Age* article of 2023-10-22 is the recurring claim that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago". The counter-argument: conceding that perception, the article calls it a stretch to attribute any decline to Google's monetisation practices — the suspicion that it uses its ubiquity to squeeze people for money even at the expense of product quality. A simpler explanation is available in the sheer growth of the web Google must index.


---


# Hypothesis: full rollout of Google's AI search will cut publisher traffic 20-40%

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20-40% of their website traffic when Google's AI products fully roll out, according to The Wall Street Journal's report as relayed in a TechCrunch article dated 2023-12-15. The expectation is falsifiable: compare per-publisher Google referral volume before and after AI-search availability, controlling for overall search demand. Two related figures from the same reporting set the stakes — Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, per data from Similarweb, and when online magazine The Atlantic modeled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website.


---


# Reach of the retracted Wired piece on Google query manipulation, October 2023

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.


---


# Wired removed Megan Gray's article alleging Google rewrites search queries for ad revenue

In October 2023, Wired published an opinion piece by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the US antitrust trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear". Google rejected the piece as misleading and inaccurate, denying it ever alters search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards.


---


# DOJ's Theory of Harm in the Google Antitrust Case: Defaults Cut Rivals Off From Data

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The theory therefore runs in two linked steps: owned distribution plus paid defaults deny rivals visibility, and denied visibility denies them the query data that would let their products reach a quality high enough to challenge Google. The claim over Google's dominance in the online search market was filed in 2020. It is separate from a claim filed in January by the Department of Justice along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind its monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising. Google's counter is that it is simply doing business, since partners want the best default engine.


---


# Google's rebuttal to Megan Gray's Wired query-rewrite allegation

In October 2023, in response to the Wired opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray — which alleged, on the example of a search for "children's clothing" being replaced with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear", that Google manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — Google rejected the piece in very strong terms, calling it misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Read as a single structure rather than two verdicts, the findings a federal jury returned against Google — reported by Tim Sweeney of Epic Games in The Verge, 2023-12-12 — describe one loop with two ends.

One end is the monopolised product: Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. The other end is the tied product: Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

Google, explained," Sean Hollister's reader-facing explainer at The Verge, published 2023-11-05 ahead of the trial that opened November 6th — "a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued"; Hollister appended a December 15th, 2023 update marking it superseded. Google rebutted Epic's market definition in Epic v. On that view, Google's app store competes with Apple's across platforms, so it is "pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general." Epic's contrary position: Android app distribution and Android in-app payment processing are each their own market.

# Epic's price-harm claim rests on monopoly-set app store and payment fees

Epic's case against Google depends on one relation: that Google's app-store and payment-processing terms are set by monopoly power rather than by competition, and that the consequence is consumers pay more for apps than they would in a contested market. Epic's earlier legal filings suggested this upshot for consumers — higher prices for apps than there would be "if there were more competition and / or lower app store and payment processing fees." Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein argued the same structure at the opening described by The Verge on 2023-11-07, showing jurors 70 percent app profit margins on $12 billion in revenue a year, per Epic, and Google "pay[ing] actual and potential competitors not to compete." Epic sued Google in 2020 over in-app purchase fees. The claim fails if the fee levels would persist under competition.


---


# Google argues its Play commission pays for more than billing

In Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google, which began November 6, 2023, Google contests the framing that the 15% to 30% commission it charges app developers on the sales it processes through Google Play's required first-party billing system is payment-processing markup. Its argument is that the commission instead funds other features and controls that keep Android users safe and guide them toward discovering new applications, plus the tools and services developers need to build and grow their apps. Google claims credit for reach beyond the mobile phone too: Android support across platforms, ranging from tablets to TVs to autos and more. It narrows the burden by noting that 99% of its developers qualify for a commission of 15% or less, based on their revenues.


---


# Epic's case against Google is weakened by never naming a reasonable store fee

Epic Games' antitrust case against Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023 — 1,180 days after Epic originally sued — argues that Google holds illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," and that developers buying for or publishing on Android are stuck paying the "Google tax." One criticism aimed at Epic's position is that it wants something for nothing: Epic has never stated what fee it would consider reasonable for Google to charge for placement in the Google Play app store. Rather than naming a defensible figure, Epic CEO Tim Sweeney instead implies that a developer who uses its own payment system should pay Google nothing at all for store listing. That silence leaves Epic's target vague: it opposes the current fee without ever describing the competitive price a court could order.


---


# Google Play as the default Android app store

Google Play is Google's app store for the Android operating system, and it is the default channel through which the vast, vast majority of Android app installs occur. It pre-empts the alternatives: the Galaxy Store, which comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone, accounts for only a tiny sliver of Android installs. In The Verge's 2023-11-07 coverage of the Epic v. Google trial, Epic's opening argument treated that installed base itself — not a closed platform — as the measure of Google's power over Android distribution.

DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.


---


# Default placement, not search quality, sets rivals' scale — the testable counterfactual from Google antitrust testimony

A testable proposition emerging from testimony in the U.S. government's Google antitrust trial (TechCrunch, 2023-10-31): a search engine of comparable product quality given equal access to paid default placement would reach competitive scale in online search. The evidence base is rival executives' own accounts. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make deals with Apple like Google's — a deal in place since 2003. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search. The proposition is falsified if a rival granted default placement of that kind failed to grow share, and it is the direct negation of Google's defense that it is default because it is the best.


---

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."

# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. In the U.S. antitrust trial over Google's search dominance, CEO Sundar Pichai defended what Google spends on default placement with a self-reinforcing account of why the money is justified. Being the default on other companies' browsers, phones and platforms produces more searches; more searches mean more data taken in; more data make Google the best engine across those devices; and being the best explains why partners choose it and why further default payments are reasonable. TechCrunch reported this on 2023-10-31, describing Pichai's testimony that Monday, two days after search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on 2023-10-28 that Google had paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default placement. # Default homepage placement causally raises search volume — Google's 2007 internal finding

Google documented internally, in 2007, that preselected placement on a user's browser homepage causally increases a search engine's query volume. Data from a 2007 Google product strategy meeting, presented at trial on October 28, 2023 by U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw to Google CEO Sundar Pichai, showed that when people changed their browser homepage to Google they performed 15% more Google searches, and when they switched away their Google searches dropped 27%. The meeting summary sent to Pichai and other Google leaders recorded that "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The relation holds user inertia and switching effort constant: default placement itself supplies the volume. Reported by TechCrunch on October 31, 2023.


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.

# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

Apple fixes that default to Google through the Information Services Agreement (ISA), in place since 2002, whose current iteration Cue negotiated with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. Cue acknowledged that the ISA doesn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup. Whether Google is "easily" changed is contested: DuckDuckGo's CEO testified it takes "too many steps."

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. GPT-4 Turbo is, in OpenAI's own description at its first developer conference, a "super-charged" version of GPT-4, the company's latest language-writing model. OpenAI named it on November 6 at OpenAI DevDay, in a batch of GPT updates that also included a multimodal API and a GPT store where users can create and monetize their own custom versions of GPT. According to TechCrunch's coverage of November 6, 2023 announcement, GPT-4 itself remains largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users, and TechCrunch's December 2023 timeline records that the ChatGPT Plus subscription includes access to both GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo.


---


# GPT Store: OpenAI's Marketplace for User-Built, Monetizable Custom GPTs

The GPT store is an OpenAI marketplace where users can create and monetize their own custom versions of GPT. OpenAI announced it on November 6 at OpenAI DevDay, the company's first developer conference, as part of a slew of updates coming to GPT that also included GPT-4 Turbo (super-charged versions of GPT-4, OpenAI's latest language-writing model) and a multimodal API. TechCrunch reported the announcement in its continuously updated ChatGPT timeline, noting the DevDay news arrived before the leadership turmoil surrounding CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return.


---


# ChatGPT's year-one capability set is a strict superset of its GPT-3.5 chat-only launch state

ChatGPT's feature set as of TechCrunch's 2023-11-30 one-year report contains everything it launched with, plus layers added on top. A year earlier, OpenAI had released ChatGPT as a "low-key research preview" — initially a basic free-to-use, web-based and chat-focused interface on top of one of OpenAI's existing models, GPT-3.5. In the months following its launch, ChatGPT gained paid tiers with additional features, including a plan geared toward enterprise customers. OpenAI also upgraded ChatGPT with web searching, document analyzing and image creating (via DALL-E 3) capabilities. And, leaning on speech recognition, voice synthesis and text-image understanding models developed in house, OpenAI gave ChatGPT the ability to "hear," "speak," "see" and take actions. The chat interface on GPT-3.5 remains the substrate; the later functions are additions, not replacements.


---


# Adoption and Investment as Grounds for AI Chatbots Outlasting OpenAI's Leadership Crisis

TechCrunch's ChatGPT coverage (published 2023-09-28, updated through December 2023) argues that AI chatbots are not going away anytime soon, resting the claim on two grounds: measured adoption and OpenAI's continued investment.

Adoption: ChatGPT reached 100 million weekly active users since its initial launch nearly a year ago, and is used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies.

Investment: OpenAI announced GPT-4 Turbo, a multimodal API and a GPT store at its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, on November 6; connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users; integrated DALL-E 3; and re-enabled ChatGPT Plus subscriptions on December 13, 2023.

The reasoning is that a user base that large and a product roadmap that active do not reverse because CEO and co-founder Sam Altman was fired and swiftly returned — a turmoil the article says may instead empower Meta's LLaMA models and rival AI startups.


---


# ChatGPT Plus

ChatGPT Plus is OpenAI's paid subscription tier for ChatGPT, the AI chatbot used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies. Its defining differentiator is access to GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo, described in a TechCrunch article published 2023-09-28. GPT-4 writes more naturally and fluently than previous models and remains largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users. OpenAI paused Plus sign-ups in November 2023 citing a "surge of usage"; CEO Sam Altman announced subscriptions re-enabled on December 13, 2023, after the company "found more gpus".


---

The article describes the store as an "app store for AI" that OpenAI will push hard as the platform for AI tools.


---

OpenAI DevDay was OpenAI's first developer conference, held on 6 November 2023 — the last major company event before the "leadership chaos" surrounding the firing and swift return of CEO and co-founder Sam Altman, which TechCrunch says raised concerns about OpenAI's direction and opened the door for competitors. At DevDay, OpenAI announced a slew of updates to GPT: GPT-4 Turbo, described as a super-charged version of GPT-4, its latest language-writing model; a multimodal API; and a GPT store where users can create and monetize their own custom versions of GPT.


---


# ChatGPT at Launch: A Free Chat Interface on GPT-3.5, Framed as a "Low-Key Research Preview"

When OpenAI released ChatGPT on 30 November 2022, it was not a new model. OpenAI published it as a "low-key research preview," reportedly prompted partly by rivalry with AI startup Anthropic, and told staff the goal was to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI to inform the development of OpenAI's future models. OpenAI never released a research paper on ChatGPT.


---


# ChatGPT as priority number one and development platform inside OpenAI

In TechCrunch's 2023-11-30 account of ChatGPT's first anniversary, the term "ChatGPT" inside OpenAI had come to mean priority number one — not simply a one-off product but a development platform to build upon. That reframing showed up in the features layered onto the original chat interface on GPT-3.5: paid tiers including an enterprise plan, web searching, document analyzing, image creation via DALL-E 3, and the ability to "hear," "speak," "see" and take actions.

# Multimodal API (OpenAI DevDay, November 6)

A multimodal API is a programmatic interface to a model that accepts and returns more than one modality — text plus another medium such as images — instead of a text-only endpoint, where a developer sends a written prompt and gets written output back. The term appears here as one of "a slew of updates coming to GPT" that OpenAI announced at OpenAI DevDay, its first developer conference, held November 6, alongside GPT-4 Turbo and a GPT store for custom, monetizable versions of GPT (TechCrunch, 2023-09-28).

Search Generative Experience (SGE) draws on the same crawler feed that powers Google's ordinary search, which means a publisher cannot refuse SGE's use of its content without also vanishing from regular search results. In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. qid: Has the news source TechCrunch reported any change in the development of AI-powered chatbots after introducing ChatGPT as a general-purpose chatbot by OpenAI, with the expectation of DeepMind's next-generation chatbot Gemini?

# ChatGPT — OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot

ChatGPT is OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot. It began as a tool to hyper-charge productivity: users write essays and code by feeding it short text prompts, and it composes the prose in response. In TechCrunch's description of it on 2023-09-28, that prompting-and-generation pattern is the core capability that made the chatbot widely known.

From that start, ChatGPT grew into something used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies for more wide-ranging needs, and it reached 100 million weekly active users since its initial launch nearly a year before that writing. Its underlying latest language-writing model is GPT-4.


---


# ChatGPT's Launch Reset Competitor Roadmaps: Bard, Amazon Q and Gemini

As ChatGPT became OpenAI's top priority, its success propagated through rivals' product roadmaps in what TechCrunch described on 2023-11-30 as a competition-driven marketplace. Google scrambled to answer it, releasing Bard, "a more or less comparable AI chatbot," in February 2023. Countless other ChatGPT rivals and derivatives reached market afterward, the most recent being Amazon Q, a more business-oriented take on ChatGPT. DeepMind, Google's premier AI research lab, was expected to debut a next-gen chatbot, Gemini, before the end of 2023. The pattern set by these three responses is that a breakout consumer product supplies the template competitors copy and reposition rather than a market they vacate.


---


# Adoption and Investment as Grounds for AI Chatbots Outlasting OpenAI's Leadership Crisis

TechCrunch's ChatGPT coverage (published 2023-09-28, updated through December 2023) argues that AI chatbots are not going away anytime soon, resting the claim on two grounds: measured adoption and OpenAI's continued investment.

Adoption: ChatGPT reached 100 million weekly active users since its initial launch nearly a year ago, and is used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies.

Investment: OpenAI announced GPT-4 Turbo, a multimodal API and a GPT store at its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, on November 6; connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users; integrated DALL-E 3; and re-enabled ChatGPT Plus subscriptions on December 13, 2023.

The reasoning is that a user base that large and a product roadmap that active do not reverse because CEO and co-founder Sam Altman was fired and swiftly returned — a turmoil the article says may instead empower Meta's LLaMA models and rival AI startups.


---


# More than 92% of Fortune 500 Companies Use ChatGPT (TechCrunch, 2023)

According to TechCrunch's ChatGPT explainer, dated 2023-09-28, more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies use ChatGPT, OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot. The figure describes how far the product had spread beyond its origins: TechCrunch characterises ChatGPT as having started as a tool to hyper-charge productivity through writing essays and code with short text prompts, then evolving into a behemoth that those large employers deploy for more wide-ranging needs. The article was last updated through December 2023.


---


# Shang: ChatGPT's target shifted from domain-specific chatbots to general-purpose systems via prompting

Ruoxi Shang, a third-year PhD student at the University of Washington studying human-AI interaction, attributes part of ChatGPT's enduring popularity in a TechCrunch article published 2023-11-30 to a change in what such systems were built to be. Chatbots had existed for decades, but the models behind ChatGPT were far more sophisticated than what users were accustomed to. Training on vast data moved the design target away from specialized, domain-specific chatbots toward general-purpose systems that people drive through instruction prompting, on the condition that users need learn no new interaction language. Shang notes that "AI models have enabled conversational agents to conduct conversations nearly indistinguishable from human dialogues."


---


# Bard: Google's ChatGPT competitor and the consumer surface for Gemini Pro

Bard is Google's consumer chatbot, which TechCrunch on 2023-12-07 describes as "Google's ChatGPT competitor," the counterpart to OpenAI's ChatGPT. It is one of the range of products and services that Gemini — Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled the same week and pitched as meeting or exceeding models like OpenAI's GPT-4 — was meant to power. A "lite" version of that model, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard the day before publication, on 2023-12-06, making Bard the surface through which ordinary users first reached Gemini Pro.


---


# ChatGPT at Launch: A Free Chat Interface on GPT-3.5, Framed as a "Low-Key Research Preview"

When OpenAI released ChatGPT on 30 November 2022, it was not a new model. As TechCrunch described it on 2023-11-30, ChatGPT was initially "a basic free-to-use, web-based and chat-focused interface on top of one of OpenAI's existing models, GPT-3.5" — the wrapping, not the engine, was the new part. OpenAI never released a research paper on ChatGPT.


---

Starting in November 2023, ChatGPT users reported that the chatbot felt "lazier" than usual, citing simpler answers and refusals to complete requested tasks, according to TechCrunch's running ChatGPT timeline. Some attributed it to the "winter break hypothesis," the argument that AI performs worse in December because it "learned" to do less work over the holidays; others suggested the chatbot was simulating seasonal depression.

OpenAI confirmed it was aware of the issue but said it was not sure why it was happening. In a post on 8 December, the company's @ChatGPTapp account stated that GPT-4 had not been updated since 11 November and that the behaviour "certainly isn't intentional," adding that model behaviour "can be unpredictable" and that OpenAI was looking into fixing it.


---


# ChatGPT Plus

ChatGPT Plus is OpenAI's paid subscription tier for ChatGPT, the AI chatbot used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies. Its defining differentiator is access to GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo, described in a TechCrunch article published 2023-09-28. GPT-4 writes more naturally and fluently than previous models and remains largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users. ---

As of TechCrunch's coverage dated 2023-09-28, ChatGPT had reached 100 million weekly active users, roughly one year after its initial launch — the timeline described as "nearly a year ago." TechCrunch attributed this user milestone to OpenAI's heavy continued investment in the chatbot, which the outlet reported was by then used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies.


---


# ChatGPT's research preview launch as a data-harvesting strategy

When OpenAI released ChatGPT "a year ago" — i.e. a year before TechCrunch's retrospective of 2023-11-30 — it did so as a "low-key research preview," reportedly spurred in part by an intense rivalry with the AI startup Anthropic. OpenAI leadership told the OpenAI rank-and-file at the time that the goal was to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI, in order to inform the development of OpenAI's future models. qid: Who is the individual implicated by Fortune and multiple TechCrunch articles as having used a colleague as a front for unauthorized access to customer funds, was once likened to a prominent investor, allegedly directed the misappropriation of billions to settle debts, and is accused by prosecutors of committing fraud for personal gain?

The Securities and Exchange Commission alleges that FTX, the cryptocurrency exchange Sam Bankman-Fried founded in 2019, was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to his crypto trading firm Alameda Research, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds," according to reporting by The Verge on 2023-09-28, shortly before Bankman-Fried's trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy began.

In his roughly 30-minute opening statement on Oct. 4, 2023, prosecutor Thane Rehn told the jury that Sam Bankman-Fried allegedly stole FTX customer funds for three purposes: to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, to donate millions of dollars to political candidates, and to finance risky bets made through Alameda Research, the crypto hedge fund he also owned.

Caroline Ellison led Alameda Research, the hedge fund at the center of the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX, and is the former girlfriend of its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried. In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. That same roundup reported Google had tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Both facts were carried into TechCrunch's roundup published on November 13, 2023.


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# Index — Five revelations from the Google antitrust trial, 30–31 October 2023

A breakdown published by TechCrunch on 30–31 October 2023, anchored on Google CEO Sundar Pichai's Monday testimony in the U.S. government's antitrust trial over Google's 2020-era search dominance, organizes the week's disclosures into five points.

1. Default-payment totals: $26.3 billion paid in 2021 across browsers, phones and platforms including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, roughly $18 billion of it to Apple, per search head Prabhakar Raghavan's 28 October testimony.
2. The Chrome-promotion ban: Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users.
3. The iPhone preinstall bid: Pichai's 2018 attempt to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device.
4. Deleted chat logs: history-off default vs. the DOJ's litigation hold.
5. Google's early letter on defaults: a 2007 email citing 15% and 27% swings.


---


# DOJ's theory in *US v. Google*: default deals capture search entry points

In *US v. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. Reporting on Apple executive Eddy Cue's testimony on 2023-09-26, The Verge states that the Justice Department is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.


---


# Apple took roughly $18 billion of Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default payments

Of the $26.3 billion Google paid in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be the default search engine, about $18 billion went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023. TechCrunch reported the figure on October 31, 2023, during the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google; the Google–Apple default deal had been in place since 2003.


---


# Google–Apple Search Deal: Payment for Default Placement, Restraint on Chrome

Under the Google–Apple search deal, in place since 2003, Google pays Apple for default search placement in Safari: of the $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults across browsers, phones and platforms in 2021, about $18 billion went to Apple, according to testimony in the U.S. antitrust trial reported by TechCrunch on October 31, 2023.

The consideration flowing back to Apple is restraint. Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, per Bloomberg, though Google had the means to do so through banners, pop-ups and similar prompts inside its other applications. That term's effect on Apple's own conduct: Apple never switched to a Google competitor as its search engine and never let iPhone users choose a browser when setting up their devices.


---


# Pichai's Loop: Default Payments, Data Intake, Search Quality

In the U.S. antitrust trial over Google's search dominance, CEO Sundar Pichai defended what Google spends on default placement with a self-reinforcing account of why the money is justified. Being the default on other companies' browsers, phones and platforms produces more searches; more searches mean more data taken in; more data make Google the best engine across those devices; and being the best explains why partners choose it and why further default payments are reasonable. TechCrunch reported this on 2023-10-31, describing Pichai's testimony that Monday, two days after search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on 2023-10-28 that Google had paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default placement. Pichai added that the decision was made with the consumer in mind. The loop is Google's own testimony about its motives, not an independently established causal finding, and the government contests its premise.


---


# Google's default-search deal with Apple dates to 2003

In its 2023-10-31 report on the U.S. antitrust trial against Google, TechCrunch stated that "Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003." That is the agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices, so it had been running roughly twenty years by the time the deal's cost came under scrutiny in court in late October 2023.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

Testifying on 28 October 2023 in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan stated that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phone makers and platforms for making Google the default search engine. Recipients included the companies Apple, Samsung and Mozilla. Of that $26.3 billion total, roughly $18 billion went directly to Apple, under a Google–Apple search deal in place since 2003.

qid: Does the Fortune article claim that Sam Bankman-Fried used Caroline Ellison as a front for secret access to customer funds at Alameda Research, while the TechCrunch article alleges that Caroline Ellison took $14 billion from customers to repay debts without Sam Bankman-Fried's knowledge, or do both articles assert different levels of involvement of Sam Bankman-Fried in the misuse of customer funds?
context:
# Caroline Ellison's $14 Billion Testimony, Week Two of the SBF Trial

In week two of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud and money laundering trial, reported by TechCrunch's Jacquelyn Melinek on 2023-10-06, the standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison. She claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. The case against Bankman-Fried covers seven counts tied to fraud and money laundering.


---


# Caroline Ellison: Alameda CEO at the Centre of Both Sides' FTX Trial Story

Caroline Ellison is the figure both sides leaned on in the opening statements of Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial, as reported by Fortune on 2023-10-04. She was the CEO of Alameda Research, the crypto hedge fund Bankman-Fried also owned, and his on-again off-again girlfriend. Prosecutor Thane Rehn alleged that Bankman-Fried used Ellison as a front to get "secret access" to customer money — both cash and crypto. Defence lawyer Mark Cohen answered that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and pointed the finger at Ellison, who, he said, did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. By then she was a former lieutenant turned government cooperator, which is why she was not among the prosecution's first two witnesses.


---


# Caroline Ellison's testimony on phony balance sheets and Alameda's use of customer funds

Caroline Ellison, Sam Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, testified at his trial that she created seven phony balance sheets. Writing in The Verge on 2023-10-26, the account of her testimony records that she was clear on two points: Alameda Research took customer funds, and Bankman-Fried knew about it. He even invested those customer funds against her advice. Ellison, alongside Gary Wang and Nishad Singh, is now a felon, with their lives irrevocably changed by possible imprisonment, house arrest, restitution requirements, barred job categories, and the publicity.


---


# The government's model of the Bankman-Fried scheme: Alameda as the conduit

In his opening statement on 2023-10-04, Fortune reported, prosecutor Thane Rehn identified Alameda Research, "a crypto hedge fund he also owned," as "the key to his alleged scheme." Using Caroline Ellison, his on-again off-again girlfriend and Alameda's CEO, as a front, Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money — both cash and crypto.


---


# Caroline Ellison: Alameda's former head and cooperating witness against Bankman-Fried

Caroline Ellison led Alameda Research, the hedge fund at the center of the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX, and is the former girlfriend of its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried. She has already pleaded guilty to criminal charges in the case: fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering. Testifying for the prosecution on 2023-10-10, the first day she took the stand in Bankman-Fried's criminal trial, she listed those crimes and said that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes," adding, "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back." Bankman-Fried is the defendant on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy.

SOURCE: The Verge, "Sam Bankman-Fried was a terrible boyfriend," 2023-10-10


---


# Caroline Ellison testified Alameda Research was already failing when she joined in 2018

Caroline Ellison testified at Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial, as reported by The Verge on October 10, 2023, that Alameda Research — the hedge fund she ran — was troubled from her earliest time there in 2018. "Shortly after I started, I learned the company was in worse shape than I realized," Ellison said. Alameda had initially been funded with loans "from acquaintances," she testified, and those loans were recalled a few weeks after she arrived. Asked why Bankman-Fried had not shared the company's shaky circumstances in her job offer, she said: "He hadn't known how to tell me."


---


# Caroline Ellison: Alameda Research head and prosecution's star witness in the FTX trial

Caroline Ellison ran Alameda Research, the sister hedge fund of the crypto exchange FTX, and had been a girlfriend of FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried. Per a CNBC report dated 2023-10-06 covering Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, she and FTX co-founder Gary Wang were integral members of Bankman-Fried's personal and professional inner circles, and both pleaded guilty in December 2022. Ellison is considered the prosecution's star witness and was expected to take the stand under a cooperation arrangement similar to Wang's.


---


# Ellison testified FTX Ventures' $2 billion came from money allocated to Alameda

During week two of Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX fraud trial, Caroline Ellison, former CEO of the trading firm Alameda Research, testified in detail that FTX Ventures — the $2 billion venture fund — was funded with money that had previously been allocated to Alameda by third-party lenders. TechCrunch reported Ellison's account of the fund's funding source in trial coverage dated 2023-10-06.


---


# Defence's counter: Alameda's risk failure lay with CEO Caroline Ellison, not Bankman-Fried's design

Countering the prosecution's Alameda-centred account, Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, told the jury on Oct. 4, 2023 at the FTX founder's trial that Caroline Ellison, the former chief executive of Alameda Research, did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. Alameda, he said, was a successful hedge fund, not a subterranean or shady front, and business practices between it and FTX were reasonable; Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor and market maker. Locating the failure in Ellison's risk management, rather than in Bankman-Fried's design, Cohen framed working at a startup as "like building a plane as you're flying it," adding that businesses sometimes fail.


---


# Caroline Ellison's "$14 billion" figure on the stand, 2023-10-10

Testifying at Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial on 2023-10-10, Caroline Ellison — head of Alameda Research during the implosion of Alameda and FTX, already pleaded guilty to fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — said Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes" and stated: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back." The remark, quoted at the end of The Verge's fifth paragraph, was repeated in the seventh as she described the losses.


---


# Alameda Research: FTX's sister hedge fund, run by Caroline Ellison

Alameda Research was the hedge fund operating as the sister firm to the bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, run by Caroline Ellison, who had been Sam Bankman-Fried's girlfriend. Media reporting in November 2022 detailed Alameda's business practices and its troubling ties to FTX, which Bankman-Fried's co-founder Gary Wang later described in October 2023 trial testimony. Alameda had a roughly $14 billion hole in its books.


---


# Ellison's named-but-unpaid role at Alameda is the Verge author's worst-ex-boyfriend test case

In its October 10, 2023 report on Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial, The Verge's author bases her verdict that Caroline Ellison is the paradigmatically terrible ex-boyfriend case on a single swapped pair: Ellison was made the named head of Alameda Research, the hedge fund at the center of the FTX collapse, while being refused equity — the author's formulation is that no ex of hers "made me the CEO of their sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give me equity." The claim's force comes from a reversal of ownership and accountability, the person whose name carried the fund's sins holding none of its upside. The author confines the argument to her personal standing as a spurned partner, not the legal record: Ellison had already pleaded guilty to fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering before testifying that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes."

qid: Which company, recently compared for its Gemini Pro's performance to OpenAI's GPT-3.5 by TechCrunch, is also the subject of a class action antitrust lawsuit by news publishers for allegedly harming their bottom line and siphoning off their content, readers, and ad revenue?

# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Complaint's core allegation: Google is "starving the free press" at a cost of billions

The central harm asserted in the class action antitrust complaint filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. is that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars." The plaintiff, Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, brings the claim against Google and parent company Alphabet under the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust law, framing Google's redistribution of news content inside its own products as anticompetitive conduct that diverts publishers' content, readers and ad revenue.


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# Vendor capability claims and user outcomes are weakly coupled — Gemini Pro, December 2023

The weakness of benchmark-derived vendor claims as evidence about real use shows up sharply in the Gemini Pro launch. In blog posts and press materials released the week of 2023-12-07, according to TechCrunch's "Early impressions of Google's Gemini aren't great," Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities and claimed the model meets or exceeds the performance of leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4. The end-user evidence that a "lite" version, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard on 2023-12-06 does not refute those claims, and that is precisely the problem. Users posting on X reported wrong 2023 Oscar winners, a seven-letter answer to a request for a six-letter French word, stale Ukraine summaries, and failed Python and HTML coding attempts. Blog-asserted capability and observed outcome are only weakly related.


---


# GPT Store: OpenAI's Marketplace for User-Built, Monetizable Custom GPTs

The GPT store is an OpenAI marketplace where users can create and monetize their own custom versions of GPT. OpenAI announced it on November 6 at OpenAI DevDay, the company's first developer conference, as part of a slew of updates coming to GPT that also included GPT-4 Turbo (super-charged versions of GPT-4, OpenAI's latest language-writing model) and a multimodal API. TechCrunch reported the announcement in its continuously updated ChatGPT timeline, noting the DevDay news arrived before the leadership turmoil surrounding CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return.


---


# Publisher's Google antitrust suit alleges spoliation of chat messages, echoing Epic Games case

The class action antitrust suit that Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023 alleges evidence of improper spoliation by Google — specifically the destruction of chat messages. The complaint ties that allegation to a known precedent: the same issue of destroyed chat messages was raised in Epic Games' recent lawsuit against Google over app-store antitrust conduct, a case Epic won. The spoliation claim sits alongside the suit's other concerns, including allegedly changed AdSense rates, and appears among the counts supporting its requests for damages and injunctive relief against Google.


---


# Bard: Google's ChatGPT competitor and the consumer surface for Gemini Pro

Bard is Google's consumer chatbot, which TechCrunch on 2023-12-07 describes as "Google's ChatGPT competitor," the counterpart to OpenAI's ChatGPT. It is one of the range of products and services that Gemini — Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled the same week and pitched as meeting or exceeding models like OpenAI's GPT-4 — was meant to power. A "lite" version of that model, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard the day before publication, on 2023-12-06, making Bard the surface through which ordinary users first reached Gemini Pro.


---


# Google calls Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit "meritless"

A Google spokesperson rejected the Helena World Chronicle class action filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. (TechCrunch, 2023-12-15) as "meritless," denying the complaint's central allegations — that Google breaks the Sherman Act by "siphoning off" publishers' content, readers and ad revenue, and that AI products including Search Generative Experience and Bard worsen the harm.


---


# Gemini: Google's flagship generative AI model family

Gemini is Google's flagship generative AI model, unveiled during the week of 2023-12-07 and meant to power a range of Google products and services. One of those services is Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor, which began receiving a "lite" version of Gemini called Gemini Pro on 2023-12-06. In blog posts and press materials published alongside that announcement, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4.


---


# OpenAI's December 2023 Axel Springer Deal Covered Both Model Training and Live ChatGPT Answers

In December 2023, OpenAI announced a content agreement with Axel Springer, the Berlin-based news publisher that owns Business Insider and Politico, which OpenAI framed as helping "provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools." The agreement had two distinct limbs. First, OpenAI would train its generative AI models on Axel Springer's journalism. Second, it would add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT, so the reporting surfaces inside answers rather than only shaping the underlying model. That combination — a licensing deal that pays for a publisher's archive as training data while also giving that publisher's newest work privileged placement in a chatbot's responses — made the deal notable beyond the parties involved, and it was reported in TechCrunch's running ChatGPT timeline alongside other December 2023 OpenAI news, including the reopening of ChatGPT Plus subscriptions on December 13, 2023.


---


# SGE rides GoogleBot, so publishers have no clean opt-out

Search Generative Experience (SGE) draws on the same crawler feed that powers Google's ordinary search, which means a publisher cannot refuse SGE's use of its content without also vanishing from regular search results. The class action antitrust suit Helena World Chronicle — an Arkansas publisher of two weekly newspapers — filed against Google and parent Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023 puts it bluntly: publishers "can't block SGE because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot." The complaint's injunction asks Google to let publishers who opt out of SGE still appear in Google search results.

- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (2020): the earlier civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

Distinct from the online search monopoly case tried in 2023 is a separate antitrust suit the U.S. Department of Justice filed in January 2023 together with eight states, including New York, California and Colorado. That ad-tech action aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising," according to TechCrunch's October 31, 2023 report on the search trial. qid: Between the portrayal of Sam Bankman-Fried's legal circumstances in the Fortune article published on October 4, 2023, and the allegations against him mentioned in the TechCrunch article published on October 7, 2023, was there consistency in the depiction of his actions related to fraud?
context:
# Bankman-Fried Visibly Upset During Wang's Testimony, October 2023

CNBC's courtroom report of 5–6 October 2023 records that Sam Bankman-Fried, 31, stayed mostly quiet at his fraud trial, listening intently to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys. But as Gary Wang testified against him, Bankman-Fried looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's appearance and demeanor in court, 2023-10-04

Reporting for The Verge on 2023-11-01 argues that the harm from search engine optimization is no longer confined to sites built for it. - U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (digital ad technology): the DOJ's monopoly suit over Google's ad-tech stack, pending alongside the publisher case in late 2023.

Epic Games sued Apple and Google on the same day, August 13th, 2020, both over in-app payment fees critics call the "Apple tax" and "Google tax," but the two cases then moved at wildly different speeds. "Humans interacting with the system inferred emotional content and a narrative through line in chat messages." # Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# Google calls Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit "meritless"

A Google spokesperson rejected the Helena World Chronicle class action filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. (TechCrunch, 2023-12-15) as "meritless," denying the complaint's central allegations — that Google breaks the Sherman Act by "siphoning off" publishers' content, readers and ad revenue, and that AI products including Search Generative Experience and Bard worsen the harm.


---


# Complaint's core allegation: Google is "starving the free press" at a cost of billions

The central harm asserted in the class action antitrust complaint filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. is that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars." The plaintiff, Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, brings the claim against Google and parent company Alphabet under the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust law, framing Google's redistribution of news content inside its own products as anticompetitive conduct that diverts publishers' content, readers and ad revenue.


---


# Hausfeld frames the Google publishers suit as a fight for AI-era press competition

Housefeeds counsel Hausfeld, in the website announcement accompanying the class action filed the week of 2023-12-15 in the U.S. District Court in D.C., cast the case against Google and parent Alphabet as necessary to restore competition in the digital news and reference publishing markets and to establish guardrails for the free marketplace of ideas in the AI era. The suit, brought on behalf of Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle and a class of news publishers, invokes both the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act. Hausfeld's framing positions the relief sought — class-wide damages plus an injunction governing how Google uses publisher content in AI products — as a structural remedy for press sustainability, not merely a compensation claim.

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

# The store–billing relation: how Epic v. Google's two findings form one loop

Read as a single structure rather than two verdicts, the findings a federal jury returned against Google — reported by Tim Sweeney of Epic Games in The Verge, 2023-12-12 — describe one loop with two ends.

One end is the monopolised product: Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. The other end is the tied product: Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The relation between the ends is the model. Whichever product a developer must accept to reach Android users also becomes the channel through which that developer's money moves, so control of distribution converts into control of payment — and the payment share Sweeney calls "huge taxes" paid to a few gatekeepers reinforces the distribution hold. Two holdings, one circuit.

# Epic's Android App Distribution Monopoly Claim Against Google

In Epic Games' antitrust suit against Google, whose trial began on November 6th, 2023, Epic's core argument concerns Android app distribution. Epic argues that Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that Google has created an illegal monopoly. The claimed harms are twofold: the monopoly unjustly enriches Google, and it artificially drives up app prices, because other app stores can't compete. Epic calls the standard in-app payment fees the "Google tax". The remedy Epic seeks is to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods, so that developers aren't stuck paying that tax or passing the fee along to players.

# Default homepage placement causally raises search volume — Google's 2007 internal finding

Google documented internally, in 2007, that preselected placement on a user's browser homepage causally increases a search engine's query volume. Data from a 2007 Google product strategy meeting, presented at trial on October 28, 2023 by U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw to Google CEO Sundar Pichai, showed that when people changed their browser homepage to Google they performed 15% more Google searches, and when they switched away their Google searches dropped 27%. The meeting summary sent to Pichai and other Google leaders recorded that "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The relation holds user inertia and switching effort constant: default placement itself supplies the volume. Reported by TechCrunch on October 31, 2023.


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.

---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

Google, the antitrust trial over Google's search business, Eddy Cue testified on 2023-09-26 about what a "default search engine" means in practice: the engine preselected on a device, which a user must actively change rather than choose. Apple fixes that default to Google through the Information Services Agreement (ISA), in place since 2002, whose current iteration Cue negotiated with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. Cue acknowledged that the ISA doesn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup. Whether Google is "easily" changed is contested: DuckDuckGo's CEO testified it takes "too many steps."

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." A testable proposition emerging from testimony in the U.S. government's Google antitrust trial (TechCrunch, 2023-10-31): a search engine of comparable product quality given equal access to paid default placement would reach competitive scale in online search. # "Unlawful Monopoly" in Epic v. Google: Legal Theory vs. Market-Leader Meaning

In Epic v. Google, tried before a jury with opening arguments reported by The Verge on 2023-11-07, the phrase "unlawful monopoly" names a legal theory, not a popularity ranking. Epic sued Google in 2020, alleging Google Play constitutes an unlawful monopoly. Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's task was proving Android *functions* as an unlawful monopoly — conduct-based: Google allegedly "bribes" or "blocks" attempts to compete with Google Play. The plain-language sense, "the most-used store," is what Google attacked. Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz countered that "Google doesn't have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general," noting "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen." Confusing the two meanings lets each side answer the other's different question.

# Market Definition in Epic v. Google: Narrow Android Market vs. All Smartphones

In Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023, "market definition" is the name The Verge gives to the question that decides the case: a monopoly on what? Epic claims Google holds illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing", so anyone who buys or develops for Android phones is stuck paying the "Google tax". Google answers that the real competition is Apple, because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead. The same conduct is lawful or unlawful depending on the boundary drawn: if the court holds the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, Google is "on the road to victory"; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic is in better shape. The court could also pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in Epic's Apple case did.

The central harm asserted in the class action antitrust complaint filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. is that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars." Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. # Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

# Default search engine, as defined in US v. Google

In US v. Google, the antitrust trial over Google's search business, Eddy Cue testified on 2023-09-26 about what a "default search engine" means in practice: the engine preselected on a device, which a user must actively change rather than choose. Beyond damages, the class action against Google and parent Alphabet filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. by Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle asks the court for two injunctive remedies. Index to The Verge's 2023-09-26 report on Eddy Cue testifying in US v. Google, the DOJ antitrust trial over Google's search business, before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC. Sub-topics covered:
