Google antitrust trial before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed Apple's senior vice president of Internet Services, Eddy Cue, on the Information Services Agreement (ISA) — the default-search deal with Google, in place since 2002, that pays Apple billions of dollars a year and which Cue renegotiated with CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. Against her point that the ISA accounts for a significant portion of Apple's profits, Cue replied that Apple does not look at the money that way: the profits figure omits the work Apple did to make its platform attractive enough for the deal to perform. Distinct from the online search monopoly case tried in 2023 is a separate antitrust suit the U.S. Department of Justice filed in January 2023 together with eight states, including New York, California and Colorado. When OpenAI released ChatGPT "a year ago" — i.e. a year before TechCrunch's retrospective of 2023-11-30 — it did so as a "low-key research preview," reportedly spurred in part by an intense rivalry with the AI startup Anthropic. # Multimodal API (OpenAI DevDay, November 6)

A multimodal API is a programmatic interface to a model that accepts and returns more than one modality — text plus another medium such as images — instead of a text-only endpoint, where a developer sends a written prompt and gets written output back. The term appears here as one of "a slew of updates coming to GPT" that OpenAI announced at OpenAI DevDay, its first developer conference, held November 6, alongside GPT-4 Turbo and a GPT store for custom, monetizable versions of GPT (TechCrunch, 2023-09-28).

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# Similarweb data: Google drives nearly 40% of news publishers' web traffic (December 2023)

Data from the analytics firm Similarweb, cited in a Wall Street Journal report that TechCrunch referenced on 2023-12-15, showed Google driving nearly 40% of news publishers' website traffic at that time. TechCrunch quoted the figure while covering the Helena World Chronicle class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet.


---


# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Google antitrust actions surrounding the Helena World Chronicle publisher suit, December 2023

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and covered by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, arrived while several other Google proceedings were live. This note indexes that surrounding docket.

- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (digital ad technology): the DOJ's monopoly suit over Google's ad-tech stack, pending alongside the publisher case in late 2023.
- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (2020): the earlier civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.
- Epic Games v. Google: the app-store antitrust case, which Epic won; the Helena complaint borrows its finding of improper spoliation of evidence — Google's destruction of chat messages.
- Canada settlement (November 2023): Google agreed to pay Canadian media $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) a year, distributed by newsroom headcount. Meta's negotiations remained unresolved; Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August.


---


# The DOJ's Separate Google Ad-Tech Lawsuit (January 2023)

Distinct from the online search monopoly case tried in 2023 is a separate antitrust suit the U.S. Department of Justice filed in January 2023 together with eight states, including New York, California and Colorado. That ad-tech action aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising," according to TechCrunch's October 31, 2023 report on the search trial. The two cases therefore target different markets — search versus digital advertising — even though both stem from the government's broader claims about Google's platforms and partner deals blocking competition.


---


# Blame for degraded Google results splits between the near-monopoly and the SEOs who game it

In a report on the search engine optimization industry published by The Verge on 2023-11-01, responsibility for bad search results is contested between two camps. In 2023, many people are unhappy with their ability to find information on the internet — which for almost everyone means the quality of Google Search results — calling the links that appear "absolutely unusable", "garbage", and "a nightmare" because "a lot of the content doesn't feel authentic." Some blame Google itself, asserting that an all-powerful, all-seeing, trillion-dollar corporation with a 90 percent market share for online search is corrupting access to the truth. Others blame the SEO practitioners, whose goal is to tell the algorithm whatever it needs to hear so a site ranks as high as possible and then shows visitors advertising. The disagreement is over agency: whether a dominant platform that rewards gaming sets the terms, or the gamers do.


---


# US v Google's ripple effect on parallel Big Tech antitrust cases

A ruling in US v Google may have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases, since enforcers need one landmark judgment to demonstrate antitrust law remains relevant. The parallel matters named in a TechCrunch roundup dated 2023-11-13: the FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power; the DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products; and there's an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, wherein the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp. The proposition is falsified if those cases proceed and settle unaffected by the Google judgment. Judge Amit Mehta hears the Google case.


---


# Hausfeld frames the Google publishers suit as a fight for AI-era press competition

Housefeeds counsel Hausfeld, in the website announcement accompanying the class action filed the week of 2023-12-15 in the U.S. District Court in D.C., cast the case against Google and parent Alphabet as necessary to restore competition in the digital news and reference publishing markets and to establish guardrails for the free marketplace of ideas in the AI era. The suit, brought on behalf of Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle and a class of news publishers, invokes both the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act. Hausfeld's framing positions the relief sought — class-wide damages plus an injunction governing how Google uses publisher content in AI products — as a structural remedy for press sustainability, not merely a compensation claim.


---


# The two injunctions sought in Helena World Chronicle's December 2023 suit against Google

Beyond damages, the class action against Google and parent Alphabet filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. by Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle asks the court for two injunctive remedies. The first would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train general-purpose artificial intelligence products — a obligation reaching not only Google's own AI offerings but those of its rivals. The second would require Google to let publishers who opt out of Search Generative Experience (SGE) continue appearing in Google's ordinary search results, addressing the complaint's allegation that publishers cannot block SGE because it shares GoogleBot, the same web crawler used by Google's general search service.


---


# Complaint's SGE argument: Google's "walled garden" built on publishers' content

The Helena World Chronicle complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in the week of 2023-12-15 and reported by TechCrunch, contends that Google's Search Generative Experience keeps users inside Google's "walled garden" while reusing publishers' material. It argues that SGE, which it says "plagiarizes" their content, offers web searchers a conversational way to seek information but ultimately keeps them on Google rather than sending them onward. According to the complaint, Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The complaint adds that publishers cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot.


---


# Google Search Antitrust Trial: the 2020 Dominance Claim

The U.S. antitrust trial being heard in October 2023 is the 2020 claim over Google's dominance in the online search market, in which Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified on the Monday covered by TechCrunch's Oct. 31, 2023 report, defending the deals that make Google the default search engine. It is distinct from the separate claim filed in January 2023 by the Department of Justice with eight states, including New York, California and Colorado, which seeks to break Google's monopoly in digital advertising, not search.

# Sam Bankman-Fried's Persona as Fast-Rich Billionaire Spending It on Existential Risk, per Michael Lewis

Michael Lewis, quoted in TechCrunch's report of 2023-10-02 on his 60 Minutes interview, described the image Sam Bankman-Fried projected when Lewis met him in early 2021 in Berkeley: a young billionaire who had made his fortune very fast and meant to give it away against catastrophe. "Eighteen months earlier, he had nothing. Now he had $22.5 billion. He was the richest person in the world under 30 [and] he was going to spend it to save humanity from extinction," Lewis said. # Wang's courtroom admission named Bankman-Fried, Singh and Ellison in his FTX frauds

Gary Wang's account of his own FTX criminality reached past himself to named others. Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos on Thursday 5 October 2023, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?", Wang answered "Yes," and said those crimes — wire and commodities fraud — were carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research. When Roos asked whether he saw any of those people in the courtroom, Wang stood, looked around, said "Yes," and identified "Sam Bankman-Fried." The argument's force is a sworn guilty plea, tempered by his six-page cooperation agreement and the up to 50 years in prison he still faces at sentencing.

# Wang's testimony: FTX platform code as the mechanism behind Alameda's access

Gary Wang's testimony at Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial in a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday, Oct. 5 and Friday, Oct. 6, 2023, put software at the center of the exposure: code baked into FTX's exchange platform gave sister hedge fund Alameda Research special access, including unlimited withdrawals on the exchange. Wang, 30, was technology chief for FTX, and those privileges, held while he ran the technology, are what he said allowed Alameda to withdraw and transfer funds derived from customers. Wang, who pleaded guilty in December and testified under a six-page cooperation agreement, faces up to 50 years in prison.

# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. # Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. # Epic v. Google after openings: what the evidence phase must settle

Following both sides' opening statements to the jury in early November 2023 — Epic Games' on Monday, 2023-11-06, and Google's later the same week, lasting 45 minutes — the Epic v. Google antitrust trial moves to its evidence phase, with several disputes deferred to later weeks. In its December 12, 2023 account of Epic's jury verdict against Google, The Verge sets "walled garden" in quotation marks as a descriptor for Apple — Epic's "rival," which the piece notes "almost entirely won a similar case two years ago." Read as a single structure rather than two verdicts, the findings a federal jury returned against Google — reported by Tim Sweeney of Epic Games in The Verge, 2023-12-12 — describe one loop with two ends.

One end is the monopolised product: Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. The other end is the tied product: Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

OpenAI was the laboratory created later in 2015 out of a private dinner in a room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road. There Elon Musk dined with Sam Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers. # TechCrunch contrasts ChatGPT's minimal launch with an unsourced "fastest-growing consumer app" claim

TechCrunch's case for ChatGPT's significance on its first birthday (November 30, 2023) rests on a contrast between an unpromising origin and a superlative outcome. The chatbot shipped a year earlier as a "low-key research preview" — initially only a basic free-to-use, web-based, chat-focused interface on top of GPT-3.5, one of OpenAI's existing models. From that, the article asserts, it became OpenAI's most popular product ever and "the fastest-growing consumer app in history," a record stated without naming the data behind it. # OpenAI as the pivot of AI's control-versus-freedom argument

In *The Age*'s report of 2023-12-09, "How ego and fear fuelled the rise of artificial intelligence," the argument over whether AI "should be controlled or set free" is shown to run through OpenAI rather than through the abstract idea of the technology. The reason is ChatGPT: thanks to that chatbot, OpenAI "has fundamentally changed the technology industry and has introduced the world to the risks and potential of artificial intelligence." A lab valued at more than $US80 billion ($A123 billion) thereby became the shared reference point for a debate conducted among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators, and one that pits Elon Musk, Larry Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI against one another.

The claim is tested by what happened inside that same company months later, when rebel board members tried to force out Altman on the belief they could no longer trust him to build AI that would benefit humanity. The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Gemini: Google's flagship generative AI model family

Gemini is Google's flagship generative AI model, unveiled during the week of 2023-12-07 and meant to power a range of Google products and services. One of those services is Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor, which began receiving a "lite" version of Gemini called Gemini Pro on 2023-12-06. In blog posts and press materials published alongside that announcement, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4.


---


# Google calls Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit "meritless"

A Google spokesperson rejected the Helena World Chronicle class action filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. (TechCrunch, 2023-12-15) as "meritless," denying the complaint's central allegations — that Google breaks the Sherman Act by "siphoning off" publishers' content, readers and ad revenue, and that AI products including Search Generative Experience and Bard worsen the harm.


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# Confabulation in generative AI: fluent statements that are untrue (Gemini Pro, Dec 2023)

Confabulation, as applied to a generative AI model, means the model producing fluent, confident statements that are simply untrue — as distinct from refusing to answer or acknowledging uncertainty. Science fiction author Charlie Stross found many examples of confabulation in a recent blog post about Gemini Pro, the "lite" version of Google's flagship generative AI model that began rolling out to Bard (Google's ChatGPT competitor) the day before TechCrunch's report of 2023-12-07. Among other mistruths recorded in that post, Gemini Pro said that Stross contributed to the Linux kernel; he never has.


---


# SGE rides GoogleBot, so publishers have no clean opt-out

Search Generative Experience (SGE) draws on the same crawler feed that powers Google's ordinary search, which means a publisher cannot refuse SGE's use of its content without also vanishing from regular search results. The class action antitrust suit Helena World Chronicle — an Arkansas publisher of two weekly newspapers — filed against Google and parent Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023 puts it bluntly: publishers "can't block SGE because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot." The complaint's injunction asks Google to let publishers who opt out of SGE still appear in Google search results.


---


# Bard: Google's ChatGPT competitor and the consumer surface for Gemini Pro

Bard is Google's consumer chatbot, which TechCrunch on 2023-12-07 describes as "Google's ChatGPT competitor," the counterpart to OpenAI's ChatGPT. It is one of the range of products and services that Gemini — Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled the same week and pitched as meeting or exceeding models like OpenAI's GPT-4 — was meant to power. A "lite" version of that model, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard the day before publication, on 2023-12-06, making Bard the surface through which ordinary users first reached Gemini Pro.


---


# Gemini: Google's flagship AI family launched with only its "lite" member

Gemini is Google's flagship AI model family, unveiled in the week of 8 December 2023 and covered in TechCrunch's Week in Review of 9 December 2023. Only its "lite" member, Gemini Pro, was released; the full model, Gemini Ultra, was withheld. In a press briefing and blog posts, Google touted Gemini's coding capabilities and multimodal prowess, claiming the model can understand images, audio and videos just as well as text. Gemini Pro is strictly text-in, text-out and has proved mistake-prone. Google was also caught faking a Gemini demo, tuning text prompts with still images off camera.


---


# Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE)

Search Generative Experience (SGE) is Google's AI-powered search product, cited in a class action antitrust suit filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in the week of December 15, 2023. The suit's plaintiff, Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle, describes SGE as offering web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode, with answers delivered inside the results page rather than through a click to the source. Google "ultimately keeps users in Google's 'walled garden' as it 'plagiarizes' their content," publishers cannot block SGE, because it runs on the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot.


---


# AI Tool Customer Withdrawal Predicted for 2024 as Marketing Claims Face Review

In an article published 2023-12-19 on TechCrunch, the hypothesis is advanced that a considerable customer withdrawal from AI tools will occur during 2024. The reasoning is that marketing claims made for machine learning systems—often adopted by companies merely to avoid falling behind—will face their quarterly and yearly reviews, and will very likely be found wanting. The measurable benefits will fail to justify the costs and risks involved. On the far end of this spectrum, lawsuits and regulatory action against AI service providers that cannot back up their claims are anticipated as a consequence of the same dynamic.


---


# Hausfeld frames the Google publishers suit as a fight for AI-era press competition

Housefeeds counsel Hausfeld, in the website announcement accompanying the class action filed the week of 2023-12-15 in the U.S. District Court in D.C., cast the case against Google and parent Alphabet as necessary to restore competition in the digital news and reference publishing markets and to establish guardrails for the free marketplace of ideas in the AI era. The suit, brought on behalf of Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle and a class of news publishers, invokes both the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act. Hausfeld's framing positions the relief sought — class-wide damages plus an injunction governing how Google uses publisher content in AI products — as a structural remedy for press sustainability, not merely a compensation claim.


---


# Hypothesis: Unsubstantiated AI marketing claims trigger lawsuits and regulatory action in 2024

TechCrunch's "8 predictions for AI in 2024" (published 2023-12-19) forecasts, in its "Marketing meets reality" section, that the far end of the 2024 AI backlash will be legal rather than commercial. After machine learning marketing claims meet quarterly and yearly reviews and are found wanting — and after customers withdraw from AI tools whose benefits fail to justify costs and risks — AI service providers "that failed to back up their claims" are likely to face lawsuits and regulatory action during 2024.

Falsified if no litigation or regulatory enforcement against such vendors follows unsubstantiated 2023 AI claims.

qid: Which company, recently discussed by both The Verge and TechCrunch, is known for making deals to be the default search engine on various platforms, altering the internet's appearance, hosting an annual hardware event to showcase new developments, and has been accused of anticompetitively affecting news publishers' content and revenue?
context:
# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# DOJ's theory in *US v. Google*: default deals capture search entry points

In *US v. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. Reporting on Apple executive Eddy Cue's testimony on 2023-09-26, The Verge states that the Justice Department is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.


---


# Microsoft and DuckDuckGo CEOs Tied Their Search Shortfalls to Missing Apple Default Deals

Earlier in October 2023, in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search. Reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, citing The Information.


---


# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.


---


# SEO's Spread Has Made Ordinary Searches commercially Shaped (The Verge, 2023)

Reporting for The Verge on 2023-11-01 argues that the harm from search engine optimization is no longer confined to sites built for it. The article states that "over time, SEO techniques have spread and become insidious, such that googling anything can now feel like looking up 'sneaker' in the dictionary and finding a definition that sounds both incorrect and suspiciously as though it were written by someone promoting Nike." By 2023, users described Google Search results as "absolutely unusable," "garbage," and "a nightmare" because "a lot of the content doesn't feel authentic." Since Google holds a 90 percent market share for online search, that commercial shaping reaches nearly every informational query, destroying "the illusion that the internet was ever about anything other than selling stuff."


---


# Google's default-search deal with Apple dates to 2003

In its 2023-10-31 report on the U.S. antitrust trial against Google, TechCrunch stated that "Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003." That is the agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices, so it had been running roughly twenty years by the time the deal's cost came under scrutiny in court in late October 2023.


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Contents index: TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup of US v Google

This TechCrunch roundup of November 13, 2023 indexes five sections. First, why US v Google matters and the remedies at stake before Judge Amit Mehta: sharing APIs, bans on anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, and surrendering data — the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. Second, Google's concurrent antitrust matters: the Match Group settlement and the November 6 trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games over Google Play. Third, the declassified list of 20 search terms ordered by revenue for the week of September 22, 2018, and vertical search. Fourth, Jamie Rosenberg's November 8 testimony on MADA (11 pre-loaded Google apps) and RSA mechanics. Fifth, Expedia and Barry Diller on ad load.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. That same roundup reported Google had tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Both facts were carried into TechCrunch's roundup published on November 13, 2023.


---


# Google's Drummond Called Microsoft's Search Default Anticompetitive in 2005

In 2005, after Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, Google legal chief David Drummond wrote to Microsoft arguing that the default was anticompetitive, according to a TechCrunch report dated 2023-10-31 on the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google. Drummond's letter rested on a claim about user behavior: most end users "do not change defaults," so the engine picked at the outset keeps the searches.


---


# Default placement, not search quality, sets rivals' scale — the testable counterfactual from Google antitrust testimony

A testable proposition emerging from testimony in the U.S. government's Google antitrust trial (TechCrunch, 2023-10-31): a search engine of comparable product quality given equal access to paid default placement would reach competitive scale in online search. The evidence base is rival executives' own accounts. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make deals with Apple like Google's — a deal in place since 2003. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search. The proposition is falsified if a rival granted default placement of that kind failed to grow share, and it is the direct negation of Google's defense that it is default because it is the best.

qid: Did TechCrunch report on Google's antitrust battle with Epic Games on November 6, 2024, and then report on a class action antitrust suit against Google on December 15, 2023, resulting in an inconsistent portrayal of Google's legal challenges related to anticompetitive practices?
context:
# Epic v. Google as a Four-Year Sequence, Originating in a September 2019 Plan Email

The Epic Games v. Google antitrust proceeding reads as a dated four-year chain rather than a single lawsuit. Its causal origin is a September 2019 email surfaced in discovery, describing Epic's plan to draw Google into a legal battle over antitrust — the document that predates and sets up everything after it. That plan became a four-week federal antitrust trial before a nine-person jury, which found on Monday, December 11, 2023 that Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems and illegally tied Google Play billing to its app store. The Verge's December 12, 2023 interview with Epic CEO Tim Sweeney frames the verdict as "four years in the making." Sweeney dates his own suspicion of Google's practices to 2018, one year earlier than the email.


---


# Google faced three search and app-store antitrust trials at once in mid-November 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was simultaneously litigating three antitrust matters touching search and app distribution, according to a TechCrunch report dated November 13, 2023. First, the Justice Department's landmark case against Google over search was roughly two months in, before Judge Amit Mehta. Second, Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the previous week. Third, on November 6, 2023 Google went to trial against Fortnite maker Epic Games, which sought to prove Google engages in anticompetitive behavior regarding its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure.


---


# Google antitrust actions surrounding the Helena World Chronicle publisher suit, December 2023

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and covered by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, arrived while several other Google proceedings were live. This note indexes that surrounding docket.

- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (digital ad technology): the DOJ's monopoly suit over Google's ad-tech stack, pending alongside the publisher case in late 2023.
- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (2020): the earlier civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.
- Epic Games v. Google: the app-store antitrust case, which Epic won; the Helena complaint borrows its finding of improper spoliation of evidence — Google's destruction of chat messages.
- Canada settlement (November 2023): Google agreed to pay Canadian media $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) a year, distributed by newsroom headcount. Meta's negotiations remained unresolved; Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August.


---


# Epic v. Google trial notes index — November 6, 2023

These notes cover TechCrunch's November 6, 2023 report on Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google, which began November 6, 2023 over Google Play and its commission structure. Sections: legal theory and statutes (Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2, Cartwright Act, Unfair Competition Law, the Microsoft/Netscape precedent); the two relevant markets; commissions and User Choice Billing; OEM agreements, AFAs and Project Hug; and Google's defenses.


---


# Publisher's Google antitrust suit alleges spoliation of chat messages, echoing Epic Games case

The class action antitrust suit that Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023 alleges evidence of improper spoliation by Google — specifically the destruction of chat messages. The complaint ties that allegation to a known precedent: the same issue of destroyed chat messages was raised in Epic Games' recent lawsuit against Google over app-store antitrust conduct, a case Epic won. The spoliation claim sits alongside the suit's other concerns, including allegedly changed AdSense rates, and appears among the counts supporting its requests for damages and injunctive relief against Google.


---


# Epic's Twin Antitrust Suits Diverged: Apple Settled in 2021, Google Waited to 2023

Epic Games sued Apple and Google on the same day, August 13th, 2020, both over in-app payment fees critics call the "Apple tax" and "Google tax," but the two cases then moved at wildly different speeds. The Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021, and a ruling came down that September mostly in Apple's favor, with both parties still waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in. The Google suit never got its day in court during those years, delayed again and again, so that Epic v. Google trial beginning November 6th, 2023 arrived "a mere 1,180 days" after Epic filed, per The Verge's article dated 2023-11-05.


---


# Epic's Antitrust Argument Against Apple Mostly Failed at Trial

Epic's antitrust argument against Apple did not succeed as its "Apple tax" campaign implied. In The Verge's explainer of Epic v. Google, published November 5th, 2023, the Apple suit is described as having gone to court in 2021, with a ruling that September "mostly decided in Apple's favor" — Epic failed to #FreeFortnite with its Llamacorn legal gambit, the August 13th, 2020 hotfix that let players buy V-Bucks directly through Epic's own payment processing and got Fortnite pulled from Apple's and Google's app stores for breaking the rules. The judge also picked a market definition "different entirely" from the one Epic pressed, and both parties ended up waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in.


---


# Sherman Act: the U.S. antitrust statute behind Epic's claims against Google

The Sherman Act is the U.S. antitrust statute Epic Games planned to invoke against Google at the trial that began November 6, 2023, taking Section 1 and Section 2 claims alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. Section 1 concerns restraints of competition; Section 2 concerns monopolization. Epic's case rested on arguing that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.


---


# Google Weaponized Epic's Internal Messages at Trial, November 2023

In opening statements in Epic Games' antitrust suit over the Google Play Store, covered by The Verge on 2023-11-07, Google displayed Epic's own internal messages to the jury, including "How do we not look like the bad guys?" and "everything we're attempting is technically a violation of Google's policy, right?" Shown without surrounding context, those lines served Google's effort to recast Epic — which had opened by painting itself as the underdog up against a bully and a cheat — as a company that knew it was breaking the rules while it was doing so.


---


# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Cartwright Act and California Unfair Competition Law in Epic v. Google

In its trial against Google over the Google Play store and its commission structure, which began November 6, 2023, Epic Games plans to plead two California anticompetitive statutes — the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law — alongside federal claims under Sections 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act. The state-law claims are the Californian legal basis for Epic's argument that Google restrains competition in Android app distribution and in payment processing for content inside Android apps.

# Wang's courtroom admission named Bankman-Fried, Singh and Ellison in his FTX frauds

Gary Wang's account of his own FTX criminality reached past himself to named others. Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos on Thursday 5 October 2023, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?", Wang answered "Yes," and said those crimes — wire and commodities fraud — were carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research. When Roos asked whether he saw any of those people in the courtroom, Wang stood, looked around, said "Yes," and identified "Sam Bankman-Fried." The argument's force is a sworn guilty plea, tempered by his six-page cooperation agreement and the up to 50 years in prison he still faces at sentencing.


---


# Caroline Ellison's $14 Billion Testimony, Week Two of the SBF Trial

In week two of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud and money laundering trial, reported by TechCrunch's Jacquelyn Melinek on 2023-10-06, the standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison. She claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. The case against Bankman-Fried covers seven counts tied to fraud and money laundering.


---


# Caroline Ellison: Alameda Research head and prosecution's star witness in the FTX trial

Caroline Ellison ran Alameda Research, the sister hedge fund of the crypto exchange FTX, and had been a girlfriend of FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried. Per a CNBC report dated 2023-10-06 covering Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, she and FTX co-founder Gary Wang were integral members of Bankman-Fried's personal and professional inner circles, and both pleaded guilty in December 2022. Ellison is considered the prosecution's star witness and was expected to take the stand under a cooperation arrangement similar to Wang's.


---


# Caroline Ellison: Alameda's former head and cooperating witness against Bankman-Fried

Caroline Ellison led Alameda Research, the hedge fund at the center of the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX, and is the former girlfriend of its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried. She has already pleaded guilty to criminal charges in the case: fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering. Testifying for the prosecution on 2023-10-10, the first day she took the stand in Bankman-Fried's criminal trial, she listed those crimes and said that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes," adding, "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back." Bankman-Fried is the defendant on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy.

SOURCE: The Verge, "Sam Bankman-Fried was a terrible boyfriend," 2023-10-10


---


# SBF Denied Bail Awaiting His FTX Fraud Trial (October 2023)

As of the TechCrunch article dated 2023-10-02, Sam Bankman-Fried — the founder and head of the collapsed crypto exchange FTX, accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history" — had been denied bail while awaiting his trial. That trial was set to begin the following Tuesday in the Manhattan Federal Court, with SBF having pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.


---


# Bankman-Fried pleaded not guilty in January to fraud charges carrying up to 115 years

In January, Sam Bankman-Fried pleaded not guilty to all counts against him, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds, according to TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account of the FTX collapse. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.


---


# Caroline Ellison's "$14 billion" figure on the stand, 2023-10-10

Testifying at Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial on 2023-10-10, Caroline Ellison — head of Alameda Research during the implosion of Alameda and FTX, already pleaded guilty to fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — said Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes" and stated: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back." The remark, quoted at the end of The Verge's fifth paragraph, was repeated in the seventh as she described the losses.


---


# SBF Criminal Trial Began 2023-10-03 on Seven Counts of Fraud and Conspiracy

The highly anticipated criminal trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, began on Tuesday, 2023-10-03, according to a TechCrunch article dated 2023-10-01. The trial was to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. A former federal prosecutor quoted in the article said: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."


---


# Ellison's named-but-unpaid role at Alameda is the Verge author's worst-ex-boyfriend test case

In its October 10, 2023 report on Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial, The Verge's author bases her verdict that Caroline Ellison is the paradigmatically terrible ex-boyfriend case on a single swapped pair: Ellison was made the named head of Alameda Research, the hedge fund at the center of the FTX collapse, while being refused equity — the author's formulation is that no ex of hers "made me the CEO of their sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give me equity." The claim's force comes from a reversal of ownership and accountability, the person whose name carried the fund's sins holding none of its upside. The author confines the argument to her personal standing as a spurned partner, not the legal record: Ellison had already pleaded guilty to fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering before testifying that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes."


---


# Caroline Ellison's testimony on phony balance sheets and Alameda's use of customer funds

Caroline Ellison, Sam Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, testified at his trial that she created seven phony balance sheets. Writing in The Verge on 2023-10-26, the account of her testimony records that she was clear on two points: Alameda Research took customer funds, and Bankman-Fried knew about it. He even invested those customer funds against her advice. Ellison, alongside Gary Wang and Nishad Singh, is now a felon, with their lives irrevocably changed by possible imprisonment, house arrest, restitution requirements, barred job categories, and the publicity.


---


# Cooperation Agreement at the Bankman-Fried Trial

A cooperation agreement, in the sense used at Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX fraud trial, is a written deal with the U.S. attorney's office in Manhattan under which a defendant who has pleaded guilty testifies for the government. Gary Wang, 30, FTX's technology chief, told jurors on Friday, Oct. 6, 2023 that his six-page cooperation agreement obliges him to meet with prosecutors, answer their questions truthfully and turn over evidence. He and Alameda Research's Caroline Ellison had pleaded guilty in December and have since been cooperating with that office.


---


# Nishad Singh's Guilty Plea: Backdated FTX Transactions and Doctored Balance Sheets

Nishad Singh, described as a longtime family friend of Sam Bankman-Fried, admitted to conduct that sounded like classic embezzlement while testifying during Bankman-Fried's trial. Singh said he backdated transactions at FTX in order to help produce doctored balance sheets to show to investors. He pleaded guilty to six charges: wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts concerning his political donations. This testimony comes from reporting by The Verge dated 2023-10-26, written as the prosecution's case against Bankman-Fried — charged with seven counts, two of wire fraud and five of conspiracy — was closing. Singh had already become a felon by that time.

qid: Does the article from The Verge defending Apple's Google Search deal suggest that there was no valid alternative to Google for search engine services, while the other article from The Verge about the public and media's understanding of search engines imply a frustration with the public's knowledge of how search engines work?
context:
# Cue's 2023-09-26 "No Valid Alternative" Argument for Apple's Google Default

Testifying on 2023-09-26 in US v. Google, Apple's Eddy Cue argued that Apple never seriously considered switching to another search provider or building its own search product, because "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time." He said there still isn't one.

The claim's scope is the 2016 renegotiation period, when Cue negotiated the current iteration of the Information Services Agreement (ISA) with Google CEO Sundar Pichai — the deal, in place since 2002, that makes Google the default search engine on Apple devices and pays Apple billions of dollars a year.

Cue's warrant was that the choice was product-driven rather than purely economic: the ISA is Apple's own evaluation, and he said "We make Google be the default search engine because we've always thought it was the best. We pick the best one and let users easily change it." Supporting that, he told DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw he'd never really considered walking away from the deal.


---


# Index: Eddy Cue testifies for Apple in US v. Google (The Verge, 2023-09-26)

Index to The Verge's 2023-09-26 report on Eddy Cue testifying in US v. Google, the DOJ antitrust trial over Google's search business, before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC. Sub-topics covered:

- **The ISA**: the Information Services Agreement making Google default search on all Apple devices, in place since 2002 and renegotiated by Cue with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016.

# DOJ's theory in *US v. Google*: default deals capture search entry points

In *US v. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. Reporting on Apple executive Eddy Cue's testimony on 2023-09-26, The Verge states that the Justice Department is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.


---


# Default search engine, as defined in US v. Google

In US v. Google, the antitrust trial over Google's search business, Eddy Cue testified on 2023-09-26 about what a "default search engine" means in practice: the engine preselected on a device, which a user must actively change rather than choose. Apple fixes that default to Google through the Information Services Agreement (ISA), in place since 2002, whose current iteration Cue negotiated with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. Cue acknowledged that the ISA doesn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup. Whether Google is "easily" changed is contested: DuckDuckGo's CEO testified it takes "too many steps."


---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# SEO's Spread Has Made Ordinary Searches commercially Shaped (The Verge, 2023)

Reporting for The Verge on 2023-11-01 argues that the harm from search engine optimization is no longer confined to sites built for it. The article states that "over time, SEO techniques have spread and become insidious, such that googling anything can now feel like looking up 'sneaker' in the dictionary and finding a definition that sounds both incorrect and suspiciously as though it were written by someone promoting Nike." By 2023, users described Google Search results as "absolutely unusable," "garbage," and "a nightmare" because "a lot of the content doesn't feel authentic." Since Google holds a 90 percent market share for online search, that commercial shaping reaches nearly every informational query, destroying "the illusion that the internet was ever about anything other than selling stuff."

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."

# Why a rapid Epic v. Google verdict did not mean Epic had lost

A quick jury decision is easy to misread as proof the plaintiffs' case was weak or that jurors never engaged with it. A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. In his courtroom account that The Verge described on 2023-10-28 as "the story of FTX, from his point of view," Sam Bankman-Fried began by informing the jury he is "somewhat introverted, naturally," then launched into a prolonged tour of his pre-Alameda Research life that the reporter skipped. Only after that detour did he reach 2017. The same morning included explanations of "Amazon Web Services" and "database."


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's path from Alameda Research to FTX, per TechCrunch

Before his criminal trial began in October 2023, Sam Bankman-Fried — aged 31 at the time, facing seven counts of fraud and conspiracy — had built the crypto firm FTX on the back of an earlier venture. Per TechCrunch's reporting on 2023-10-01, he co-founded the crypto-trading firm Alameda Research in 2017, then co-founded FTX in 2019 as a complement to it, to bring in revenue and liquidity for the trading arm. FTX became the third-largest crypto exchange, reaching a peak valuation of $32 billion.


---


# Bankman-Fried's Account of When He Learned About fiat@ftx, October 2022

Testifying at his own trial on 2023-10-31, reported by The Verge, Sam Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account — the account tracking how much Alameda owed FTX — in June 2022, while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug. He said he did not discover what the account was for until October.

# Index: "Sam Bankman-Fried didn't ask where the $8 billion went" (The Verge, Oct 31, 2023)

Navigation index for The Verge's October 31, 2023 courtroom report on the June 2022 thread of Sam Bankman-Fried's self-testimony at his fraud trial — seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. The decomposition entries attach to these parts of the article: the software bug overestimating Alameda's debt to FTX by about $8 billion, found by Adam Yedidia; Bankman-Fried's discovery of the fiat@ftx account in June 2022 but not its purpose until October; staff telling him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting"; his "no, no, and no" on directions, policies and measures protecting FTX customer money; Yedidia's padel tennis court exchange in June or July, and Judge Lewis Kaplan's intervention; and the Alameda balance sheet of June 13, 2022 listing the borrowed money as "ftx borrows."

# Alameda Research: Bankman-Fried's 2017 crypto arbitrage trading firm

Alameda Research is the cryptocurrency trading firm Sam Bankman-Fried started in 2017, during a crypto bull run. Testifying at his own fraud trial on October 28, 2023, Bankman-Fried told the jury he knew "basically nothing" about cryptocurrency at the time he founded it, but said he wanted to do arbitrage on it anyway. He described the firm's early arbitrage trading as wildly successful, citing annualized returns of 50 percent to 100 percent, before he went on to found the cryptocurrency exchange FTX. Bankman-Fried was the CEO and majority owner of Alameda Research.


---


# FTX funding made Bankman-Fried's parents and brother politically undesirable

Sam Bankman-Fried's family lost the political access FTX money had once bought them, according to The Verge's account of his fraud trial on 2023-10-26. Joe Bankman and Barbara Fried — whose political action committee, Mind the Gap, was among the entities to receive FTX customer money as political donations, and who an FTX bankruptcy estate lawsuit alleges were given $10 million of that money — and Gabe Bankman-Fried, whose nonprofit Guarding Against Pandemics received millions from FTX, are described as having tarnished reputations. In the political arenas where they once operated, the article writes, they are suddenly undesirable.

# FTX's Spot Margin Program Was Not Equivalent to Alameda's Credit Line

During cross-examination of FTX chief technology officer Gary Wang on 2023-10-10, at Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial, defense attorney Christian Everdell raised FTX's spot margin program as a counter to Wang's claim that Alameda Research received a special credit line. The two arrangements look alike but are not equivalent. Wang had testified that Alameda got access to a special credit line and an option to take its balance into the negative without triggering liquidation — something he alleged other accounts at FTX didn't get. The spot margin program let users lend each other assets for margin trading, and in those cases it was possible to have a negative balance in a specific coin. An FTX software bug overestimated the amount that Alameda Research owed to FTX by about $8 billion, according to testimony at Sam Bankman-Fried's wire-fraud trial reported by The Verge on 2023-10-31. # Alameda Research: FTX's sister hedge fund, run by Caroline Ellison

Alameda Research was the hedge fund operating as the sister firm to the bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, run by Caroline Ellison, who had been Sam Bankman-Fried's girlfriend. Media reporting in November 2022 detailed Alameda's business practices and its troubling ties to FTX, which Bankman-Fried's co-founder Gary Wang later described in October 2023 trial testimony. qid: Which company, according to TechCrunch articles, invested $26.3 billion in 2021 to maintain its status as the primary search engine on multiple devices and is also accused of harming news publishers' revenue and content through anticompetitive practices?

# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. That same roundup reported Google had tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Both facts were carried into TechCrunch's roundup published on November 13, 2023.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

Testifying on 28 October 2023 in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan stated that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phone makers and platforms for making Google the default search engine. Recipients included the companies Apple, Samsung and Mozilla. Of that $26.3 billion total, roughly $18 billion went directly to Apple, under a Google–Apple search deal in place since 2003.


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Apple took roughly $18 billion of Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default payments

Of the $26.3 billion Google paid in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be the default search engine, about $18 billion went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023. TechCrunch reported the figure on October 31, 2023, during the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google; the Google–Apple default deal had been in place since 2003.

The central harm asserted in the class action antitrust complaint filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. is that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars." The plaintiff, Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, brings the claim against Google and parent company Alphabet under the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust law, framing Google's redistribution of news content inside its own products as anticompetitive conduct that diverts publishers' content, readers and ad revenue.

# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." # Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. # Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. # Index — Five revelations from the Google antitrust trial, 30–31 October 2023

A breakdown published by TechCrunch on 30–31 October 2023, anchored on Google CEO Sundar Pichai's Monday testimony in the U.S. government's antitrust trial over Google's 2020-era search dominance, organizes the week's disclosures into five points.

1. Default-payment totals: $26.3 billion paid in 2021 across browsers, phones and platforms including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, roughly $18 billion of it to Apple, per search head Prabhakar Raghavan's 28 October testimony.

3. The iPhone preinstall bid: Pichai's 2018 attempt to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device.

# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.

# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.

# Rosenberg's Nov 8 Defense of Google's Android Pre-install and RSA Payments

In the US v Google antitrust trial, Jamie Rosenberg, a Google employee who focuses on Android and Google Play, testified on November 8, 2023 in Google's defense that the deals putting Google Search and Chrome on Android amount to fair competition rather than exclusion. Rosenberg described a mobile app distribution agreement (MADA) that requires Android smartphone makers such as Samsung or Oppo to pre-load a bundle of 11 Google apps, including Search, Chrome and Play, and stressed that those apps need not be the default choices, according to Bloomberg's account of the testimony. Rosenberg also cited revenue share agreements (RSAs) with smartphone makers and wireless carriers such as Verizon — payments that, in Google's telling, reward partners for building and selling more Android devices, in a rivalry with Apple he called "as intense as it gets."


---


# "Walled garden" in The Verge's Epic v. Google coverage: a closed platform controlling distribution and payment

In its December 12, 2023 account of Epic's jury verdict against Google, The Verge sets "walled garden" in quotation marks as a descriptor for Apple — Epic's "rival," which the piece notes "almost entirely won a similar case two years ago." In that usage, the term denotes a closed mobile platform whose owner controls both app distribution and in-app payment: the same two powers the nine-person federal jury found Google held an illegal monopoly over, in "Android app distribution and in-app payment systems," and had illegally tied together through "its Google Play billing system to its app store." Apple's verdict, by contrast, went Epic's way only in part.


---


# Google's counter-argument: iPhone substitution, not Android app stores, defines the market

Google rebutted Epic's market definition in Epic v. Google — which went to trial on Nov. 6, 2023, some 1,180 days after Epic first sued — by arguing the real competition is Apple, because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead. On that view, Google's app store competes with Apple's across platforms, so it is "pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general." Epic's contrary position: Android app distribution and Android in-app payment processing are each their own market.


---


# Revenue Share Agreement (RSA): Google's Payment Deal for Default Search and Chrome

A revenue share agreement (RSA) is the payment arrangement Google strikes with Android device makers and wireless carriers, conditioning Google's money on those partners setting Google Search and the Chrome browser as the defaults on the devices they ship. Jamie Rosenberg, a Google employee who focuses on Android and Google Play, described the structure while testifying in Google's defense on November 8, 2023, in the Justice Department's antitrust trial against Google (US v Google). He contrasted RSAs, held with makers and with carriers such as Verizon, with the mobile app distribution agreement (MADA): that requires Android smartphone makers like Samsung or Oppo to pre-load a bundle of 11 Google apps, including Search, Chrome and Play, which he said need not be defaults. TechCrunch reported this on November 13, 2023.


---


# DOJ's Theory of Harm in the Google Antitrust Case: Defaults Cut Rivals Off From Data

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The theory therefore runs in two linked steps: owned distribution plus paid defaults deny rivals visibility, and denied visibility denies them the query data that would let their products reach a quality high enough to challenge Google. The claim over Google's dominance in the online search market was filed in 2020. It is separate from a claim filed in January by the Department of Justice along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind its monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising. Google's counter is that it is simply doing business, since partners want the best default engine.
