qid: What company, as reported by TechCrunch, spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to maintain its default search engine status on multiple devices and is also accused of harming news publishers' revenue and content through anticompetitive practices?
context:
# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. That same roundup reported Google had tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Both facts were carried into TechCrunch's roundup published on November 13, 2023.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

Testifying on 28 October 2023 in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan stated that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phone makers and platforms for making Google the default search engine. Recipients included the companies Apple, Samsung and Mozilla. Of that $26.3 billion total, roughly $18 billion went directly to Apple, under a Google–Apple search deal in place since 2003.


---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Apple took roughly $18 billion of Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default payments

Of the $26.3 billion Google paid in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be the default search engine, about $18 billion went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023. TechCrunch reported the figure on October 31, 2023, during the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google; the Google–Apple default deal had been in place since 2003.


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.


---


# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# Google–Apple Search Deal: Payment for Default Placement, Restraint on Chrome

Under the Google–Apple search deal, in place since 2003, Google pays Apple for default search placement in Safari: of the $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults across browsers, phones and platforms in 2021, about $18 billion went to Apple, according to testimony in the U.S. antitrust trial reported by TechCrunch on October 31, 2023.

The consideration flowing back to Apple is restraint. Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, per Bloomberg, though Google had the means to do so through banners, pop-ups and similar prompts inside its other applications. That term's effect on Apple's own conduct: Apple never switched to a Google competitor as its search engine and never let iPhone users choose a browser when setting up their devices.


---


# Index — Five revelations from the Google antitrust trial, 30–31 October 2023

A breakdown published by TechCrunch on 30–31 October 2023, anchored on Google CEO Sundar Pichai's Monday testimony in the U.S. government's antitrust trial over Google's 2020-era search dominance, organizes the week's disclosures into five points.

1. Default-payment totals: $26.3 billion paid in 2021 across browsers, phones and platforms including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, roughly $18 billion of it to Apple, per search head Prabhakar Raghavan's 28 October testimony.
2. The Chrome-promotion ban: Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users.
3. The iPhone preinstall bid: Pichai's 2018 attempt to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device.
4. Deleted chat logs: history-off default vs. the DOJ's litigation hold.
5. Google's early letter on defaults: a 2007 email citing 15% and 27% swings.


---


# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Microsoft and DuckDuckGo CEOs Tied Their Search Shortfalls to Missing Apple Default Deals

Earlier in October 2023, in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search. Reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, citing The Information.

# Epic's Sideloading Problem: The Obvious Weakness in Its Google Antitrust Case

The most obvious objection to the case Epic Games brought against Google, tried from November 6, 2023, is structural: Android permits sideloading apps, so Epic cannot allege there is no alternative path to install apps on the platform — the claim it made against Apple, where no such route exists. That distinction is why the Google trial "will differ slightly" from the Apple fight. Epic's fallback, that Google makes sideloading cumbersome, is a weaker position than a closed door, and it leaves the bulk of the case resting on agreements with device manufacturers and developers rather than on any outright installation ban.


---


# Epic's Google case rests on the Microsoft browser-monopoly precedent

Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google, which began on November 6, 2023 and concerns Google Play's app distribution and its 15% to 30% commissions, is analogically dependent on the Microsoft antitrust rulings, as reported by TechCrunch. In those earlier cases, courts found that Microsoft had a monopoly over the operating system and was abusing it by making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. The analogy carries weight because Android, unlike Apple's iOS, permits sideloading — so Epic's theory of the case runs on a dominant platform owner's agreements constraining rivals rather than on the absence of any alternative.


---


# Epic v. Google reached trial 1,180 days after Epic first sued

Epic v. Google went to trial on 2023-11-06, "a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued," according to The Verge's 2023-11-05 explainer. The delay is the comparison: Epic's parallel antitrust suit against Apple — both filed after the 2020-08-13 Fortnite hotfix and the app stores' removal of the game — went to court in 2021, with a ruling that September mostly in Apple's favor. The Google case was "delayed again and again" until late 2023.

# Epic v. Google trial notes index — November 6, 2023

These notes cover TechCrunch's November 6, 2023 report on Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google, which began November 6, 2023 over Google Play and its commission structure. Sections: legal theory and statutes (Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2, Cartwright Act, Unfair Competition Law, the Microsoft/Netscape precedent); the two relevant markets; commissions and User Choice Billing; OEM agreements, AFAs and Project Hug; and Google's defenses.

# Epic's OEM evidence: the cancelled OnePlus deal and the Google–Samsung agreement

Epic Games' antitrust case against Google, tried from November 6, 2023, leads with an agreement theory, because Android allows sideloading and Epic cannot claim, as it did against Apple, that no other way exists to load apps. Two episodes carry that theory. Epic had an agreement with the device maker OnePlus to make Epic games available on OnePlus devices through the Epic Games app, and OnePlus cancelled the deal over concerns that the arrangement would have it bypassing the Google Play Store. The trial will also examine a deal between Google and Samsung that Epic says was designed to prevent the Galaxy Store from becoming a competitive threat and to require Google Play Billing on apps distributed by Samsung. Epic places both inside the "Anti-Fragmentation Agreements" (AFAs) it cites, which prevent Android OEMs from modifying Android to allow frictionless downloading of apps outside Google Play.


---


# Epic's case against Google is weakened by never naming a reasonable store fee

Epic Games' antitrust case against Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023 — 1,180 days after Epic originally sued — argues that Google holds illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," and that developers buying for or publishing on Android are stuck paying the "Google tax." One criticism aimed at Epic's position is that it wants something for nothing: Epic has never stated what fee it would consider reasonable for Google to charge for placement in the Google Play app store. Rather than naming a defensible figure, Epic CEO Tim Sweeney instead implies that a developer who uses its own payment system should pay Google nothing at all for store listing. That silence leaves Epic's target vague: it opposes the current fee without ever describing the competitive price a court could order.

Google trial beginning November 6th, 2023 arrived "a mere 1,180 days" after Epic filed, per The Verge's article dated 2023-11-05.

# Judge Rogers' Market Definition Gave Apple the Epic Case — and Haunts Google

In Epic's antitrust case against Apple, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers defined the relevant market for Fortnite as "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than iPhone apps, and that definitional choice carried much of Apple's mostly favorable September 2021 victory. It is the precedent hanging over Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023 — a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued. There, Epic's proposed markets are "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing"; Google counters that the real competition is the iPhone.

# Epic's Core Argument: Google's OEM and Developer Agreements Are Unlawful Restraints

Epic Games' claim against Google, tried from November 6, 2023, rests on one argument: Google's agreements with Android device manufacturers and app developers are anticompetitive restraints under Sections 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act and under California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law, regardless of whether Android permits sideloading.

# Epic frames two separate markets in its Google antitrust case

In its antitrust trial against Google, which began November 6, 2023, Epic Games — the Fortnite maker — frames Google as restraining competition in two separate markets rather than one: the distribution of apps to Android users, and payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps. Epic brings the case under Sections 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act, the U.S. antitrust law, and under California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. The split lets Epic attack two distinct sets of contracts: Google's agreements with Android device manufacturers and developers, and Google's requirement that apps use its own first-party billing system, which charges a 15% to 30% commission on the sales it processes.


---


# Sherman Act: the U.S. antitrust statute behind Epic's claims against Google

The Sherman Act is the U.S. antitrust statute Epic Games planned to invoke against Google at the trial that began November 6, 2023, taking Section 1 and Section 2 claims alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. Section 1 concerns restraints of competition; Section 2 concerns monopolization. Epic's case rested on arguing that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.


---


# Epic's price-harm claim rests on monopoly-set app store and payment fees

Epic's case against Google depends on one relation: that Google's app-store and payment-processing terms are set by monopoly power rather than by competition, and that the consequence is consumers pay more for apps than they would in a contested market. Epic's earlier legal filings suggested this upshot for consumers — higher prices for apps than there would be "if there were more competition and / or lower app store and payment processing fees." Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein argued the same structure at the opening described by The Verge on 2023-11-07, showing jurors 70 percent app profit margins on $12 billion in revenue a year, per Epic, and Google "pay[ing] actual and potential competitors not to compete." Epic sued Google in 2020 over in-app purchase fees. The claim fails if the fee levels would persist under competition.


---


# Epic's Two Named Monopoly Markets in Epic v. Google: Android App Distribution and Android In-App Payment Processing

In Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023 — a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued — Epic Games names two markets in which it alleges Google holds illegal monopolies: "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing." Epic's theory is that if you buy or develop for Android phones, you are stuck paying the "Google tax," the in-app payment fee that attached to a Fortnite V-Bucks purchase until August 13th, 2020. The dispute over those boundaries is "market definition": the narrower the market, the stronger Epic's monopoly claim.


---


# Epic v. Google as a Four-Year Sequence, Originating in a September 2019 Plan Email

The Epic Games v. Google antitrust proceeding reads as a dated four-year chain rather than a single lawsuit. Its causal origin is a September 2019 email surfaced in discovery, describing Epic's plan to draw Google into a legal battle over antitrust — the document that predates and sets up everything after it. That plan became a four-week federal antitrust trial before a nine-person jury, which found on Monday, December 11, 2023 that Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems and illegally tied Google Play billing to its app store. The Verge's December 12, 2023 interview with Epic CEO Tim Sweeney frames the verdict as "four years in the making." Sweeney dates his own suspicion of Google's practices to 2018, one year earlier than the email.


---


# Publisher's Google antitrust suit alleges spoliation of chat messages, echoing Epic Games case

The class action antitrust suit that Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023 alleges evidence of improper spoliation by Google — specifically the destruction of chat messages. The complaint ties that allegation to a known precedent: the same issue of destroyed chat messages was raised in Epic Games' recent lawsuit against Google over app-store antitrust conduct, a case Epic won. The spoliation claim sits alongside the suit's other concerns, including allegedly changed AdSense rates, and appears among the counts supporting its requests for damages and injunctive relief against Google.


---


# Judge Rogers' Market Definition Gave Apple the Epic Case — and Haunts Google

In Epic's antitrust case against Apple, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers defined the relevant market for Fortnite as "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than iPhone apps, and that definitional choice carried much of Apple's mostly favorable September 2021 victory. It is the precedent hanging over Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023 — a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued. There, Epic's proposed markets are "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing"; Google counters that the real competition is the iPhone.


---


# Epic's August 13, 2020 Fortnite hotfix triggered app-store removals and two antitrust suits

On August 13th, 2020, Epic Games, the studio behind Fortnite — a free-to-play game that sells in-game items with its virtual currency V-Bucks — publicly announced it was bypassing Apple and Google's app store fees. It deployed a hotfix update to Fortnite without either company's knowledge, letting players purchase V-Bucks directly through Epic's own payment processing option at a discount. Until that date, such purchases on Android or iOS devices installed through an official app store triggered an in-app payment fee to Google or Apple. Apple and Google almost immediately reacted by kicking Fortnite off their app stores for breaking the rules. Then Epic, per The Verge's November 5th, 2023 account, sprung a pre-planned response: two lawsuits and an attack ad depicting a Fortnite hero throwing a unicorn-llama hammer into a giant screen reminiscent of Apple's famous "1984" Macintosh ad.


---


# Epic's Android App Distribution Monopoly Claim Against Google

In Epic Games' antitrust suit against Google, whose trial began on November 6th, 2023, Epic's core argument concerns Android app distribution. Epic argues that Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that Google has created an illegal monopoly. The claimed harms are twofold: the monopoly unjustly enriches Google, and it artificially drives up app prices, because other app stores can't compete. Epic calls the standard in-app payment fees the "Google tax". The remedy Epic seeks is to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods, so that developers aren't stuck paying that tax or passing the fee along to players.

Source: The Verge, "Epic v. Google, explained" (2023-11-05).


---


# Epic's case against Google is weakened by never naming a reasonable store fee

Epic Games' antitrust case against Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023 — 1,180 days after Epic originally sued — argues that Google holds illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," and that developers buying for or publishing on Android are stuck paying the "Google tax." One criticism aimed at Epic's position is that it wants something for nothing: Epic has never stated what fee it would consider reasonable for Google to charge for placement in the Google Play app store. Rather than naming a defensible figure, Epic CEO Tim Sweeney instead implies that a developer who uses its own payment system should pay Google nothing at all for store listing. That silence leaves Epic's target vague: it opposes the current fee without ever describing the competitive price a court could order.


---


# Epic's own mention of Project Liberty blunts Google's bad-faith angle

Google's attempt to cast Epic's Project Liberty as proof of bad faith runs into one complication: in the opening statements of Epic's 2020 monopoly suit against Google, reported by The Verge on 2023-11-07, Epic mentioned Project Liberty in its own opening. A fact the jury hears first from the side it is supposed to embarrass lands as disclosure, not exposure — so the same detail is a weaker sting when Google reaches for it later. Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein spoke first, portraying Google as a bully that pays competitors not to compete.

context:
# The Sam Bankman-Fried Fraud Trial Before Judge Lewis Kaplan

The Sam Bankman-Fried fraud trial is the six-week federal criminal proceeding over the collapse of the bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, held in a Manhattan courtroom before U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan and begun in early October 2023. The trial is scheduled to resume on Tuesday 10 October 2023 with key testimony expected from Caroline Ellison, the prosecution's star witness. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges.


---


# Judge Kaplan Forced a Concession on Whether Yedidia Warned Bankman-Fried About the $8 Billion

Adam Yedidia — Sam Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — testified that he had asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July 2022. In his own testimony on 2023-10-31, The Verge reported, Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny that conversation ever took place. Only after Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had told him about that money, "in words or in substance," did Bankman-Fried admit he had been told.


---


# Ellison's named-but-unpaid role at Alameda is the Verge author's worst-ex-boyfriend test case

In its October 10, 2023 report on Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial, The Verge's author bases her verdict that Caroline Ellison is the paradigmatically terrible ex-boyfriend case on a single swapped pair: Ellison was made the named head of Alameda Research, the hedge fund at the center of the FTX collapse, while being refused equity — the author's formulation is that no ex of hers "made me the CEO of their sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give me equity." The claim's force comes from a reversal of ownership and accountability, the person whose name carried the fund's sins holding none of its upside. The author confines the argument to her personal standing as a spurned partner, not the legal record: Ellison had already pleaded guilty to fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering before testifying that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes."


---


# Know what "epistemology" means? Don't testify in your own defense

The Verge's FTX trial reporter (31 Oct 2023) draws one rule from Sam Bankman-Fried's cross-examination by Danielle Sassoon: "if you know the meaning of the word 'epistemology,' you absolutely should not testify in your own defense." Wire-fraud liability turns on what a defendant knew and when he asked — so Bankman-Fried's quarrels over precision ("hole isn't really the word I would use"; wanting "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it") wrote the jury the record of his own inquiry. He conceded he knew of the fiat@ftx account in June 2022 but not its purpose until October, and admitted Judge Lewis Kaplan pressed him into admitting Adam Yedidia had told him about the missing $8 billion.


---


# The Verge's Assessment: Prosecution Built a Strong Case of Orchestration and Direct Participation by Bankman-Fried

In a column published 2023-10-26, as the government's case against Sam Bankman-Fried neared its end, The Verge argued that the prosecution "has made a strong case" that Bankman-Fried presided over the various forms of fraud played out at his trading firm Alameda Research and at the FTX exchange — orchestrating some of that conduct and engaging in some of it directly. Bankman-Fried then faced seven counts: two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges. The claim's scope is explicitly limited to the trial evidence presented up to that date, and it is a journalist's assessment of the government's persuasiveness rather than any verdict — testimony still to come included from former colleagues who had already pleaded guilty and were felons.


---


# The judge, not the witness, defines legal terms like "market manipulation"

During Sam Bankman-Fried's direct testimony at his FTX trial on 2023-10-28, reported by The Verge, Bankman-Fried offered his own definition of "market manipulation." Judge Lewis Kaplan cut in and told the jury that he, Kaplan, was the final authority on that term. The morning had already been spent largely explaining vocabulary, including "Amazon Web Services" and "database," which the reporter judged too detail-oriented. The exchange illustrated a standing allocation of roles in the courtroom: the witness supplies facts within his experience, and the court supplies the legal meaning of charged terms such as market manipulation.


---


# Damian Williams: Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history"

At a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history," according to TechCrunch's report of 2023-10-01 — the public characterization by the prosecutor bringing the FTX case, as Bankman-Fried's criminal trial on fraud and conspiracy charges began.


---


# Prosecution's claim beyond diversion: concealed money flows and forged documents

In the opening statement reported by Fortune on 2023-10-04, prosecutor Thane Rehn pushed the government's case past the taking of FTX customer funds: Bankman-Fried allegedly directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers and forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged.


---


# Wang's courtroom admission named Bankman-Fried, Singh and Ellison in his FTX frauds

Gary Wang's account of his own FTX criminality reached past himself to named others. Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos on Thursday 5 October 2023, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?", Wang answered "Yes," and said those crimes — wire and commodities fraud — were carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research. When Roos asked whether he saw any of those people in the courtroom, Wang stood, looked around, said "Yes," and identified "Sam Bankman-Fried." The argument's force is a sworn guilty plea, tempered by his six-page cooperation agreement and the up to 50 years in prison he still faces at sentencing.


---


# Kaplan scolded Bankman-Fried for non-answers on two consecutive days at FTX trial

On two consecutive days at Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial, Judge Lewis Kaplan repeatedly scolded the defendant for not answering questions. Yesterday, during an evidentiary hearing, Kaplan scolded Bankman-Fried for not answering prosecutor Danielle Sassoon's questions on cross-examination. Today, 2023-10-28, Kaplan scolded Bankman-Fried for not answering his counsel Mark Cohen's questions on direct examination. Bankman-Fried also occasionally interrupted Cohen with "yes" and "yup." The repetition spans two distinct settings and two different examining lawyers, one adverse and one friendly.


---


# SEC Alleges FTX Was a Fraud "From the Start," Caused by Bankman-Fried's Own Misappropriation

The SEC's allegation against Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, goes further than the criminal charges he was facing at trial — seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. The Securities and Exchange Commission alleges that FTX was a fraud “from the start,” which frames the misstatement as running through the exchange's whole existence rather than arising only as it collapsed. The element that separates the SEC's theory from a plain story of a failed exchange is the source of the shortfall: it alleges a “multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds,” naming Bankman-Fried personally and specifying customer money as what went missing.


---


# SBF Faces Seven Counts of Fraud and Money Laundering from FTX and Alameda Leadership

Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO and co-founder of the collapsed crypto exchange FTX, faces seven counts tied to fraud and money laundering allegedly committed while leading FTX and its sister trading firm Alameda Research. As of October 6, 2023, the trial was entering the defense phase after the prosecution had concluded its case and Bankman-Fried was set to testify in his own defense.

qid: What company, which was reported by both TechCrunch and The Verge to be involved in antitrust cases, has spent billions to maintain its default search engine status across various platforms and is accused of harming news publishers' revenues through its competitive practices?
context:
# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. That same roundup reported Google had tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Both facts were carried into TechCrunch's roundup published on November 13, 2023.


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.


---


# DOJ's Theory of Harm in the Google Antitrust Case: Defaults Cut Rivals Off From Data

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The theory therefore runs in two linked steps: owned distribution plus paid defaults deny rivals visibility, and denied visibility denies them the query data that would let their products reach a quality high enough to challenge Google. The claim over Google's dominance in the online search market was filed in 2020. It is separate from a claim filed in January by the Department of Justice along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind its monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising. Google's counter is that it is simply doing business, since partners want the best default engine.


---


# Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.


---


# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

Testifying on 28 October 2023 in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan stated that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phone makers and platforms for making Google the default search engine. Recipients included the companies Apple, Samsung and Mozilla. Of that $26.3 billion total, roughly $18 billion went directly to Apple, under a Google–Apple search deal in place since 2003.


---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Default placement, not search quality, sets rivals' scale — the testable counterfactual from Google antitrust testimony

A testable proposition emerging from testimony in the U.S. government's Google antitrust trial (TechCrunch, 2023-10-31): a search engine of comparable product quality given equal access to paid default placement would reach competitive scale in online search. The evidence base is rival executives' own accounts. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make deals with Apple like Google's — a deal in place since 2003. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search. The proposition is falsified if a rival granted default placement of that kind failed to grow share, and it is the direct negation of Google's defense that it is default because it is the best.

qid: Which company, recently covered by TechCrunch, has been involved in showcasing new hardware developments at an annual event, has faced criticism for not releasing the full version of a product named Gemini Ultra, and is accused in a class action antitrust suit of harming news publishers' revenue through anticompetitive practices?
context:
# Gemini: Google's flagship AI family launched with only its "lite" member

Gemini is Google's flagship AI model family, unveiled in the week of 8 December 2023 and covered in TechCrunch's Week in Review of 9 December 2023. Only its "lite" member, Gemini Pro, was released; the full model, Gemini Ultra, was withheld. In a press briefing and blog posts, Google touted Gemini's coding capabilities and multimodal prowess, claiming the model can understand images, audio and videos just as well as text. Gemini Pro is strictly text-in, text-out and has proved mistake-prone. Google was also caught faking a Gemini demo, tuning text prompts with still images off camera.


---

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The list runs all the way to the ornamental — ChatGPT can even emulate a Linux machine. # ChatGPT — OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot

ChatGPT is OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot. It began as a tool to hyper-charge productivity: users write essays and code by feeding it short text prompts, and it composes the prose in response. ---

TechCrunch's hub article "ChatGPT: Everything you need to know about the AI-powered chatbot" (published 2023-09-28) splits into two navigational layers. ---


# Shang: ChatGPT's target shifted from domain-specific chatbots to general-purpose systems via prompting

Ruoxi Shang, a third-year PhD student at the University of Washington studying human-AI interaction, attributes part of ChatGPT's enduring popularity in a TechCrunch article published 2023-11-30 to a change in what such systems were built to be. Chatbots had existed for decades, but the models behind ChatGPT were far more sophisticated than what users were accustomed to. Training on vast data moved the design target away from specialized, domain-specific chatbots toward general-purpose systems that people drive through instruction prompting, on the condition that users need learn no new interaction language. Shang notes that "AI models have enabled conversational agents to conduct conversations nearly indistinguishable from human dialogues."

Stella Biderman, an AI researcher at Booz Allen Hamilton and the open research group EleutherAI, told TechCrunch on 2023-11-30 that ChatGPT's influence on the AI field came from lowering a barrier to use, not from a jump in capability. She does not consider it an AI breakthrough per se, but a "user experience breakthrough" that took generative AI mainstream — and its primary effect, she says, was "encouraging people training AIs to try to mimic it, or encouraging people studying AIs to use it as their central object of study." The mechanism she gives: "Previously you needed to have some skill, albeit not be an expert, to consistently get usable stuff out of [text-generating models]." Once that requirement disappeared, ChatGPT "brought a very large amount of attention to and discussion about the technology."

Adam Hyland, a PhD student studying AI at the University of Washington, draws out the emotional component of ChatGPT: conversations with it have a palpably different "feel" than with more rudimentary chatbots. He points back to ELIZA, the chatbot created by MIT computer scientist Joseph Weizenbaum in 1966. "In the 1960s, ELIZA offered a chatbot, the response to which was very similar to how people reacted to ChatGPT," Hyland said. "Humans interacting with the system inferred emotional content and a narrative through line in chat messages." Guidance issued by the U.K. Judicial Office permits judges in the United Kingdom to use ChatGPT, along with other AI tools, to write legal rulings and perform court duties. Google scrambled to answer it, releasing Bard, "a more or less comparable AI chatbot," in February 2023. Countless other ChatGPT rivals and derivatives reached market afterward, the most recent being Amazon Q, a more business-oriented take on ChatGPT. The pattern set by these three responses is that a breakout consumer product supplies the template competitors copy and reposition rather than a market they vacate.

Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. # Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.

# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. That same roundup reported Google had tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Both facts were carried into TechCrunch's roundup published on November 13, 2023.

# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. Of the $26.3 billion Google paid in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be the default search engine, about $18 billion went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023. TechCrunch reported the figure on October 31, 2023, during the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google; the Google–Apple default deal had been in place since 2003.

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.

# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The theory therefore runs in two linked steps: owned distribution plus paid defaults deny rivals visibility, and denied visibility denies them the query data that would let their products reach a quality high enough to challenge Google. The Epic Games v. Google antitrust proceeding reads as a dated four-year chain rather than a single lawsuit. The Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021, and a ruling came down that September mostly in Apple's favor, with both parties still waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in. A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. # Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. # Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

Testifying on 28 October 2023 in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan stated that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phone makers and platforms for making Google the default search engine. Recipients included the companies Apple, Samsung and Mozilla. Of that $26.3 billion total, roughly $18 billion went directly to Apple, under a Google–Apple search deal in place since 2003.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. That same roundup reported Google had tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Both facts were carried into TechCrunch's roundup published on November 13, 2023.


---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Apple took roughly $18 billion of Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default payments

Of the $26.3 billion Google paid in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be the default search engine, about $18 billion went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023. TechCrunch reported the figure on October 31, 2023, during the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google; the Google–Apple default deal had been in place since 2003.


---


# Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.


---


# Google–Apple Search Deal: Payment for Default Placement, Restraint on Chrome

Under the Google–Apple search deal, in place since 2003, Google pays Apple for default search placement in Safari: of the $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults across browsers, phones and platforms in 2021, about $18 billion went to Apple, according to testimony in the U.S. antitrust trial reported by TechCrunch on October 31, 2023.

The consideration flowing back to Apple is restraint. Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, per Bloomberg, though Google had the means to do so through banners, pop-ups and similar prompts inside its other applications. That term's effect on Apple's own conduct: Apple never switched to a Google competitor as its search engine and never let iPhone users choose a browser when setting up their devices.


---


# Microsoft and DuckDuckGo CEOs Tied Their Search Shortfalls to Missing Apple Default Deals

Earlier in October 2023, in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search. Reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, citing The Information.


---


# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.


---


# Index — Five revelations from the Google antitrust trial, 30–31 October 2023

A breakdown published by TechCrunch on 30–31 October 2023, anchored on Google CEO Sundar Pichai's Monday testimony in the U.S. government's antitrust trial over Google's 2020-era search dominance, organizes the week's disclosures into five points.

1. Default-payment totals: $26.3 billion paid in 2021 across browsers, phones and platforms including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, roughly $18 billion of it to Apple, per search head Prabhakar Raghavan's 28 October testimony.
2. The Chrome-promotion ban: Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users.
3. The iPhone preinstall bid: Pichai's 2018 attempt to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device.
4. Deleted chat logs: history-off default vs. the DOJ's litigation hold.
5. Google's early letter on defaults: a 2007 email citing 15% and 27% swings.


---


# Nadella Said Microsoft Would Pay $15 Billion a Year for Apple's Default Search Slot

During the U.S. antitrust trial against Google in October 2023, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search placement, per The Information's reporting, as covered by TechCrunch on October 31, 2023. Nadella and DuckDuckGo's CEO testified that week that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they made similar deals with Apple.

Epic's case against Google depends on one relation: that Google's app-store and payment-processing terms are set by monopoly power rather than by competition, and that the consequence is consumers pay more for apps than they would in a contested market. In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The theory therefore runs in two linked steps: owned distribution plus paid defaults deny rivals visibility, and denied visibility denies them the query data that would let their products reach a quality high enough to challenge Google. The claim over Google's dominance in the online search market was filed in 2020. It is separate from a claim filed in January by the Department of Justice along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind its monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising. As of mid-November 2023, Google was simultaneously litigating three antitrust matters touching search and app distribution, according to a TechCrunch report dated November 13, 2023. First, the Justice Department's landmark case against Google over search was roughly two months in, before Judge Amit Mehta. Second, Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the previous week. Third, on November 6, 2023 Google went to trial against Fortnite maker Epic Games, which sought to prove Google engages in anticompetitive behavior regarding its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure.


---


# US v Google's ripple effect on parallel Big Tech antitrust cases

A ruling in US v Google may have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases, since enforcers need one landmark judgment to demonstrate antitrust law remains relevant. The parallel matters named in a TechCrunch roundup dated 2023-11-13: the FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power; the DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products; and there's an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, wherein the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp. The proposition is falsified if those cases proceed and settle unaffected by the Google judgment. Judge Amit Mehta hears the Google case.


---


# Google antitrust actions surrounding the Helena World Chronicle publisher suit, December 2023

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and covered by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, arrived while several other Google proceedings were live. This note indexes that surrounding docket.

- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (digital ad technology): the DOJ's monopoly suit over Google's ad-tech stack, pending alongside the publisher case in late 2023.
- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (2020): the earlier civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.
- Epic Games v. Google: the app-store antitrust case, which Epic won; the Helena complaint borrows its finding of improper spoliation of evidence — Google's destruction of chat messages.
- Canada settlement (November 2023): Google agreed to pay Canadian media $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) a year, distributed by newsroom headcount. Meta's negotiations remained unresolved; Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August.


---


# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# The DOJ's Separate Google Ad-Tech Lawsuit (January 2023)

Distinct from the online search monopoly case tried in 2023 is a separate antitrust suit the U.S. Department of Justice filed in January 2023 together with eight states, including New York, California and Colorado. That ad-tech action aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising," according to TechCrunch's October 31, 2023 report on the search trial. The two cases therefore target different markets — search versus digital advertising — even though both stem from the government's broader claims about Google's platforms and partner deals blocking competition.


---


# Google calls Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit "meritless"

A Google spokesperson rejected the Helena World Chronicle class action filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. (TechCrunch, 2023-12-15) as "meritless," denying the complaint's central allegations — that Google breaks the Sherman Act by "siphoning off" publishers' content, readers and ad revenue, and that AI products including Search Generative Experience and Bard worsen the harm.


---


# Remedies floated against Google if Judge Mehta finds liability

In TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup of the US v. Google antitrust trial, the remedies sketched for Google all hinge on one condition: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google. The article names three. First, Google may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers. Second, it may be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and with wireless carriers. Third, Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines, so those rivals can improve their products and attract more users. The DOJ has said that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday, and the government's case is that Google uses its platforms and partner deals to block competition in search and advertising, cutting rivals off from the data they would need to improve their products.


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# Publisher's Google antitrust suit alleges spoliation of chat messages, echoing Epic Games case

The class action antitrust suit that Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023 alleges evidence of improper spoliation by Google — specifically the destruction of chat messages. The complaint ties that allegation to a known precedent: the same issue of destroyed chat messages was raised in Epic Games' recent lawsuit against Google over app-store antitrust conduct, a case Epic won. The spoliation claim sits alongside the suit's other concerns, including allegedly changed AdSense rates, and appears among the counts supporting its requests for damages and injunctive relief against Google.


---


# Contents index: TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup of US v Google

This TechCrunch roundup of November 13, 2023 indexes five sections. First, why US v Google matters and the remedies at stake before Judge Amit Mehta: sharing APIs, bans on anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, and surrendering data — the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. Second, Google's concurrent antitrust matters: the Match Group settlement and the November 6 trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games over Google Play. Third, the declassified list of 20 search terms ordered by revenue for the week of September 22, 2018, and vertical search. Fourth, Jamie Rosenberg's November 8 testimony on MADA (11 pre-loaded Google apps) and RSA mechanics. Fifth, Expedia and Barry Diller on ad load.


---


# SGE rides GoogleBot, so publishers have no clean opt-out

Search Generative Experience (SGE) draws on the same crawler feed that powers Google's ordinary search, which means a publisher cannot refuse SGE's use of its content without also vanishing from regular search results. The class action antitrust suit Helena World Chronicle — an Arkansas publisher of two weekly newspapers — filed against Google and parent Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023 puts it bluntly: publishers "can't block SGE because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot." The complaint's injunction asks Google to let publishers who opt out of SGE still appear in Google search results.

qid: Which company invested $26.3 billion to maintain its default search engine status across various devices and platforms, and is also accused by news publishers of adversely affecting their business through anticompetitive practices, while using relevance, distance, and prominence to rank local search results?
context:
# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. That same roundup reported Google had tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Both facts were carried into TechCrunch's roundup published on November 13, 2023.


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

Testifying on 28 October 2023 in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan stated that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phone makers and platforms for making Google the default search engine. Recipients included the companies Apple, Samsung and Mozilla. Of that $26.3 billion total, roughly $18 billion went directly to Apple, under a Google–Apple search deal in place since 2003.


---


# Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.


---


# Google's Drummond Called Microsoft's Search Default Anticompetitive in 2005

In 2005, after Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, Google legal chief David Drummond wrote to Microsoft arguing that the default was anticompetitive, according to a TechCrunch report dated 2023-10-31 on the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google. Drummond's letter rested on a claim about user behavior: most end users "do not change defaults," so the engine picked at the outset keeps the searches.


---


# Blame for degraded Google results splits between the near-monopoly and the SEOs who game it

In a report on the search engine optimization industry published by The Verge on 2023-11-01, responsibility for bad search results is contested between two camps. In 2023, many people are unhappy with their ability to find information on the internet — which for almost everyone means the quality of Google Search results — calling the links that appear "absolutely unusable", "garbage", and "a nightmare" because "a lot of the content doesn't feel authentic." Some blame Google itself, asserting that an all-powerful, all-seeing, trillion-dollar corporation with a 90 percent market share for online search is corrupting access to the truth. Others blame the SEO practitioners, whose goal is to tell the algorithm whatever it needs to hear so a site ranks as high as possible and then shows visitors advertising. The disagreement is over agency: whether a dominant platform that rewards gaming sets the terms, or the gamers do.


---


# DOJ's theory in *US v. Google*: default deals capture search entry points

In *US v. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. Reporting on Apple executive Eddy Cue's testimony on 2023-09-26, The Verge states that the Justice Department is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.


---


# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.


---


# Default search engine, as defined in US v. Google

In US v. Google, the antitrust trial over Google's search business, Eddy Cue testified on 2023-09-26 about what a "default search engine" means in practice: the engine preselected on a device, which a user must actively change rather than choose. Apple fixes that default to Google through the Information Services Agreement (ISA), in place since 2002, whose current iteration Cue negotiated with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. Cue acknowledged that the ISA doesn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup. Whether Google is "easily" changed is contested: DuckDuckGo's CEO testified it takes "too many steps."
