# Caroline Ellison: Alameda Research head and prosecution's star witness in the FTX trial

Caroline Ellison ran Alameda Research, the sister hedge fund of the crypto exchange FTX, and had been a girlfriend of FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried. Per a CNBC report dated 2023-10-06 covering Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, she and FTX co-founder Gary Wang were integral members of Bankman-Fried's personal and professional inner circles, and both pleaded guilty in December 2022. Ellison is considered the prosecution's star witness and was expected to take the stand under a cooperation arrangement similar to Wang's.


---


# The judge, not the witness, defines legal terms like "market manipulation"

During Sam Bankman-Fried's direct testimony at his FTX trial on 2023-10-28, reported by The Verge, Bankman-Fried offered his own definition of "market manipulation." Judge Lewis Kaplan cut in and told the jury that he, Kaplan, was the final authority on that term. The morning had already been spent largely explaining vocabulary, including "Amazon Web Services" and "database," which the reporter judged too detail-oriented. The exchange illustrated a standing allocation of roles in the courtroom: the witness supplies facts within his experience, and the court supplies the legal meaning of charged terms such as market manipulation.


---


# The Sam Bankman-Fried Fraud Trial Before Judge Lewis Kaplan

The Sam Bankman-Fried fraud trial is the six-week federal criminal proceeding over the collapse of the bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, held in a Manhattan courtroom before U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan and begun in early October 2023. The trial is scheduled to resume on Tuesday 10 October 2023 with key testimony expected from Caroline Ellison, the prosecution's star witness. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges.


---


# FTX: the cryptocurrency exchange whose founder was convicted on seven counts

FTX is the failed cryptocurrency exchange founded by Sam Bankman-Fried, who was found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud, as reported by The Verge on 2023-10-28 while Bankman-Fried was testifying at his own trial. The Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." Bankman-Fried, who started his cryptocurrency trading firm in 2017 and testified he expected only a 20 percent chance of success with the exchange, characterized not creating a risk team as a "big mistake."


---


# Wang's courtroom admission named Bankman-Fried, Singh and Ellison in his FTX frauds

Gary Wang's account of his own FTX criminality reached past himself to named others. Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos on Thursday 5 October 2023, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?", Wang answered "Yes," and said those crimes — wire and commodities fraud — were carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research. When Roos asked whether he saw any of those people in the courtroom, Wang stood, looked around, said "Yes," and identified "Sam Bankman-Fried." The argument's force is a sworn guilty plea, tempered by his six-page cooperation agreement and the up to 50 years in prison he still faces at sentencing.


---


# Alameda Research: FTX's sister hedge fund, run by Caroline Ellison

Alameda Research was the hedge fund operating as the sister firm to the bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, run by Caroline Ellison, who had been Sam Bankman-Fried's girlfriend. Media reporting in November 2022 detailed Alameda's business practices and its troubling ties to FTX, which Bankman-Fried's co-founder Gary Wang later described in October 2023 trial testimony. Alameda had a roughly $14 billion hole in its books.


---


# Bankman-Fried Could Not Recall Who Decided to Spend $8 Billion of FTX Customer Funds

During his trial testimony on October 31, 2023, Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of the collapsed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, said he could not recall knowing anything about who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, as prosecutor Danielle Sassoon questioned him in the wire fraud trial. Asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, and whether there were rules for risk management, Bankman-Fried answered only, "I was concerned with overall risk management." He also said he wasn't trying to build blame for the spending, and had fired no one.


---


# Lutke's Objection: Sympathetic Coverage of SBF, Hostility Toward Value-Creating Founders

An objection to the framing of Michael Lewis's account of Sam Bankman-Fried came from Shopify founder tobi lutke, posting on October 2, 2023 about a Lewis appearance on 60 Minutes discussing "Going Infinite," the book debuting on the first day of SBF's trial. Not disputing the profile's facts, lutke wrote: "60 Minutes got rightly community noted here. How is it that SBF is _still_ getting super positive media coverage when the media has nothing good to say about the founders that have actually created things and brought value into the world?" The counter-argument is that the press keeps extending a fraud defendant sympathetic, close-access treatment while withholding equivalent coverage from founders who build things.


---


# The two-step path to proving intent in the FTX trial against Sam Bankman-Fried

At the criminal trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, the government faces a two-step burden in the element Christopher LaVigne, a former federal prosecutor, identifies as the crucial one: intent. The procedure splits cleanly in difficulty.

Step one is the mechanical part. Prosecutors must show that certain transactions actually took place. This is "pretty simple and a little boring," LaVigne says — whatever records the Southern District of New York holds for those transactions will simply be entered and shown. It establishes movement of money, nothing more.

Step two, where LaVigne notes "all the drama is likely to co"me, is the one that decides the case: connecting those recorded transactions to Bankman-Fried personally by proving he knew what he was doing was wrong and lied about it anyway. The transactions prove themselves; the state of mind behind them must be demonstrated separately.


---


# Alameda's missing risk team as an active governance choice, not a neutral fact

In The Verge's FTX trial coverage ("The jury finally hears from Sam Bankman-Fried," 2023-10-28), the reporter treats Alameda Research's lack of a risk team as an indictment rather than a neutral detail: "Not having a risk team, when you are any kind of financial anything, is certainly a choice." The logic given is that risk is inherent to a futures exchange, which she calls "even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency," so the absence is something a person decided, not an oversight of scale. Sam Bankman-Fried, Alameda's CEO and majority owner, testified he did not create one and has since called it a "big mistake" — a choice reclassified as an accident.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article on Epic Games' antitrust battle with Google suggest a different level of transparency in legal discovery compared to the TechCrunch article on the class action antitrust suit filed by a news publisher against Google, with the former discussing Google's disclosure of evidence and the latter addressing Google's alleged anticompetitive behavior?

# Publisher's Google antitrust suit alleges spoliation of chat messages, echoing Epic Games case

The class action antitrust suit that Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023 alleges evidence of improper spoliation by Google — specifically the destruction of chat messages. The complaint ties that allegation to a known precedent: the same issue of destroyed chat messages was raised in Epic Games' recent lawsuit against Google over app-store antitrust conduct, a case Epic won. The spoliation claim sits alongside the suit's other concerns, including allegedly changed AdSense rates, and appears among the counts supporting its requests for damages and injunctive relief against Google.


---


# Google antitrust actions surrounding the Helena World Chronicle publisher suit, December 2023

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and covered by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, arrived while several other Google proceedings were live. This note indexes that surrounding docket.

- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (digital ad technology): the DOJ's monopoly suit over Google's ad-tech stack, pending alongside the publisher case in late 2023.
- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (2020): the earlier civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.
- Epic Games v. Google: the app-store antitrust case, which Epic won; the Helena complaint borrows its finding of improper spoliation of evidence — Google's destruction of chat messages.
- Canada settlement (November 2023): Google agreed to pay Canadian media $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) a year, distributed by newsroom headcount. Meta's negotiations remained unresolved; Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August.


---


# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# The Article's Argument: The Burden of Proof Makes the Google Case an Uphill Battle

In "Is Google Search better than the rest? And is that fair?", published by The Age on 22 October 2023, the author argues that the US antitrust suit against Google "could be an uphill battle" because the government "has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo" — that is, show that Google's dominance as the default search provider was unlawfully won rather than earned by being, as Google contends, simply the best product. The same paragraph grants the case a countervailing value: for everyone outside the courtroom it "offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share," specifically whether Google is still focused on being the best, or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money even at the expense of product quality, and how "organic" its results are.


---


# Google faced three search and app-store antitrust trials at once in mid-November 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was simultaneously litigating three antitrust matters touching search and app distribution, according to a TechCrunch report dated November 13, 2023. First, the Justice Department's landmark case against Google over search was roughly two months in, before Judge Amit Mehta. Second, Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the previous week. Third, on November 6, 2023 Google went to trial against Fortnite maker Epic Games, which sought to prove Google engages in anticompetitive behavior regarding its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure.


---


# Epic's Twin Antitrust Suits Diverged: Apple Settled in 2021, Google Waited to 2023

Epic Games sued Apple and Google on the same day, August 13th, 2020, both over in-app payment fees critics call the "Apple tax" and "Google tax," but the two cases then moved at wildly different speeds. The Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021, and a ruling came down that September mostly in Apple's favor, with both parties still waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in. The Google suit never got its day in court during those years, delayed again and again, so that Epic v. Google trial beginning November 6th, 2023 arrived "a mere 1,180 days" after Epic filed, per The Verge's article dated 2023-11-05.


---


# Epic v. Google trial notes index — November 6, 2023

These notes cover TechCrunch's November 6, 2023 report on Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google, which began November 6, 2023 over Google Play and its commission structure. Sections: legal theory and statutes (Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2, Cartwright Act, Unfair Competition Law, the Microsoft/Netscape precedent); the two relevant markets; commissions and User Choice Billing; OEM agreements, AFAs and Project Hug; and Google's defenses.


---


# Epic v. Google as a Four-Year Sequence, Originating in a September 2019 Plan Email

The Epic Games v. Google antitrust proceeding reads as a dated four-year chain rather than a single lawsuit. Its causal origin is a September 2019 email surfaced in discovery, describing Epic's plan to draw Google into a legal battle over antitrust — the document that predates and sets up everything after it. That plan became a four-week federal antitrust trial before a nine-person jury, which found on Monday, December 11, 2023 that Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems and illegally tied Google Play billing to its app store. The Verge's December 12, 2023 interview with Epic CEO Tim Sweeney frames the verdict as "four years in the making." Sweeney dates his own suspicion of Google's practices to 2018, one year earlier than the email.


---


# Complaint's core allegation: Google is "starving the free press" at a cost of billions

The central harm asserted in the class action antitrust complaint filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. is that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars." The plaintiff, Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, brings the claim against Google and parent company Alphabet under the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust law, framing Google's redistribution of news content inside its own products as anticompetitive conduct that diverts publishers' content, readers and ad revenue.


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# Google calls Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit "meritless"

A Google spokesperson rejected the Helena World Chronicle class action filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. (TechCrunch, 2023-12-15) as "meritless," denying the complaint's central allegations — that Google breaks the Sherman Act by "siphoning off" publishers' content, readers and ad revenue, and that AI products including Search Generative Experience and Bard worsen the harm.

qid: Between the TechCrunch report on Sam Bankman-Fried's intentions with his wealth published on October 2, 2023, and the TechCrunch report on the allegations against Sam Bankman-Fried published on October 7, 2023, was there no change in the portrayal of Sam Bankman-Fried's actions and intentions?
context:
# Prosecutors' intent theory: Bankman-Fried's tweets and interviews vs. the record

In its August 14th superseding indictment, prosecutors called Sam Bankman-Fried's November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." In The Verge's September 28, 2023 trial coverage, the government's plan is to use Bankman-Fried's own public statements — on Twitter and in the many interviews he sat for — to show a gap between what he said and what actually happened at FTX, supplying the evidence needed to prove intent.


---


# Bankman-Fried Visibly Upset During Wang's Testimony, October 2023

CNBC's courtroom report of 5–6 October 2023 records that Sam Bankman-Fried, 31, stayed mostly quiet at his fraud trial, listening intently to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys. But as Gary Wang testified against him, Bankman-Fried looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX Trial in Session at Manhattan Federal Court, Week Ending 7 October 2023

As of the week ending 7 October 2023, the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried — the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of cryptocurrency exchange FTX — was in session at the Manhattan Federal Court, and TechCrunch reported that its team had been stationed there to cover the proceedings. The observation appears in TechCrunch's Week in Review digest of that week, in the item headlined "SBF allegedly tried to buy off Trump," which described the trial as the setting for emerging details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings.


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's appearance and demeanor in court, 2023-10-04

Fortune's account of day two of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial in New York on 2023-10-04 records what it observed in the courtroom: his cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, and he spent most of his day there staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys.


---


# Cooperating co-conspirators' conversations as intent evidence in the Bankman-Fried trial

In the fraud trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of FTX and Alameda Research, the government's second burden is proving intent — where The Verge, on 2023-09-28, expected the drama: "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?"


---


# Bankman-Fried's Physical Demeanour Shifted Between Two Testimonies, 2023-10-10

In The Verge's courtroom coverage of 2023-10-10 — the fifth day of Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial, in which he faces seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — the reporter recorded a change in the defendant's posture as the witnesses changed. Bankman-Fried "had been vibrating slightly" during the testimony of Gary Wang, FTX's chief technology officer. During Caroline Ellison's testimony later the same day, the reporter wrote, "his bouncing became more noticeable." By day's end, the defence's cross-examination of Wang "seemed like a sideshow." The observation is the journalist's own visual impression, not a measured or courtroom-documented fact.


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried Faces Seven Federal Charges Carrying Life Exposure, October 2023

As his fraud trial over the collapsed crypto exchange FTX proceeded on 6 October 2023, Sam Bankman-Fried, 31, faced seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering — charges that could put him in prison for the rest of his life.


---


# Bankman-Fried Faced Seven Counts at Close of Prosecution's Case, October 2023

At the close of the prosecution's case in October 2023, Sam Bankman-Fried faced seven counts: two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges, according to The Verge's reporting on 2023-10-26. The trial concerned fraud at the FTX exchange and his trading firm Alameda Research.


---


# Bankman-Fried on trial for seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy, October 2023

As reported by The Verge on 2023-10-10, Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, was standing trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. In the same passage, The Verge records the Securities and Exchange Commission's allegation that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The report places the trial in progress on the day Caroline Ellison took the stand.


---


# Cohen's Closing Argument: Bankman-Fried Gave Up Wealth Rather Than Steal, Fortune Says

Mark Cohen, defending Sam Bankman-Fried at FTX's criminal trial in New York, argued in his opening statement on 2023-10-04 that when the walls came closing in and his "plane approached the 'eye of the storm'," Bankman-Fried behaved as an innocent would, being willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. Cohen concluded that the founder of two billion-dollar businesses "didn't steal any money."

Source: Fortune, 2023-10-04.


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried fraud trial opened at Manhattan Federal Court on 3 October 2023

Sam Bankman-Fried, the cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history" through the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the exchange he founded and led, stood trial from Tuesday 3 October 2023 at Manhattan Federal Court. Bankman-Fried had pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.


---


# Ayelet Noff attributes Sam Bankman-Fried's poor on-camera performance to inexperience at scale

In TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 report on Michael Lewis and *Going Infinite*, the closing assessment comes from Ayelet Noff, CEO and founder of the PR firm Sliced Brand: Sam Bankman-Fried performed badly on camera because he had never managed an undertaking of that size and was in over his head. The warrant she leans on is behaviour visible in the 60 Minutes footage Lewis appeared on — Bankman-Fried shuffling cards with a nervously twitching leg behind his desk, and his eyes going back and forth during his first television appearance because he was trying to win a video game on air. Noff's claim sets its own scope: it is about the impression of competence Bankman-Fried projected, not about his legal culpability on the roughly seven fraud and conspiracy charges he pleaded not-guilty to.


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Persona as Fast-Rich Billionaire Spending It on Existential Risk, per Michael Lewis

Michael Lewis, quoted in TechCrunch's report of 2023-10-02 on his 60 Minutes interview, described the image Sam Bankman-Fried projected when Lewis met him in early 2021 in Berkeley: a young billionaire who had made his fortune very fast and meant to give it away against catastrophe. "Eighteen months earlier, he had nothing. Now he had $22.5 billion. He was the richest person in the world under 30 [and] he was going to spend it to save humanity from extinction," Lewis said. "My jaw was on the floor." Lewis had gone to "evaluate his character" for a friend and came away deciding to write about him instead.


---


# Rehn's Core Allegation: SBF's Success "Was Built on Lies"

In his roughly 30-minute government opening statement on Oct. 4, 2023, in Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial, prosecutor Thane Rehn's central claim was that Bankman-Fried's apparent success — "all of that, all of it, was built on lies" — because "behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." The warrant is the divergence between Bankman-Fried repeatedly telling FTX customers their money was "safe and secure" and his alleged "secret access" to that customer money via Alameda Research.

qid: After TechCrunch reported on September 28, 2023, that OpenAI would make GPT-4 with vision available alongside the launch of GPT-4 Turbo API, did the same news source maintain consistency in its view of OpenAI's strategy when reporting on December 19, 2023, about OpenAI pushing an "app store for AI" as the primary platform for obtaining AI tools and toys?
context:
# GPT store launch delayed past December 2023 by OpenAI's C-suite crisis

TechCrunch's predictions piece of 2023-12-19 reports that OpenAI's GPT store was originally planned for launch in December but was "understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas" — the leadership shake-up of November 2023. The article describes the store as an "app store for AI" that OpenAI will push hard as the platform for AI tools.


---


# Hypothesis: OpenAI's GPT store becomes the default "app store for AI" in 2024

In a TechCrunch piece dated 2023-12-19, the prediction is that OpenAI will push its GPT store hard through 2024 as the default "app store for AI" — the platform people get their AI tools from — following Apple's store model "all the way to the bank," and at the expense of Hugging Face and open-source models. Originally planned for a December launch, the store was delayed by the November C-suite upheaval that left Sam Altman more fully in charge, accelerating OpenAI's shift toward a "ship it" mindset.

Falsification: the store fails to ship, or becomes only a minor distribution channel for AI tools.


---


# OpenAI's product-company turn: Altman's post-November 2023 authority displaces board caution with appetite for markets

TechCrunch's 2023-12-19 predictions essay argues that OpenAI will run as a product company in 2024 because the leadership shake-up in November 2023 left Sam Altman more fully in charge, displacing the previous board. The consequence trickles down at every level of the company as a "ship it" mindset, exemplified by the GPT store — the "app store for AI" originally planned for launch in December but delayed due to the C-suite fracas — which OpenAI will push hard as the place to get AI toys and tools, never mind Hugging Face or any open source models. The mechanism is a swap of governing temperament: the caution and academic reserve that the previous board exerted gives way, in TechCrunch's phrasing, to an unseemly lust for markets and customers.


---


# OpenAI DevDay: OpenAI's First Developer Conference, 6 November 2023

OpenAI DevDay was OpenAI's first developer conference, held on 6 November 2023 — the last major company event before the "leadership chaos" surrounding the firing and swift return of CEO and co-founder Sam Altman, which TechCrunch says raised concerns about OpenAI's direction and opened the door for competitors. At DevDay, OpenAI announced a slew of updates to GPT: GPT-4 Turbo, described as a super-charged version of GPT-4, its latest language-writing model; a multimodal API; and a GPT store where users can create and monetize their own custom versions of GPT.


---


# GPT Store: OpenAI's Marketplace for User-Built, Monetizable Custom GPTs

The GPT store is an OpenAI marketplace where users can create and monetize their own custom versions of GPT. OpenAI announced it on November 6 at OpenAI DevDay, the company's first developer conference, as part of a slew of updates coming to GPT that also included GPT-4 Turbo (super-charged versions of GPT-4, OpenAI's latest language-writing model) and a multimodal API. TechCrunch reported the announcement in its continuously updated ChatGPT timeline, noting the DevDay news arrived before the leadership turmoil surrounding CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return.


---


# GPT-4 Turbo: OpenAI's "super-charged" GPT-4, announced at DevDay on Nov 6

GPT-4 Turbo is, in OpenAI's own description at its first developer conference, a "super-charged" version of GPT-4, the company's latest language-writing model. OpenAI named it on November 6 at OpenAI DevDay, in a batch of GPT updates that also included a multimodal API and a GPT store where users can create and monetize their own custom versions of GPT. According to TechCrunch's coverage of November 6, 2023 announcement, GPT-4 itself remains largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users, and TechCrunch's December 2023 timeline records that the ChatGPT Plus subscription includes access to both GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo.


---


# Adoption and Investment as Grounds for AI Chatbots Outlasting OpenAI's Leadership Crisis

TechCrunch's ChatGPT coverage (published 2023-09-28, updated through December 2023) argues that AI chatbots are not going away anytime soon, resting the claim on two grounds: measured adoption and OpenAI's continued investment.

Adoption: ChatGPT reached 100 million weekly active users since its initial launch nearly a year ago, and is used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies.

Investment: OpenAI announced GPT-4 Turbo, a multimodal API and a GPT store at its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, on November 6; connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users; integrated DALL-E 3; and re-enabled ChatGPT Plus subscriptions on December 13, 2023.

The reasoning is that a user base that large and a product roadmap that active do not reverse because CEO and co-founder Sam Altman was fired and swiftly returned — a turmoil the article says may instead empower Meta's LLaMA models and rival AI startups.


---


# Multimodal API (OpenAI DevDay, November 6)

A multimodal API is a programmatic interface to a model that accepts and returns more than one modality — text plus another medium such as images — instead of a text-only endpoint, where a developer sends a written prompt and gets written output back. The term appears here as one of "a slew of updates coming to GPT" that OpenAI announced at OpenAI DevDay, its first developer conference, held November 6, alongside GPT-4 Turbo and a GPT store for custom, monetizable versions of GPT (TechCrunch, 2023-09-28).


---


# ChatGPT at Launch: A Free Chat Interface on GPT-3.5, Framed as a "Low-Key Research Preview"

When OpenAI released ChatGPT on 30 November 2022, it was not a new model. As TechCrunch described it on 2023-11-30, ChatGPT was initially "a basic free-to-use, web-based and chat-focused interface on top of one of OpenAI's existing models, GPT-3.5" — the wrapping, not the engine, was the new part. OpenAI published it as a "low-key research preview," reportedly prompted partly by rivalry with AI startup Anthropic, and told staff the goal was to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI to inform the development of OpenAI's future models. OpenAI never released a research paper on ChatGPT.


---


# ChatGPT Plus

ChatGPT Plus is OpenAI's paid subscription tier for ChatGPT, the AI chatbot used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies. Its defining differentiator is access to GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo, described in a TechCrunch article published 2023-09-28. GPT-4 writes more naturally and fluently than previous models and remains largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users. OpenAI paused Plus sign-ups in November 2023 citing a "surge of usage"; CEO Sam Altman announced subscriptions re-enabled on December 13, 2023, after the company "found more gpus".


---


# ChatGPT's research preview launch as a data-harvesting strategy

When OpenAI released ChatGPT "a year ago" — i.e. a year before TechCrunch's retrospective of 2023-11-30 — it did so as a "low-key research preview," reportedly spurred in part by an intense rivalry with the AI startup Anthropic. OpenAI leadership told the OpenAI rank-and-file at the time that the goal was to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI, in order to inform the development of OpenAI's future models. ChatGPT was not a new model at all in that framing: initially a basic free-to-use, web-based, chat-focused interface on top of one of OpenAI's existing models, GPT-3.5.

qid: Who was once portrayed as a trustworthy figure in the cryptocurrency industry by The Verge, was not considered the white horse of crypto by TechCrunch, had the wealth and ambition to potentially influence political events according to TechCrunch, and is now facing allegations of fraud as reported by TechCrunch?
context:
# Bankman-Fried's pre-collapse persona as crypto's trustworthy face

Before his fall, Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX (founded 2019) and the trading firm Alameda Research, made himself out to be the "Good Boy of crypto" — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry, as reported by The Verge on 2023-09-28. He sat for many interviews both before and after FTX's collapse, and the quick rise of FTX as an industry force was at least in part due to his appetite for attention. At one point he told a colleague at FTX: "I honestly think it's negative EV for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy."


---


# FTX: the cryptocurrency exchange whose founder was convicted on seven counts

FTX is the failed cryptocurrency exchange founded by Sam Bankman-Fried, who was found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud, as reported by The Verge on 2023-10-28 while Bankman-Fried was testifying at his own trial. The Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." Bankman-Fried, who started his cryptocurrency trading firm in 2017 and testified he expected only a 20 percent chance of success with the exchange, characterized not creating a risk team as a "big mistake."

The DOJ has said that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday, and the government's case is that Google uses its platforms and partner deals to block competition in search and advertising, cutting rivals off from the data they would need to improve their products.

# Activision's denial undercuts Epic's $360 million "payment not to compete" narrative

Epic's account of Google buying off rivals rests heavily on a $360 million figure. At the opening day of the Epic v. Google trial on Monday, 2023-11-06, Epic attorney Gary Bornstein told jurors Google "pays actual and potential competitors not to compete," citing $360 million as "an actual number you'll hear about" — the alleged payment that kept Activision from opening an app store that could compete with Google Play. The Verge's 2023-11-07 report contests that characterization at its foundation: Activision told The Verge in 2022 that it "never entered into an agreement that Activision would not open its own app store," and Google now says it is armed with the evidence to prove it. That is not a quibble over margin size; it removes the named recipient and the documented quid pro quo from Epic's most concrete-sounding example. Bornstein conceded on Monday that Google "was too clever" to draw up contracts specifically forcing developers not to compete with the Play Store, which compounds the gap between the narrative and the paper trail.


---


# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.


---


# Epic's own mention of Project Liberty blunts Google's bad-faith angle

Google's attempt to cast Epic's Project Liberty as proof of bad faith runs into one complication: in the opening statements of Epic's 2020 monopoly suit against Google, reported by The Verge on 2023-11-07, Epic mentioned Project Liberty in its own opening. A fact the jury hears first from the side it is supposed to embarrass lands as disclosure, not exposure — so the same detail is a weaker sting when Google reaches for it later. Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein spoke first, portraying Google as a bully that pays competitors not to compete.


---


# The store–billing relation: how Epic v. Google's two findings form one loop

Read as a single structure rather than two verdicts, the findings a federal jury returned against Google — reported by Tim Sweeney of Epic Games in The Verge, 2023-12-12 — describe one loop with two ends.

One end is the monopolised product: Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. The other end is the tied product: Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The relation between the ends is the model. Whichever product a developer must accept to reach Android users also becomes the channel through which that developer's money moves, so control of distribution converts into control of payment — and the payment share Sweeney calls "huge taxes" paid to a few gatekeepers reinforces the distribution hold. Two holdings, one circuit.


---


# The Epic v. Google hypothesis: paid exclusion, not consumer preference, kept rival app stores off Android

Testable proposition from the Epic v. Google trial record, stated by Epic CEO Tim Sweeney in his interview with The Verge published 2023-12-12: rival Android app stores failed to reach devices because Google paid for that outcome — paying "other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores" and "paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores." Sweeney says he suspected these practices since 2018, early enough that critics called him a conspiracy theorist, and says the testimony confirmed them; when Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with manufacturers like OnePlus and carriers of all sorts, they told him Google had already done a secret deal with them. Falsified if carriers, OEMs or developers declined competition for reasons documented independently of Google payments.


---


# Google's User Choice Billing Counter to Epic's Payment-Processing Market Claim

Facing Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google that began November 6, 2023, Google answers Epic's claim of a foreclosed market for payment-processing solutions inside Android apps by pointing to its own alternative-billing program, User Choice Billing — and to Epic's refusal to use it. Introduced in November 2022 and still in pilot testing at trial time, User Choice Billing is open to all developers selling apps in the 35 markets where it is available, including the U.S., and cuts the standard commission — otherwise 15% to 30% under Google Play's first-party billing requirement — by 4% for companies that use their own payment processing. Spotify and Bumble were the initial testers, and Match, having settled with Google the week before the trial started, will also take advantage of the option. In Google's framing, developers who want to process payments themselves are invited to do so at a lower rate; Epic simply declined the offer.

# Multimodal API (OpenAI DevDay, November 6)

A multimodal API is a programmatic interface to a model that accepts and returns more than one modality — text plus another medium such as images — instead of a text-only endpoint, where a developer sends a written prompt and gets written output back. The term appears here as one of "a slew of updates coming to GPT" that OpenAI announced at OpenAI DevDay, its first developer conference, held November 6, alongside GPT-4 Turbo and a GPT store for custom, monetizable versions of GPT (TechCrunch, 2023-09-28).

# Adam Yedidia, MIT friend of Bankman-Fried, testified under a grant of immunity

Adam Yedidia, a fast-talking MIT graduate and close college friend of Sam Bankman-Fried, testified for the prosecution on the second day of the FTX founder's New York trial, reported Fortune on 2023-10-04. Adam Yedidia — Sam Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and an employee at FTX — testified that he had asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July. Bankman-Fried, testifying in his own defense at his fraud trial, appeared to deny that conversation had ever taken place. It was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Bankman-Fried had ever been told by Yedidia about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. ---


# Judge Kaplan Forced a Concession on Whether Yedidia Warned Bankman-Fried About the $8 Billion

Adam Yedidia — Sam Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — testified that he had asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July 2022. Adam Yedidia, college roommate of FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, testified at Bankman-Fried's fraud trial with immunity because Yedidia was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud. Those messages were sent before Yedidia realized FTX had stolen customer funds — at which point, Yedidia resigned.

# Damian Williams: Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history"

At a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history," according to TechCrunch's report of 2023-10-01 — the public characterization by the prosecutor bringing the FTX case, as Bankman-Fried's criminal trial on fraud and conspiracy charges began.

# Yedidia's Explained Reason for His Government Deal, 2023-10-04

Asked by lead prosecutor Danielle Sassoon why he made a deal with the government, Adam Yedidia testified on 2023-10-04: "I was concerned that I had unwittingly written code that contributed to a crime." That quoted concern is the reason Yedidia gave for his immunity agreement, in the FTX proceedings reported by Fortune.

# Know what "epistemology" means? Don't testify in your own defense

The Verge's FTX trial reporter (31 Oct 2023) draws one rule from Sam Bankman-Fried's cross-examination by Danielle Sassoon: "if you know the meaning of the word 'epistemology,' you absolutely should not testify in your own defense." Wire-fraud liability turns on what a defendant knew and when he asked — so Bankman-Fried's quarrels over precision ("hole isn't really the word I would use"; wanting "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it") wrote the jury the record of his own inquiry. He conceded he knew of the fiat@ftx account in June 2022 but not its purpose until October, and admitted Judge Lewis Kaplan pressed him into admitting Adam Yedidia had told him about the missing $8 billion.


---


# Index: "Sam Bankman-Fried didn't ask where the $8 billion went" (The Verge, Oct 31, 2023)

Navigation index for The Verge's October 31, 2023 courtroom report on the June 2022 thread of Sam Bankman-Fried's self-testimony at his fraud trial — seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. The decomposition entries attach to these parts of the article: the software bug overestimating Alameda's debt to FTX by about $8 billion, found by Adam Yedidia; Bankman-Fried's discovery of the fiat@ftx account in June 2022 but not its purpose until October; staff telling him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting"; his "no, no, and no" on directions, policies and measures protecting FTX customer money; Yedidia's padel tennis court exchange in June or July, and Judge Lewis Kaplan's intervention; and the Alameda balance sheet of June 13, 2022 listing the borrowed money as "ftx borrows."

# The FTX Trial's Real Story: Fraud Plus a Destroyed Inner Circle

The Verge's argument on 2023-10-26, as the prosecution's case neared its end, is that the FTX trial matters on two tracks at once. The first is familiar: the prosecution made a strong case that Sam Bankman-Fried presided over the frauds at FTX and his trading firm Alameda Research, which purloined customers' funds, and he faces seven counts, two of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges. What gives the trial its weight, however, is "a simultaneous drama of ruined lives playing out in the courtroom" among the people closest to him. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity after having texted "I love you Sam… I'm not going anywhere." Gary Wang, co-founder of FTX and Alameda, "sang like a canary"; Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, pleaded guilty to six charges; Caroline Ellison, his ex-girlfriend, described the seven phony balance sheets she created. In the opening statement reported by Fortune on 2023-10-04, prosecutor Thane Rehn pushed the government's case past the taking of FTX customer funds: Bankman-Fried allegedly directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers and forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. In his opening statement on Oct 4, 2023, as reported by Fortune, defence lawyer Mark Cohen offered a model of the FTX–Alameda relationship at odds with the prosecution's two-entity structure. Alameda was not subterranean or shady but a successful hedge fund, he said; FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." "Sam didn't defraud anyone," he said.

As of the TechCrunch article dated 2023-10-02, Sam Bankman-Fried — the founder and head of the collapsed crypto exchange FTX, accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history" — had been denied bail while awaiting his trial. That trial was set to begin the following Tuesday in the Manhattan Federal Court, with SBF having pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Google antitrust actions surrounding the Helena World Chronicle publisher suit, December 2023

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and covered by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, arrived while several other Google proceedings were live. This note indexes that surrounding docket.

- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (digital ad technology): the DOJ's monopoly suit over Google's ad-tech stack, pending alongside the publisher case in late 2023.
- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (2020): the earlier civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.
- Epic Games v. Google: the app-store antitrust case, which Epic won; the Helena complaint borrows its finding of improper spoliation of evidence — Google's destruction of chat messages.
- Canada settlement (November 2023): Google agreed to pay Canadian media $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) a year, distributed by newsroom headcount. Meta's negotiations remained unresolved; Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August.


---


# Hausfeld frames the Google publishers suit as a fight for AI-era press competition

Housefeeds counsel Hausfeld, in the website announcement accompanying the class action filed the week of 2023-12-15 in the U.S. District Court in D.C., cast the case against Google and parent Alphabet as necessary to restore competition in the digital news and reference publishing markets and to establish guardrails for the free marketplace of ideas in the AI era. The suit, brought on behalf of Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle and a class of news publishers, invokes both the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act. Hausfeld's framing positions the relief sought — class-wide damages plus an injunction governing how Google uses publisher content in AI products — as a structural remedy for press sustainability, not merely a compensation claim.


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# SGE rides GoogleBot, so publishers have no clean opt-out

Search Generative Experience (SGE) draws on the same crawler feed that powers Google's ordinary search, which means a publisher cannot refuse SGE's use of its content without also vanishing from regular search results. The class action antitrust suit Helena World Chronicle — an Arkansas publisher of two weekly newspapers — filed against Google and parent Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023 puts it bluntly: publishers "can't block SGE because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot." The complaint's injunction asks Google to let publishers who opt out of SGE still appear in Google search results.


---


# AI Tool Customer Withdrawal Predicted for 2024 as Marketing Claims Face Review

In an article published 2023-12-19 on TechCrunch, the hypothesis is advanced that a considerable customer withdrawal from AI tools will occur during 2024. The reasoning is that marketing claims made for machine learning systems—often adopted by companies merely to avoid falling behind—will face their quarterly and yearly reviews, and will very likely be found wanting. The measurable benefits will fail to justify the costs and risks involved. On the far end of this spectrum, lawsuits and regulatory action against AI service providers that cannot back up their claims are anticipated as a consequence of the same dynamic.


---


# Post/Allen Institute finding: News and Media sites are the third-largest category of AI training data

A Washington Post analysis conducted with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI found that News and Media sites form the third-largest category of material in AI training datasets. The Helena World Chronicle's class action antitrust suit against Google and parent Alphabet — reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15 — cited that finding, together with a 2023 News Media Alliance report, in arguing that Google's Bard was trained on "news, magazine and digital publications."


---


# Axel Springer licenses its news content to OpenAI, week of 15 December 2023

In the week of 15 December 2023, German publisher Axel Springer signed a deal with OpenAI to license its news for AI model training, a TechCrunch article on that date reported. The agreement was cited as one example of publishers "trying to get ahead of" the threat that AI-powered search poses to their traffic. Overall, publishers expected to lose 20-40% of website traffic once Google's AI products fully rolled out, per The WSJ, and Google then drove nearly 40% of publisher traffic (Similarweb).


---


# Helena World Chronicle, Arkansas Weekly Newspaper Publisher and Google Antitrust Plaintiff

Helena World Chronicle is a publisher based in Arkansas that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in that state. It is the named plaintiff in the class action antitrust lawsuit filed this week — in the news reports of 2023-12-15 — in the U.S. District Court in D.C. against Google and parent company Alphabet, which it says is "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars".


---


# Google Bard trained on news publisher content, Helena World Chronicle complaint alleges

In the class action antitrust complaint Helena World Chronicle filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023, the Arkansas publisher alleges that Google's Bard AI chatbot was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications." Beyond damages, the class action against Google and parent Alphabet filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. by Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle asks the court for two injunctive remedies. The first would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train general-purpose artificial intelligence products — a obligation reaching not only Google's own AI offerings but those of its rivals. The second would require Google to let publishers who opt out of Search Generative Experience (SGE) continue appearing in Google's ordinary search results, addressing the complaint's allegation that publishers cannot block SGE because it shares GoogleBot, the same web crawler used by Google's general search service.

# Google calls Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit "meritless"

A Google spokesperson rejected the Helena World Chronicle class action filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. (TechCrunch, 2023-12-15) as "meritless," denying the complaint's central allegations — that Google breaks the Sherman Act by "siphoning off" publishers' content, readers and ad revenue, and that AI products including Search Generative Experience and Bard worsen the harm.

qid: After the report by The Age on October 22, 2023, which maintained that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue, and the subsequent report by TechCrunch on November 13, 2023, detailing Google's expenditure to be the default search engine, was there consistency in the portrayal of Google's business practices in the TechCrunch article published on December 15, 2023, regarding the class action antitrust suit against Google?

# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Reach of the retracted Wired piece on Google query manipulation, October 2023

In October 2023, Wired published, then removed for not meeting its standards, an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had revealed during the US antitrust trial that it manipulates search queries for ad revenue — for example replacing "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear". The Age reports that the extent of its sharing on social media and boosting in write-ups at other outlets shows how willing people are to accept foul play by Google, amid a standing suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling.

SOURCE: The Age, "Is Google Search better than the rest? And is that fair?", 2023-10-22.


---


# Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.


---


# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."

# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. # Google's default-search deal with Apple dates to 2003

In its 2023-10-31 report on the U.S. antitrust trial against Google, TechCrunch stated that "Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003." That is the agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices, so it had been running roughly twenty years by the time the deal's cost came under scrutiny in court in late October 2023.


---


# Apple took roughly $18 billion of Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default payments

Of the $26.3 billion Google paid in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be the default search engine, about $18 billion went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023. TechCrunch reported the figure on October 31, 2023, during the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google; the Google–Apple default deal had been in place since 2003.

In 2005, after Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, Google legal chief David Drummond wrote to Microsoft arguing that the default was anticompetitive, according to a TechCrunch report dated 2023-10-31 on the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google. Drummond's letter rested on a claim about user behavior: most end users "do not change defaults," so the engine picked at the outset keeps the searches.


---


# Default search engine, as defined in US v. Google

In US v. Google, the antitrust trial over Google's search business, Eddy Cue testified on 2023-09-26 about what a "default search engine" means in practice: the engine preselected on a device, which a user must actively change rather than choose. Apple fixes that default to Google through the Information Services Agreement (ISA), in place since 2002, whose current iteration Cue negotiated with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. Cue acknowledged that the ISA doesn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup. Whether Google is "easily" changed is contested: DuckDuckGo's CEO testified it takes "too many steps."


---


# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.

# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

Testifying on 28 October 2023 in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan stated that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phone makers and platforms for making Google the default search engine. Recipients included the companies Apple, Samsung and Mozilla. Of that $26.3 billion total, roughly $18 billion went directly to Apple, under a Google–Apple search deal in place since 2003.


---


# Google Search Antitrust Trial: the 2020 Dominance Claim

The U.S. antitrust trial being heard in October 2023 is the 2020 claim over Google's dominance in the online search market, in which Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified on the Monday covered by TechCrunch's Oct. 31, 2023 report, defending the deals that make Google the default search engine. It is distinct from the separate claim filed in January 2023 by the Department of Justice with eight states, including New York, California and Colorado, which seeks to break Google's monopoly in digital advertising, not search.

Bard is Google's consumer chatbot, which TechCrunch on 2023-12-07 describes as "Google's ChatGPT competitor," the counterpart to OpenAI's ChatGPT. # Gemini: Google's flagship generative AI model family

Gemini is Google's flagship generative AI model, unveiled during the week of 2023-12-07 and meant to power a range of Google products and services. One of those services is Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor, which began receiving a "lite" version of Gemini called Gemini Pro on 2023-12-06. In blog posts and press materials published alongside that announcement, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4.

# Vendor capability claims and user outcomes are weakly coupled — Gemini Pro, December 2023

The weakness of benchmark-derived vendor claims as evidence about real use shows up sharply in the Gemini Pro launch. Google trial record, stated by Epic CEO Tim Sweeney in his interview with The Verge published 2023-12-12: rival Android app stores failed to reach devices because Google paid for that outcome — paying "other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores" and "paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores." # Why the Same Bet Is Priced Differently at Every Sportsbook

The Sporting News guide to line shopping (Nov 6, 2023) argues that price differences between sportsbooks are structural, not accidental, and that this is the reason line shopping "always makes sense."

Each sportsbook sets its own market: some employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms, while other betting apps simply copy those lines. Some books therefore open at different prices "right from the jump." Then each book responds to its own money. Since a sportsbook's goal is to even out betting on both sides so it can earn the profit built into the odds without worrying which side wins, it moves a line or changes odds when the public bets heavily on one side.

The decisive point is independence: one sportsbook may be forced to move a line because of betting, while another is not. That produces a divergence on the identical bet, and the divergence is the opportunity — a chance to lay less, win more, and improve your chances.


---


# The Sportsbook Business Model: Balanced Action Wins Either Way

Per Sporting News (2023-11-06), a sportsbook's objective on each market is balanced action, not picking winners. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," which lets it earn the profit already built into the odds and lines — the margin commonly called the vig — without worrying about which side wins. Lines move when the public bets heavily on one side; the originals come from oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms fed by analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data.


---


# Sportsbook Opening Lines Come From Computer Models Run by Oddsmakers

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), the best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and dedicated oddsmaking services to produce their lines and odds. Those oddsmakers and oddsmaking services run computer models and algorithms that weigh analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, among other inputs, to develop the lines and odds before betting opens. Not every operator does this work itself: other sports betting apps simply copy the lines that the oddsmakers and oddsmaking services set. The models' inputs are therefore the origin point for the prices that later move on public betting.


---


# DraftKings Runs More Open Betting Markets Than Most Online Sportsbooks

In its guide to line shopping, Sporting News (2023-11-06) reports that DraftKings Sportsbook "has more open betting markets than most online sportsbooks, and the lines and odds are always competitive." # Sports Betting Lines Move With Public Action and New Information

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), betting lines and odds are not static once posted by sportsbooks. They are subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that comes to light ahead of the game — sportsbooks will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side. Because the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook, one may be forced to move a line while another is not.

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. # Google's Gemini multimodal claims outrun the model it actually shipped

Google's launch messaging for Gemini, described in TechCrunch's Week in Review on 2023-12-09, ran ahead of what was actually available. In an interview published by TechCrunch on 2023-11-30, Stella Biderman, an AI researcher at Booz Allen Hamilton and the open research group EleutherAI, separated an "AI breakthrough" from what she called a bonafide "user experience breakthrough." # Index: Eddy Cue testifies for Apple in US v. Google (The Verge, 2023-09-26)

Index to The Verge's 2023-09-26 report on Eddy Cue testifying in US v. Google, the DOJ antitrust trial over Google's search business, before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC. Sub-topics covered:

- **The ISA**: the Information Services Agreement making Google default search on all Apple devices, in place since 2002 and renegotiated by Cue with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016.
- **The 2016 revenue-share renegotiation**: Apple sought a larger share of Google's search revenue from Apple-directed users; specific numbers were reserved for closed court sessions.
- **The no-alternative defence**: "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time" — Cue never considered switching providers or building Apple's own search.
- **Setup-choice arguments**: DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's iPhone setup screenshots (Appearance, location tracking, App Tracking Transparency) against Cue's "Setup is just critical stuff," plus the disputed ease of changing defaults.
- **Privacy versus payments**: Apple's privacy claims set against emails in which Cue railed at Google's privacy policies.


---


# Cue's 2023-09-26 "No Valid Alternative" Argument for Apple's Google Default

Testifying on 2023-09-26 in US v. Google, Apple's Eddy Cue argued that Apple never seriously considered switching to another search provider or building its own search product, because "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time." He said there still isn't one.

The claim's scope is the 2016 renegotiation period, when Cue negotiated the current iteration of the Information Services Agreement (ISA) with Google CEO Sundar Pichai — the deal, in place since 2002, that makes Google the default search engine on Apple devices and pays Apple billions of dollars a year.

Cue's warrant was that the choice was product-driven rather than purely economic: the ISA is Apple's own evaluation, and he said "We make Google be the default search engine because we've always thought it was the best. We pick the best one and let users easily change it." Supporting that, he told DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw he'd never really considered walking away from the deal.


---


# DOJ's theory in *US v. Google*: default deals capture search entry points

In *US v. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. Reporting on Apple executive Eddy Cue's testimony on 2023-09-26, The Verge states that the Justice Department is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.


---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Default search engine, as defined in US v. Google

In US v. Google, the antitrust trial over Google's search business, Eddy Cue testified on 2023-09-26 about what a "default search engine" means in practice: the engine preselected on a device, which a user must actively change rather than choose. Apple fixes that default to Google through the Information Services Agreement (ISA), in place since 2002, whose current iteration Cue negotiated with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. Cue acknowledged that the ISA doesn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup. Whether Google is "easily" changed is contested: DuckDuckGo's CEO testified it takes "too many steps."


---


# SEO's Spread Has Made Ordinary Searches commercially Shaped (The Verge, 2023)

Reporting for The Verge on 2023-11-01 argues that the harm from search engine optimization is no longer confined to sites built for it. The article states that "over time, SEO techniques have spread and become insidious, such that googling anything can now feel like looking up 'sneaker' in the dictionary and finding a definition that sounds both incorrect and suspiciously as though it were written by someone promoting Nike." By 2023, users described Google Search results as "absolutely unusable," "garbage," and "a nightmare" because "a lot of the content doesn't feel authentic." Since Google holds a 90 percent market share for online search, that commercial shaping reaches nearly every informational query, destroying "the illusion that the internet was ever about anything other than selling stuff."


---


# Google's behavioural data as the personalisation engine across Search, mobile widgets and other services

# Black-and-White Moderation Policy

A black-and-white moderation policy is a rule set that classifies content in binary terms — permitted or forbidden — with no graded middle category. Because of this binary design, such policies cannot effectively moderate nuanced speech, as illustrated by Meta Platforms, whose content rules are described in a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: "The company's black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic, like content that discusses violence without condoning it." # Meta's moderation bias against Palestinian users: effect, not intent

Disparate moderation outcomes for Palestinian users on Meta's platforms are a function of the company's policy and tooling design, not of declared intent: absent intent to censor is fully compatible with systematically unequal effect. # The store–billing relation: how Epic v. Google's two findings form one loop

Read as a single structure rather than two verdicts, the findings a federal jury returned against Google — reported by Tim Sweeney of Epic Games in The Verge, 2023-12-12 — describe one loop with two ends.

One end is the monopolised product: Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. The other end is the tied product: Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The relation between the ends is the model. Whichever product a developer must accept to reach Android users also becomes the channel through which that developer's money moves, so control of distribution converts into control of payment — and the payment share Sweeney calls "huge taxes" paid to a few gatekeepers reinforces the distribution hold. Two holdings, one circuit.

Rather than naming a defensible figure, Epic CEO Tim Sweeney instead implies that a developer who uses its own payment system should pay Google nothing at all for store listing. Procedure as practiced by Teddy Jirapraphanan and Felix Silva (The Verge, 2023-10-26).

First, establish the literal query phrase customers already type. Jirapraphanan, co-owner of the New York restaurant Thai Food Near Me, based the name on his own habit: "Everywhere I go, I'm craving Thai food. I have to search 'Thai food near me' all the time."

# Deriving Qualification Permutations Before a Final Matchday

A Champions League group permutation is worked out by taking a club's position in the table before a matchday is played and enumerating the results — in that club's own fixture and in the other fixture of the same matchday — that would leave it inside the qualifying places. The output is a checkable list, not a prediction: each combination can be compared against the actual scores once the matches finish.

A black-and-white moderation policy is a rule set that classifies content in binary terms — permitted or forbidden — with no graded middle category. Because of this binary design, such policies cannot effectively moderate nuanced speech, as illustrated by Meta Platforms, whose content rules are described in a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: "The company's black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic, like content that discusses violence without condoning it."
