On September 26, 2023, in the US v. Google antitrust trial before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed Apple's senior vice president of Internet Services, Eddy Cue, on the Information Services Agreement (ISA) — the default-search deal with Google, in place since 2002, that pays Apple billions of dollars a year and which Cue renegotiated with CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. Against her point that the ISA accounts for a significant portion of Apple's profits, Cue replied that Apple does not look at the money that way: the profits figure omits the work Apple did to make its platform attractive enough for the deal to perform. He had already argued the deal was about more than economics, and that "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time."


---


# Hypothesis: Apple ships its AI under the Siri brand, not a new one

Testable claim drawn from a TechCrunch predictions piece dated 2023-12-19: Apple will release its AI in 2024 under the existing Siri brand rather than launching a separately named service such as "Apple AI", because the incumbency of "hey Siri" voice habits outweighs that assistant's reputation for mediocrity. The reasoning sits on the article's observation that Apple has an established pattern of waiting, watching and learning from other companies' failures, then arriving with a refined and polished take that puts others to shame, and that the timing is right partly because waiting too long risks competitors eating up the market. Falsified if Apple introduces a distinct AI brand.


---


# The DOJ's implied case that Apple's "best product" defence is pretextual

In US v. Google, on 26 September 2023 in Washington, DC, Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed Eddy Cue on a question she did not have to state: whether Apple placed Google at the centre of its platform for the money rather than the product. The source names this directly — "whether Apple picked Google because it's the most lucrative choice or the best product" was "a key part of the DOJ's entire case."

The warrant is Apple's own paper and its own ledger. The Information Services Agreement, in place since 2002 and renegotiated by Cue with Sundar Pichai in 2016, "pays Apple billions of dollars a year" and makes Google the default search engine on all Apple devices; in 2016 Apple sought a higher percentage of Google's revenue from Apple-directed users, and Cue conceded he never considered walking away: "I always felt like it was in Google's best interest, and our best interest, to get a deal done." Then Bellshaw showed emails and slides in which Cue and Apple "railed against Google's privacy policies" — after Cue had testified that user privacy is "Absolutely" important to Apple, and that the ISA bars Apple from offering a choice of search engines during setup.


---


# Nike shares jumped 6.7 per cent on better-than-expected quarterly profit

On 29 September 2023, on Wall Street, Nike jumped 6.7 per cent after reporting better profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strength overseas helped it make up for some declines in North America. The rise came on a day the S&P 500 slipped 0.3 per cent as Wall Street closed out its worst month and quarter of the year.

# Index: Eddy Cue testifies for Apple in US v. Google (The Verge, 2023-09-26)

Index to The Verge's 2023-09-26 report on Eddy Cue testifying in US v. Google, the DOJ antitrust trial over Google's search business, before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC. Sub-topics covered:

- **The ISA**: the Information Services Agreement making Google default search on all Apple devices, in place since 2002 and renegotiated by Cue with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016.
- **The 2016 revenue-share renegotiation**: Apple sought a larger share of Google's search revenue from Apple-directed users; specific numbers were reserved for closed court sessions.
- **The no-alternative defence**: "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time" — Cue never considered switching providers or building Apple's own search.
- **Setup-choice arguments**: DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's iPhone setup screenshots (Appearance, location tracking, App Tracking Transparency) against Cue's "Setup is just critical stuff," plus the disputed ease of changing defaults.
- **Privacy versus payments**: Apple's privacy claims set against emails in which Cue railed at Google's privacy policies.


---


# Apple's ISA revenue-share percentage stayed out of the public record via closed sessions

During Eddy Cue's 2023-09-26 testimony in US v. Google, the specific revenue-share figures behind Apple's Information Services Agreement (ISA) — the deal dating from 2002 that he renegotiated with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016 — were discussed only in closed court sessions. Cue said he wanted a higher percentage and Pichai wanted the existing terms; the resulting compromised number went unspoken in open court, and Google has paid Apple that undisclosed amount since.

Source: The Verge, 2023-09-26.

# Wall Street's 29 September 2023 close: S&P 500 down 0.3 per cent, Dow down 0.5 per cent, Nasdaq up 0.1 per cent

Wall Street ended September 2023 — its worst month and quarter of the year — with further losses on Friday 29 September 2023. The S&P 500 slipped 0.3 per cent, or 11.65 points, to close at 4288.05, with the majority of stocks within the index sinking. The Dow Jones fell 0.5 per cent, 158.84 points, to 33,507.50. The Nasdaq composite edged 0.1 per cent higher, up 18.05 points, to 13,219.32. # The Apple–Google ISA revenue-share: a percentage of Google's search ad revenue from Apple users

Under the Information Services Agreement (ISA) — the deal that makes Google the default search engine on Apple's products, in place since 2002 and renegotiated in its current form in 2016 by Eddy Cue with Google CEO Sundar Pichai — Google pays Apple a share of the advertising revenue Google earns from Apple users it directs toward Google Search. The model is a percentage, not a fixed sum. At the 2016 renegotiation, Apple pressed for a higher percentage of that revenue; Pichai wanted to keep the deal as it was. They compromised on a figure neither disclosed in open court: on 26 September 2023, in US v. Google before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, Cue testified that discussion of specific numbers was reserved for closed court sessions. Google has paid Apple that percentage ever since, a sum the reporting describes as billions of dollars a year.

The Sydney Morning Herald market briefing of 1 October 2023, "ASX set to open lower as Wall Street closes September with more losses", opens with the day's largest local decliners — Treasury Wine Estates (down 1.9 per cent), Woolworths (down 1.2 per cent) in a consumer staples sector down 1.1 per cent, Pilbara Minerals (down 2.1 per cent) and Qantas (down 1.5 per cent) — then its "The lowdown" section covers iron ore strength, the RBA's Tuesday meeting and NAB's November hike forecast to 4.35 per cent. # Google's default-search deal with Apple dates to 2003

In its 2023-10-31 report on the U.S. antitrust trial against Google, TechCrunch stated that "Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003." That is the agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices, so it had been running roughly twenty years by the time the deal's cost came under scrutiny in court in late October 2023.

# Deriving Qualification Permutations Before a Final Matchday

A Champions League group permutation is worked out by taking a club's position in the table before a matchday is played and enumerating the results — in that club's own fixture and in the other fixture of the same matchday — that would leave it inside the qualifying places. The output is a checkable list, not a prediction: each combination can be compared against the actual scores once the matches finish.

Sporting News applied this on 2023-12-12, reviewing the UEFA Champions League group stage ahead of its final match night and examining what teams from each group needed to qualify for the Round of 16, of which 16 places were at stake.

Group A shows the method at its simplest. Bayern Munich had already qualified, but Copenhagen, Galatasaray and Manchester United all entered the final matchweek with a chance of joining them. Galatasaray knew that if they beat Copenhagen at Parken they would go through. Copenhagen won 1-0 through Lukas Lerager's only goal, which took Copenhagen into the knockout rounds and left Galatasaray on 5 points from 6 games. Manchester United were eliminated after a 1-0 defeat to Bayern at Old Trafford, Kingsley Coman scoring, leaving them bottom of the group on 4 points.


---


# Atlético Madrid's 13 December 2023 win over Lazio settled Group E's top spot

On 13 December 2023, Atlético Madrid beat Lazio 2-0 in the Spanish capital to claim first place in their UEFA Champions League Group E. Both clubs had already secured qualification for the Round of 16 before that fixture, so only the seeding order was at stake. The result falls a day after Sporting News's 12 December 2023 dateline on its Champions League permutations and scenarios article, which reviewed the group stage ahead of its final match night and listed Atlético Madrid alongside Real Sociedad as Spain's remaining representatives in the next round.

# Swift's Eagles fandom makes her Chiefs cheering a signal — but only of affiliation

In The Age's 2023-09-26 timeline of Taylor Swift's NFL takeover, the evidential weight of Swift's Arrowhead appearance rests on a fandom conflict. Swift is known as an Eagles supporter: she is originally from Pennsylvania and references the team in "Gold Rush". So her visible backing of the Kansas City Chiefs — shouting "let's f—ing go" after Travis Kelce's touchdown, then chest-bumping other Chiefs fans, at the game following his 2023-09-21 invitation on The Pat McAfee Show — reads as abandoning her own civic team, which points to personal affiliation with Kelce. The warrant reaches fan behaviour only. It does not establish relationship status: a supporter switching teams signals affinity, not romance.

# At Swift's first Chiefs game, only observed behavior — no statement from her

CBSSports.com's Oct. 12, 2023 timeline documents observable behavior at the first Kansas City Chiefs game Taylor Swift attended, the Week 3 game against the Chicago Bears on Sept. 24, 2023 — roughly a month before that article, and not any statement by Swift herself. There she was seen chatting with Donna Kelce, tight end Travis Kelce's mother, and cheering emphatically when No. 87 scored. That touchdown, a three-yard catch, put Kansas City up 41-0.

# Caroline Ellison: Alameda Research head and prosecution's star witness in the FTX trial

Caroline Ellison ran Alameda Research, the sister hedge fund of the crypto exchange FTX, and had been a girlfriend of FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried. Per a CNBC report dated 2023-10-06 covering Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, she and FTX co-founder Gary Wang were integral members of Bankman-Fried's personal and professional inner circles, and both pleaded guilty in December 2022. Ellison is considered the prosecution's star witness and was expected to take the stand under a cooperation arrangement similar to Wang's.


---


# Copenhagen 1-0 Galatasaray, Parken, 12 December 2023: Group A's decider went the hosts' way

In UEFA Champions League Group A on 12 December 2023, FC Copenhagen beat Galatasaray 1-0 at Parken, Lukas Lerager scoring the only goal. Going into that final matchweek Galatasaray knew that a win over Copenhagen would take them through; the defeat ended that route. Copenhagen instead finished second in the group on 8 points, behind Bayern Munich on 16, with Galatasaray on 5.

*Source: Sporting News, "Champions League permutations, scenarios: What teams need to qualify from groups for 2023/24 Round of 16 stage," 2023-12-12.*

# Ellison put dates on three phases of her relationship with Bankman-Fried

On the first day of her testimony against former boss Sam Bankman-Fried, reported by The Verge on 2023-10-10, Caroline Ellison put specific dates on their personal relationship. She testified that the two slept together on and off from autumn 2018, while she was a trader at Alameda Research and Bankman-Fried was chief executive of FTX. After that, she described two discrete periods of dating: summer 2020 to summer 2021, which Ellison said the couple kept secret, and autumn 2021 to spring 2022, when the two lived together. Ellison had already pleaded guilty to criminal charges stemming from the relationship before taking the stand.


---


# Caroline Ellison testified Alameda Research was already failing when she joined in 2018

Caroline Ellison testified at Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial, as reported by The Verge on October 10, 2023, that Alameda Research — the hedge fund she ran — was troubled from her earliest time there in 2018. "Shortly after I started, I learned the company was in worse shape than I realized," Ellison said. Alameda had initially been funded with loans "from acquaintances," she testified, and those loans were recalled a few weeks after she arrived. Asked why Bankman-Fried had not shared the company's shaky circumstances in her job offer, she said: "He hadn't known how to tell me."


---


# Caroline Ellison: Alameda CEO at the Centre of Both Sides' FTX Trial Story

Caroline Ellison is the figure both sides leaned on in the opening statements of Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial, as reported by Fortune on 2023-10-04. She was the CEO of Alameda Research, the crypto hedge fund Bankman-Fried also owned, and his on-again off-again girlfriend. Prosecutor Thane Rehn alleged that Bankman-Fried used Ellison as a front to get "secret access" to customer money — both cash and crypto. Defence lawyer Mark Cohen answered that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and pointed the finger at Ellison, who, he said, did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. By then she was a former lieutenant turned government cooperator, which is why she was not among the prosecution's first two witnesses.

# Google faced three search and app-store antitrust trials at once in mid-November 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was simultaneously litigating three antitrust matters touching search and app distribution, according to a TechCrunch report dated November 13, 2023. First, the Justice Department's landmark case against Google over search was roughly two months in, before Judge Amit Mehta. Second, Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the previous week. Third, on November 6, 2023 Google went to trial against Fortnite maker Epic Games, which sought to prove Google engages in anticompetitive behavior regarding its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure.


---


# Manchester United and Newcastle United Out of Europe After Finishing Bottom of Their 2023/24 Champions League Groups

Manchester United and Newcastle United will play no further part in European competition in 2023/24, having been eliminated by finishing bottom of their UEFA Champions League groups, Sporting News reported on 12 December 2023. Manchester United ended Group A last on 4 points from six matches, with one win, one draw and four defeats.

# "Search-optimized hellhole" as a 2023 phrase for traffic-shaped online life

A November 2023 Verge feature on the people accused of ruining the internet describes the professionals turning online life into what one tech writer recently called a "search-optimized hellhole" — a phrase capturing internet content reshaped to satisfy search algorithms and earn traffic rather than inform.

# OpenAI valued at more than US$80 billion in its latest funding round

OpenAI is valued at more than US$80 billion (A$123 billion), according to two people familiar with the company's latest funding round, as reported by The Age on 2023-12-09. That valuation attaches to the startup created in 2015 from a dinner between Elon Musk and Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, and backed by hundreds of millions of dollars from Musk and other funders.


---


# Epic's own mention of Project Liberty blunts Google's bad-faith angle

Google's attempt to cast Epic's Project Liberty as proof of bad faith runs into one complication: in the opening statements of Epic's 2020 monopoly suit against Google, reported by The Verge on 2023-11-07, Epic mentioned Project Liberty in its own opening. A fact the jury hears first from the side it is supposed to embarrass lands as disclosure, not exposure — so the same detail is a weaker sting when Google reaches for it later. Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein spoke first, portraying Google as a bully that pays competitors not to compete.


---


# "Thai Food Near Me" as Google's Quiet Part, Spoken Out Loud

The central argument of The Verge's 2023-10-26 profile of the New York restaurant Thai Food Near Me is that the name is "a small but powerful symbol of Google's far-reaching impact on businesses over the past two decades and the lengths their owners will go to try to optimize their operations for the company's platforms." The restaurant is named after a literal Google search query and is optimized for the digital platforms diners use to find places nearby, not for the person walking past on the street or getting a recommendation from a friend.

The reasoning is circular by design, and that is its force: the name is "both notable and obvious," because anyone who has spent time searching online understands the reference immediately. The turn the article claims is that 25 years after Google Search first arrived, the name "says the quiet part out loud."


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# OpenAI's December 2023 Axel Springer Deal Covered Both Model Training and Live ChatGPT Answers

In December 2023, OpenAI announced a content agreement with Axel Springer, the Berlin-based news publisher that owns Business Insider and Politico, which OpenAI framed as helping "provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools." The agreement had two distinct limbs. First, OpenAI would train its generative AI models on Axel Springer's journalism. Second, it would add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT, so the reporting surfaces inside answers rather than only shaping the underlying model. That combination — a licensing deal that pays for a publisher's archive as training data while also giving that publisher's newest work privileged placement in a chatbot's responses — made the deal notable beyond the parties involved, and it was reported in TechCrunch's running ChatGPT timeline alongside other December 2023 OpenAI news, including the reopening of ChatGPT Plus subscriptions on December 13, 2023.


---


# Source text breaks off before Sweeney's "Project Hug" characterization is stated

In The Verge's December 12, 2023 interview with Epic CEO Tim Sweeney after the jury verdict in Epic v. Google, the published text stops mid-sentence — "You'd think a trillion-dollar compa" — so Sweeney's characterization of Google's "Project Hug" as a corrupt payment programme at massive scale, and the deal structure he is said to compare it with, are not stated in this source and cannot be attributed from it. The verifiable content at that point is Sweeney describing Google "paying other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores" and "paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores," with OnePlus and carriers telling Epic they could not bundle Fortnite because of a secret Google deal.


---


# "Walled garden" in The Verge's Epic v. Google coverage: a closed platform controlling distribution and payment

In its December 12, 2023 account of Epic's jury verdict against Google, The Verge sets "walled garden" in quotation marks as a descriptor for Apple — Epic's "rival," which the piece notes "almost entirely won a similar case two years ago." In that usage, the term denotes a closed mobile platform whose owner controls both app distribution and in-app payment: the same two powers the nine-person federal jury found Google held an illegal monopoly over, in "Android app distribution and in-app payment systems," and had illegally tied together through "its Google Play billing system to its app store." Apple's verdict, by contrast, went Epic's way only in part.


---


# The SEO Business Model: Ranking High to Convert Google's Objectivity Into Ad Traffic

According to a 2023-11-01 Verge report on search engine optimization, the SEO business model works by borrowing the appearance of neutrality that Google lends to organic results. The practitioner's goal is to tell the algorithm whatever it needs to hear for a site to appear as high up as possible in search results, then use that placement — Google's supposed objectivity — to lure people in and, usually, show them some kind of advertising. The article distinguishes this from simply buying the advertising space labeled "Sponsored" above organic results, comparing SEO instead to the Wizard of Oz projecting his voice to magnify his authority. The scheme is contingent on ranking: it pays only insofar as the site actually reaches the top of results, against a backdrop in which Google holds a 90 percent market share for online search.


---


# The store–billing relation: how Epic v. Google's two findings form one loop

Read as a single structure rather than two verdicts, the findings a federal jury returned against Google — reported by Tim Sweeney of Epic Games in The Verge, 2023-12-12 — describe one loop with two ends.

One end is the monopolised product: Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. The other end is the tied product: Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The relation between the ends is the model. Whichever product a developer must accept to reach Android users also becomes the channel through which that developer's money moves, so control of distribution converts into control of payment — and the payment share Sweeney calls "huge taxes" paid to a few gatekeepers reinforces the distribution hold. Two holdings, one circuit.


---


# The Sportsbook Business Model: Balanced Action Wins Either Way

Per Sporting News (2023-11-06), a sportsbook's objective on each market is balanced action, not picking winners. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," which lets it earn the profit already built into the odds and lines — the margin commonly called the vig — without worrying about which side wins. Lines move when the public bets heavily on one side; the originals come from oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms fed by analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data.


---


# Epic's case against Google is weakened by never naming a reasonable store fee

Epic Games' antitrust case against Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023 — 1,180 days after Epic originally sued — argues that Google holds illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," and that developers buying for or publishing on Android are stuck paying the "Google tax." One criticism aimed at Epic's position is that it wants something for nothing: Epic has never stated what fee it would consider reasonable for Google to charge for placement in the Google Play app store. Rather than naming a defensible figure, Epic CEO Tim Sweeney instead implies that a developer who uses its own payment system should pay Google nothing at all for store listing. That silence leaves Epic's target vague: it opposes the current fee without ever describing the competitive price a court could order.

# Fed's data-dependence at risk if US economic reports get postponed

Stated as a hypothesis: postponements of scheduled US economic reports could undermine the Federal Reserve's insistence that it will make its upcoming interest-rate decisions based on what incoming data say about the economy.

Testable because of the reporting calendar itself, per The Sydney Morning Herald on 2023-10-01: the latest monthly update on the US jobs market is due the week after that date, with a couple of important inflation reports coming the following week, and the Fed's next meeting on rates ends on November 1.

Falsification condition: if the Fed's October–November guidance tracks the published data cleanly, the postponements have not impaired its stated data-dependent approach, and the hypothesis fails.


---


# US Economic Data Calendar After 1 October 2023: Jobs, Inflation, and the Fed Meeting

As reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 1 October 2023, the latest monthly update on the US jobs market was due the following week, with a couple of important reports on inflation coming the week after that. The Federal Reserve's next meeting on interest rates ends on 1 November 2023. The Fed has insisted it will make upcoming rate decisions based on what incoming data say about the economy.


---


# Jacobsen's three drags on US consumer spending, October 2023

Brian Jacobsen, chief economist at Annex Wealth Management, identified three factors that in combination depressed the growth of US consumer spending in late 2023: higher energy prices, student loan debt repayments, and "real disposable incomes that have been on a declining trajectory since June". His verdict on the trio was blunt — it "doesn't bode well". He described the slowdown of US consumer spending growth as having "come to a boil during a hot summer, and the temperature is really starting to come down". The written opinion was reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 1 October 2023. Supporting the first factor, US crude settled at $US90.79 a barrel on the Friday before, down 92¢ that day but far above the $US70 of June, at the highest level in more than a year. The article dated this assessment to the 29 September 2023 close, when August data showed US consumer spending growth cooler than expected alongside slightly cooler inflation — a reading positive for inflation but a risk to the spending that had kept the US economy out of recession, since resumed US student-loan repayments diverted dollars away from purchases.


---


# NAB's forecast of an RBA hike to 4.35 per cent in November 2023

In a report covered by The Sydney Morning Herald on 2023-10-01, the National Australia Bank forecasts the Reserve Bank of Australia will lift the cash rate again in November 2023, to 4.35 per cent. The forecast sits against the market expectation cited in the same article that the RBA will keep rates on hold at its October meeting, with interest-rate sensitive sectors such as healthcare and consumer companies among the weakest on that view.

The proposition is falsifiable by the RBA's November 2023 decision: either the cash rate moves to 4.35 per cent, or it does not.

# Google's November 2023 Canadian Agreement: $73.5 Million a Year to News Organisations, Allocated by Headcount

Under an agreement Google reached with the Canadian government in November 2023 — the month before the Helena World Chronicle class action was filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. on 2023-12-15 — the search giant will pay Canadian media for use of their content. The terms set Google's contribution at $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) every year to news organisations in the country, with the funds distributed according to each news outlet's headcount. The same reporting notes that negotiations between the Canadian government and Meta remained unresolved at that point; Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August.

The Sydney Morning Herald market briefing of 1 October 2023, "ASX set to open lower as Wall Street closes September with more losses", opens with the day's largest local decliners — Treasury Wine Estates (down 1.9 per cent), Woolworths (down 1.2 per cent) in a consumer staples sector down 1.1 per cent, Pilbara Minerals (down 2.1 per cent) and Qantas (down 1.5 per cent) — then its "The lowdown" section covers iron ore strength, the RBA's Tuesday meeting and NAB's November hike forecast to 4.35 per cent. Follow-on sections track Wall Street's September close, the Treasury-yield mechanism, US inflation and consumer-spending data, oil, the US economic calendar and single stocks. The trailing "Tweek of the day" and "Quote of the day" placeholders are empty in the source.

# Cooler US consumer spending cuts both ways: easing inflation, weakening growth

Economic data released Friday and reported on 1 October 2023 showed growth in spending by US consumers was cooler than expected in August, alongside inflation that was also a touch cooler than expected. That slowdown runs in two opposing directions. Fewer dollars pouring into purchases eases demand-pull pressure, giving companies less encouragement to try to raise prices further and supporting the Federal Reserve's attempt to push still-high inflation down to its target. But softer consumption may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession. Brian Jacobsen, chief economist at Annex Wealth Management, said spending growth had "come to a boil during a hot summer" and was cooling, citing higher energy prices, student-loan repayments and real disposable incomes declining since June.


---


# "Higher-for-longer": the market's assumption that central banks hold rates elevated rather than cut quickly

"Higher-for-longer" names the market's assumption that a central bank keeps policy rates elevated well past the near term instead of cutting quickly — as Sydney Morning Herald reporting on 2023-10-01 put it, "Wall Street accepts a new normal where the Federal Reserve is likely to keep interest rates high for longer."

The concept describes expectations, not announced policy. Anchors cited then: the US Federal Reserve's main rate at its highest level since 2001, with the central bank signalling in the week before that it may cut in 2024 by less than earlier expected, and its next rate meeting ending November 1. In Australia, the RBA was expected to hold at its Tuesday meeting, with National Australia Bank forecasting another hike to 4.35 per cent in November.

Consequences observed: the 10-year US Treasury yield back at 4.58 per cent, near its highest since 2007; interest-rate-sensitive healthcare and consumer stocks weakest; the S&P 500 down 4.9 per cent in September.

In The Verge's December 12, 2023 interview with Epic CEO Tim Sweeney after the jury verdict in Epic v. Google, the published text stops mid-sentence — "You'd think a trillion-dollar compa" — so Sweeney's characterization of Google's "Project Hug" as a corrupt payment programme at massive scale, and the deal structure he is said to compare it with, are not stated in this source and cannot be attributed from it. The verifiable content at that point is Sweeney describing Google "paying other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores" and "paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores," with OnePlus and carriers telling Epic they could not bundle Fortnite because of a secret Google deal.

# Cue's 2023-09-26 "No Valid Alternative" Argument for Apple's Google Default

Testifying on 2023-09-26 in US v. Google, Apple's Eddy Cue argued that Apple never seriously considered switching to another search provider or building its own search product, because "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time." He said there still isn't one.

The claim's scope is the 2016 renegotiation period, when Cue negotiated the current iteration of the Information Services Agreement (ISA) with Google CEO Sundar Pichai — the deal, in place since 2002, that makes Google the default search engine on Apple devices and pays Apple billions of dollars a year.

Cue's warrant was that the choice was product-driven rather than purely economic: the ISA is Apple's own evaluation, and he said "We make Google be the default search engine because we've always thought it was the best. We pick the best one and let users easily change it." Supporting that, he told DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw he'd never really considered walking away from the deal.

# Jane Street: Sam Bankman-Fried's Pre-FTX Trading Employer

Jane Street, the high-frequency trading firm, is the finance employer Sam Bankman-Fried worked for before founding the crypto exchange FTX and its hedge fund Alameda Research. # Meta's moderation bias against Palestinian users: effect, not intent

Disparate moderation outcomes for Palestinian users on Meta's platforms are a function of the company's policy and tooling design, not of declared intent: absent intent to censor is fully compatible with systematically unequal effect. Meta told TechCrunch on 2023-10-19 that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, stated "we apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." That denial of motive does not reach the documented record: a lengthy history of incidents reflecting inherent bias in Meta's processes, from both inside and outside the company, plus a third-party report Meta commissioned after the 2021 Hamas-Israel violence finding an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation. The mechanism is design. Meta struggles with Arabic's more than 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversified language resources; its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuanced content, such as material discussing violence without condoning it; and advocacy groups have raised concerns that partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Calling removals a "bug" localizes harm to a single defect, while the bias here is distributed across language coverage, policy architecture, and escalation channels.
